parts.text: State why the shape of a protein is important for its function, using an enzyme as an example.
parts.answer: The amino acid sequence determines how the protein folds; an enzyme's active site must have a specific shape complementary to its substrate.
parts.working: B1 sequence determines shape; B1 active site shape complementary to substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a change in the base sequence of a gene can result in a protein that does not work.
parts.answer: The base sequence determines the sequence of amino acids; a different amino acid sequence changes how the protein folds (its shape); e.g. an enzyme's active site no longer fits its substrate.
parts.working: B1 base sequence → amino acid sequence; B1 changed shape; B1 consequence for function, e.g. active site / binding site.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Most body cells do not express the gene for haemoglobin, though they contain it. Suggest one advantage of switching off unneeded genes.
parts.answer: Saves energy and materials (amino acids) by not making proteins the cell does not need.
parts.working: B1 saves energy / resources; accept prevents proteins interfering with the cell's own function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the molecule that carries a copy of a gene from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
parts.answer: mRNA (messenger RNA)
parts.working: B1 mRNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the units that are joined together to make a protein.
parts.answer: Amino acids
parts.working: B1 amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what determines the order in which these units are joined.
parts.answer: The sequence of bases in the gene / mRNA.
parts.working: B1 base sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A protein is made of 285 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of bases in the mRNA that codes for it, given three bases code for one amino acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gene in the DNA is longer than this. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: Not all of the DNA of a gene codes for amino acids, e.g. start/stop signals or regions that are removed / do not code.
parts.working: B1 non-coding regions / stop signal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why DNA does not leave the nucleus to make proteins, but mRNA does.
parts.answer: DNA is very large / is the master copy, which must be protected from damage in the cytoplasm; mRNA is a small, short-lived copy of one gene that can pass through the nuclear pores.
parts.working: B1 DNA too large / kept safe; B1 mRNA small copy of a single gene that can leave nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the statement 'a person's genotype for eye colour is homozygous recessive'.
parts.answer: Homozygous: has two identical alleles of the gene; recessive: the allele only expressed when no dominant allele is present (e.g. bb).
parts.working: B1 two identical alleles; B1 recessive alleles (only expressed when homozygous).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define (i) phenotype and (ii) genotype.
parts.answer: (i) The observable features of an organism; (ii) the genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A father has blood group AB and a mother has blood group O. Which blood groups could their children have?
A A or B only
B AB or O only
C A, B, AB or O
D A only
parts.answer: A A or B only
parts.working: Father IᴬIᴮ gives Iᴬ or Iᴮ; mother IᴼIᴼ gives Iᴼ; children are IᴬIᴼ (group A) or IᴮIᴼ (group B). No child can be AB or O.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A man with normal vision and a woman who is a carrier have a son. What is the probability that the son is colour blind?
A 0
B 0.25
C 0.5
D 1.0
parts.working: A son gets Y from his father and one X from his mother: Xᴮ or Xᵇ with equal chance, so 0.5. 0.25 (B) is the probability for any child (son or daughter) being colour blind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by codominance, using the ABO blood group alleles as an example.
parts.answer: Both alleles in a heterozygote are expressed in the phenotype; e.g. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant so a person with IᴬIᴮ has blood group AB.
parts.working: B1 both alleles expressed in heterozygote; B1 IᴬIᴮ gives AB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of children from a father who is IᴬIᴼ and a mother who is IᴮIᴼ. Give the probability of a child having blood group O.
parts.answer: Parental genotypes IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ; gametes Iᴬ, Iᴼ and Iᴮ, Iᴼ; offspring IᴬIᴮ (AB), IᴬIᴼ (A), IᴮIᴼ (B), IᴼIᴼ (O); probability of O = 0.25 (1 in 4).
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring genotypes (Punnett square); B1 phenotypes; B1 probability 0.25 / 25 % / 1 in 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why red-green colour blindness is more common in men than in women.
parts.answer: The allele is on the X chromosome (sex-linked) and the Y chromosome carries no copy of the gene; a man has only one X, so one recessive allele (XᵇY) makes him colour blind; a woman needs two recessive alleles (XᵇXᵇ), which is less likely.
parts.working: B1 gene on X chromosome / not on Y; B1 males need only one recessive allele; B1 females need two / heterozygous females are carriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A colour-blind man (XᵇY) and a woman with normal vision who is not a carrier (XᴮXᴮ) have children. Use a genetic diagram to give the probability that (i) a daughter is a carrier and (ii) a son is colour blind.
parts.answer: Gametes Xᵇ, Y and Xᴮ; daughters XᴮXᵇ, sons XᴮY. (i) 1 (all daughters carriers); (ii) 0.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 (i) 1 / 100 %; B1 (ii) 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the blood group of a person with each genotype: (i) IᴮIᴼ, (ii) IᴬIᴮ, (iii) IᴼIᴼ.
parts.answer: (i) B; (ii) AB; (iii) O.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A couple both have blood group A. Their first child has blood group O. State the genotypes of the parents and the probability that their next child will have blood group A.
parts.answer: Both parents IᴬIᴼ; probability of group A = 0.75.
parts.working: B1 both IᴬIᴼ; M1 offspring IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴼIᴼ; A1 0.75 (3/4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A woman whose father was colour blind has normal vision. She has children with a man who has normal vision. Give the woman's genotype and explain how you worked it out.
parts.answer: XᴮXᵇ; she has normal vision so has at least one Xᴮ, and she must have received Xᵇ from her colour-blind father (fathers pass their X to daughters).
parts.working: B1 XᴮXᵇ; B1 reasoning – father gives his only X (Xᵇ) to daughter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first child is a colour-blind boy.
parts.working: M1 offspring XᴮXᴮ, XᴮXᵇ, XᴮY, XᵇY; A1 1/4 = 0.25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the probability that two of their children are both colour-blind boys.

stem: A class of 40 students in Hyderabad recorded their blood groups: A – 9, B – 13, AB – 4, O – 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the 40 students with blood group O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which blood group shows that two alleles are codominant.
parts.answer: AB
parts.working: B1 AB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable way of displaying these results and give a reason.
parts.answer: A bar chart (with gaps between bars), because blood group is a discontinuous (categoric) variable.
parts.working: B1 bar chart; B1 discontinuous / categories.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the sex chromosomes of (i) a human male and (ii) a human female.
parts.answer: (i) XY; (ii) XX.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a genetic diagram to show why the chance of a baby being a boy is 50 %.
parts.answer: Parents XX × XY; gametes X (egg) and X or Y (sperm); offspring XX (girl) and XY (boy) in a 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: B1 parental chromosomes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring XX : XY 1 : 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the father's sperm determines the sex of the child.
parts.answer: All eggs carry an X chromosome; half of sperm carry X and half carry Y.
parts.working: B1 eggs all X, sperm X or Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many chromosomes are present in each cell produced when a human body cell (46 chromosomes) divides by mitosis?
A 23
B 46
C 92
D 69
parts.working: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells with the same chromosome number as the parent, 46. 23 (A) is the result of meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three roles of mitosis in the human body.
parts.answer: Growth; repair of damaged tissues; replacement of cells (e.g. skin, red blood cells).
parts.working: B1 each; accept asexual reproduction only for other organisms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of cell division that produces sperm cells.
parts.answer: Meiosis
parts.working: B1 meiosis.

stem: A patient in a hospital in Lahore needs treatment to replace damaged blood-forming tissue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term stem cell.
parts.answer: An unspecialised cell that divides by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions.
parts.working: B1 unspecialised; B1 divides by mitosis to give cells that can become specialised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stem cells taken from a patient's own bone marrow can be used to replace damaged cells without being rejected.
parts.answer: The new cells are genetically identical to the patient's (made by mitosis), so they have the same antigens and are not recognised as foreign by the immune system.
parts.working: B1 genetically identical / same DNA; B1 same antigens / not attacked by immune system.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to chromosomes before and during mitosis so that the two daughter cells are genetically identical.
parts.answer: Each chromosome is copied (replicated / DNA copied) before division; the two copies separate, one copy going to each end of the cell; each new nucleus receives an exact copy of every chromosome; cell then divides (cytoplasm).
parts.working: B1 chromosomes replicate before mitosis; B1 copies separate (to opposite poles); B1 each daughter nucleus gets full identical set.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that gametes are produced by meiosis, not by mitosis.
parts.answer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number (diploid 46 → haploid 23); at fertilisation two gametes fuse to restore the diploid number; otherwise the chromosome number would double every generation; meiosis also produces genetic variation.
parts.working: B1 halves chromosome number / haploid; B1 fertilisation restores diploid; B1 prevents doubling each generation / gives variation.

stem: A student examined a stained squash of an onion root tip under a microscope. In one field of view 150 cells were counted and 24 of them showed chromosomes that were visible (dividing).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells that were dividing (mitotic index).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student used the tip of the root rather than a region further back.
parts.answer: Cells divide by mitosis mainly at the root tip (growth region); further back cells are elongating / specialising.
parts.working: B1 mitosis occurs at tip / growth region.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the estimate more reliable.
parts.answer: Count cells in more fields of view / from more roots and calculate a mean.
parts.working: B1 more fields / more roots / repeats.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many cells would be produced from one fertilised egg after 12 rounds of mitosis, assuming every cell divides each time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Red blood cells have no nucleus and live for only about four months. Explain why stem cells in the bone marrow must keep dividing throughout a person's life.
parts.answer: Red blood cells cannot divide (no nucleus) and are constantly being destroyed, so they must be replaced; stem cells divide by mitosis to make new cells that become specialised as red blood cells.
parts.working: B1 red blood cells cannot divide / are continually lost and need replacing; B1 stem cells divide by mitosis and the daughter cells become specialised (as red blood cells).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the chromosome number in the egg of a dog, whose body cells have 78 chromosomes, and name the division producing it.
parts.answer: 39; meiosis.
parts.working: B1 39; B1 meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define (i) a haploid nucleus and (ii) a diploid nucleus.
parts.answer: (i) A nucleus containing a single set of chromosomes; (ii) a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a haploid cell and one example of a diploid cell in a human.
parts.answer: Haploid: sperm or egg cell; diploid: any body cell, e.g. a cheek cell or zygote.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare mitosis and meiosis by giving three differences.
parts.answer: Mitosis gives 2 cells, meiosis gives 4 (cells / gametes); mitosis gives genetically identical cells, meiosis gives genetically different cells; mitosis keeps chromosome number (diploid), meiosis halves it (haploid); mitosis for growth/repair, meiosis for gamete production.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mitosis is also used in asexual reproduction. Explain why a field of potato plants grown from tubers of one plant all show the same disease susceptibility.
parts.answer: Tubers are produced by mitosis so all the plants are genetically identical (clones); none has alleles giving resistance, so all are equally affected.
parts.working: B1 mitosis → genetically identical / clones; B1 same alleles / no variation for resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two plants that are heterozygous for flower colour (Rr) are crossed. Red (R) is dominant to white (r). What is the expected ratio of red to white offspring?
A 1 : 1
B 3 : 1
C 1 : 3
D all red
parts.working: Rr × Rr gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr: three red to one white. 1 : 1 (A) is the result of a test cross Rr × rr.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a farmer could use a test cross to find out whether a black-coated goat is homozygous (BB) or heterozygous (Bb). Black (B) is dominant to brown (b).
parts.answer: Cross the black goat with a brown goat (bb, homozygous recessive); if any offspring are brown, the black goat is Bb; if all offspring (in a large number) are black, it is probably BB.
parts.working: B1 cross with homozygous recessive / brown goat; B1 any brown offspring → Bb; B1 all black → BB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram for the cross if the black goat is heterozygous. State the expected ratio of offspring phenotypes.
parts.answer: Bb × bb; gametes B, b and b; offspring Bb (black), bb (brown); ratio 1 black : 1 brown.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 1 : 1 black : brown.

stem: A family pedigree is described: Persons 1 (father) and 2 (mother) are both unaffected. They have three children: person 3 (son, unaffected), person 4 (daughter, unaffected) and person 5 (son, has cystic fibrosis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Use the pedigree to state the genotypes of persons 1 and 2. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Both Ff. They are unaffected, so each has at least one F; their child 5 has cystic fibrosis (ff) and received one f from each parent.
parts.working: B1 both Ff; B1 unaffected so have dominant allele; B1 affected child must have received f from each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that the next child of persons 1 and 2 will have cystic fibrosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Person 4 is unaffected. Calculate the probability that person 4 is a carrier (Ff).
parts.working: M1 unaffected offspring of Ff × Ff are FF, Ff, Ff (ff excluded); A1 2/3.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student in Multan grew 810 pea seeds from a cross between two tall plants. 612 plants were tall and 198 were dwarf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of tall to dwarf plants, to the nearest whole number : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotypes of the parent plants. Use T for tall and t for dwarf.
parts.answer: Tt × Tt
parts.working: B1 both Tt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the ratio is not exactly the expected ratio.
parts.answer: Fertilisation is random / chance; sample is too small to give the exact ratio.
parts.working: B1 random fusion of gametes / chance.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of (i) homozygous and (ii) heterozygous.
parts.answer: (i) Having two identical alleles of a particular gene; (ii) having two different alleles of a particular gene.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why two heterozygous individuals do not 'breed true' for a characteristic.
parts.answer: Each can pass on either allele, so offspring can be homozygous dominant, heterozygous or homozygous recessive – some offspring show a different phenotype from the parents.
parts.working: B1 gametes carry different alleles; B1 offspring can be recessive / different phenotype.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For which disease would a doctor prescribe an antibiotic?
A influenza
B measles
C cholera
D the common cold
parts.answer: C cholera
parts.working: Cholera is caused by a bacterium, and antibiotics act on bacteria. Influenza, measles and colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not affect.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why do antibiotics not cure diseases caused by viruses?
A Viruses are too small to be seen by the immune system.
B Viruses lack the structures and processes, such as cell walls, that antibiotics act on.
C Viruses are always resistant to antibiotics because of mutations.
D Antibiotics only work in the gut, and viruses live in the lungs.
parts.answer: B Viruses lack the structures and processes, such as cell walls, that antibiotics act on.
parts.working: Antibiotics damage bacterial structures or processes (e.g. cell wall formation); viruses have no cell wall or cell processes of their own and reproduce inside host cells. Resistance (C) is a property of some bacteria, not the reason viruses are unaffected.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is MRSA?
A a virus that causes pneumonia
B a strain of bacteria resistant to several commonly used antibiotics
C an antibiotic used in hospitals
D a fungus that produces penicillin
parts.answer: B a strain of bacteria resistant to several commonly used antibiotics
parts.working: MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to methicillin and several other antibiotics, making infections hard to treat.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which action is most likely to reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a community?
A taking antibiotics at the first sign of any sore throat
B stopping a course of antibiotics as soon as symptoms disappear
C using antibiotics only when essential and finishing the full course
D giving leftover antibiotics to family members with similar symptoms
parts.answer: C using antibiotics only when essential and finishing the full course
parts.working: Using antibiotics only when needed reduces the chance of selecting resistant bacteria, and finishing the course kills as many bacteria as possible so fewer survive to multiply. Stopping early (B) leaves the less susceptible bacteria alive.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Paper discs soaked in four antibiotics, P, Q, R and S, were placed on agar spread with one type of bacterium. After incubation the diameters of the clear zones were P 6 mm, Q 21 mm, R 0 mm, S 14 mm (all discs 6 mm wide). Which conclusion is correct?
A P is the most effective antibiotic.
B The bacteria are resistant to R, and Q is the most effective.
C S is more effective than Q.
D All four antibiotics killed the bacteria.
parts.answer: B The bacteria are resistant to R, and Q is the most effective.
parts.working: The largest clear zone (Q, 21 mm) shows the most bacteria killed or prevented from growing. A zone no wider than the disc (P 6 mm) or none at all (R) means no effect, i.e. resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what an antibiotic is used for.
parts.answer: To treat bacterial infections (kill bacteria or stop them growing) in the body.
parts.working: B1 treat bacterial infection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student with a bad cold asks a doctor for antibiotics. Explain why the doctor refuses.
parts.answer: Colds are caused by viruses; antibiotics have no effect on viruses (and unnecessary use encourages resistant bacteria).
parts.working: B1 cold caused by virus; B1 antibiotics do not kill viruses / encourage resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one disease, caused by bacteria, that can be treated with antibiotics.
parts.answer: e.g. cholera, tuberculosis, typhoid, bacterial pneumonia, strep throat.
parts.working: B1 any bacterial disease. Do not accept viral diseases (e.g. HIV, flu, COVID-19).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why some bacterial infections are now difficult to treat with antibiotics.
parts.answer: Some bacteria are resistant to antibiotics, which reduces the effectiveness of the antibiotics.
parts.working: B1 resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one example of a strain of bacteria that is resistant to several antibiotics.
parts.answer: MRSA
parts.working: B1 MRSA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the development of resistant bacteria, such as MRSA, can be minimised.
parts.answer: Use antibiotics only when essential (not for viral infections); doctors prescribe only when needed / avoid unnecessary prescriptions; patients complete the full course so all bacteria are killed; do not use antibiotics routinely in farm animals; good hygiene in hospitals reduces spread of resistant strains.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: only use when essential; not for viral infections; complete the course; do not share / keep leftover; limit use in livestock; hospital hygiene / hand washing / isolate infected patients; use the correct antibiotic (after testing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why patients are told to finish the full course of antibiotics even when they feel better.
parts.answer: Some bacteria may still be alive (the more resistant ones survive longest); if the course is stopped they can multiply, causing the infection to return and spreading resistance.
parts.working: B1 not all bacteria killed / surviving bacteria; B1 they multiply / infection returns / resistant bacteria increase.

stem: The number of antibiotic prescriptions per 1000 people per day in one district was 5.2 in 2021 and 3.9 in 2024, after a campaign to reduce unnecessary use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in antibiotic prescriptions between 2021 and 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why health authorities wanted to reduce the number of prescriptions.
parts.answer: To slow the development / spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria; many prescriptions were for viral infections where antibiotics have no effect; to save money / reduce side effects.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Over the same period, the percentage of infections caused by resistant bacteria in the district did not fall. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: Resistant bacteria already present continue to spread (e.g. in hospitals); antibiotics still used in livestock / bought without prescription; resistance takes many years to decline.
parts.working: B1 any sensible reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In one country, 202 tonnes of antibiotics were used in a year: 71 tonnes in human medicine and 131 tonnes in farm animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total antibiotics used that were given to farm animals. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why giving antibiotics routinely to healthy farm animals can affect human health.
parts.answer: Bacteria in animals are exposed to antibiotics, so resistant bacteria survive and multiply; resistant bacteria (or their resistance) can pass to humans through meat, contact or the environment; antibiotics may then not work against human infections.
parts.working: B1 routine use selects for resistant bacteria; B1 resistant bacteria spread to humans (food / contact / manure); B1 infections in humans harder to treat.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student placed discs soaked in antibiotics A and B on agar plates spread with a harmless bacterium and incubated them at 25 °C for 2 days. Diameter of clear zone / mm:
A: 26, 24, 25
B: 14, 15, 31, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the clear zone for antibiotic A.
parts.answer: 25 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result for antibiotic B and calculate the mean without it.
parts.answer: Anomaly 31 mm; mean 14 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which antibiotic would be most effective against this bacterium. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Antibiotic A; it has the largest clear zone, showing the most bacteria were killed / prevented from growing.
parts.working: B1 A; B1 largest zone / more inhibition.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the plates were incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C.
parts.answer: To reduce the chance of growing bacteria that are pathogenic to humans (which grow best at body temperature).
parts.working: B1 avoids growth of human pathogens.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Clear zones around two antibiotic discs on a bacterial lawn had diameters of 2.2 cm (antibiotic X) and 1.1 cm (antibiotic Y).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of each clear zone. Use area = πr² and give your answers to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Antibiotic X: 3.8 cm²; antibiotic Y: 0.95 cm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the clear zone area is for X than for Y.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is better to compare areas rather than diameters.
parts.answer: The area shows the actual region where bacteria failed to grow; doubling the diameter gives four times the area, so diameters underestimate the difference.
parts.working: B1 area represents amount of agar cleared / area ∝ diameter².

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of an antibiotic affects the growth of a harmless bacterium on agar plates.
parts.answer: Prepare at least five concentrations of antibiotic by dilution (e.g. 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 %); spread bacteria evenly on agar plates using aseptic technique (sterile spreader, flame neck of bottle, lift lid only slightly); soak equal-sized filter paper discs in each concentration for the same time; place on plates at equal spacing; tape the lid with two strips (not sealed), incubate upside down at 25 °C for 48 hours; measure diameter of clear zone with a ruler; repeat three times and calculate means; control: disc soaked in sterile water; controlled variables: same bacterium, same agar volume, disc size, temperature, time; safety: do not open plates after incubation, dispose by autoclaving, wash hands.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of ≥5 concentrations with how made; aseptic technique (one detail); same-size discs soaked for equal time; incubate at 25 °C for stated time; measure diameter / area of clear zone; two controlled variables; control disc (water); repeats and mean; safety (taped lid not sealed / do not open / autoclave).

stem: A student prepared an agar plate to test the effect of penicillin on a harmless bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student flamed the inoculating loop until it glowed red before use.
parts.answer: To kill any microorganisms on the loop (sterilise it), so the plate is not contaminated.
parts.working: B1 sterilise / kill microorganisms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lid was held with two pieces of tape but not sealed all the way round.
parts.answer: Tape stops the lid being opened accidentally (safety); not sealing allows oxygen in, preventing the growth of harmful anaerobic bacteria.
parts.working: B1 prevents lid being lifted / contamination; B1 oxygen can enter so anaerobic (pathogenic) bacteria do not grow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the plate was stored upside down during incubation.
parts.answer: Prevents condensation dripping onto the agar surface and spreading colonies.
parts.working: B1 condensation does not drip onto agar.

parts.label: d
parts.text: After incubation a clear zone appeared around a disc containing penicillin. Explain what this shows.
parts.answer: The penicillin diffused into the agar and killed the bacteria / stopped them growing near the disc.
parts.working: B1 antibiotic diffused out and prevented bacterial growth.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the use of an antibiotic leads to an increase in the proportion of resistant bacteria in a population.
parts.answer: There is variation in a bacterial population; some bacteria have (by random mutation) an allele giving resistance; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance allele; over many generations most of the population is resistant.
parts.working: B1 variation / random mutation already present (not caused by antibiotic); B1 non-resistant killed; B1 resistant survive and reproduce; B1 pass on allele / proportion increases over generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student writes 'the antibiotic makes the bacteria become immune'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Bacteria do not have an immune system / immunity refers to the body's response to pathogens; the antibiotic does not cause the resistance – it selects bacteria that were already resistant.
parts.working: B1 'immune' is wrong term (immunity is in the host); B1 resistance pre-exists, selected not caused.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Antibiotics affect bacteria but do not affect viruses. Name one structure found in bacteria that is not found in viruses.
parts.answer: Cell wall / cell membrane / ribosomes / cytoplasm.
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether each disease can be treated with antibiotics: (i) tuberculosis; (ii) HIV/AIDS; (iii) cholera; (iv) influenza.
parts.answer: (i) yes; (ii) no; (iii) yes; (iv) no.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

stem: A survey in a city found that many people bought antibiotics for coughs and fevers without seeing a doctor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some places antibiotics can be bought from a pharmacy without a doctor's prescription. Explain two ways this can increase antibiotic resistance.
parts.answer: People take antibiotics for viral illnesses where they have no benefit, exposing their bacteria to antibiotics unnecessarily; people buy only a few tablets / do not complete a full course, so some bacteria survive; wrong antibiotic or dose may be chosen, so bacteria are not killed. In each case resistant bacteria are favoured and multiply.
parts.working: Two ways, each B1 practice + B1 link to resistance (surviving / selected resistant bacteria multiply).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of a doctor testing a sample of bacteria from the patient before choosing an antibiotic.
parts.answer: The doctor can choose an antibiotic that the bacteria are not resistant to, so it will work and unnecessary antibiotics are avoided.
parts.working: B1 choose effective antibiotic / avoid ineffective use.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A doctor in Peshawar prescribed amoxicillin capsules of 500 mg, one capsule three times a day for 7 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of antibiotic taken during the full course and the number of capsules needed.
parts.answer: 10 500 mg (10.5 g); 21 capsules

parts.label: b
parts.text: After 3 days the patient feels better and stops taking the capsules. Calculate the number of capsules not taken.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the risk of stopping the course early.
parts.answer: Not all the bacteria have been killed; the surviving ones (often the least sensitive / resistant) multiply, so the infection can return and is harder to treat.
parts.working: B1 bacteria survive; B1 infection returns / resistant bacteria increase.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for one resistant bacterium to produce over 4000 bacteria if it divides every 20 minutes. Show your working.
parts.answer: 4 hours (12 divisions give 2¹² = 4096)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why resistance can spread through a bacterial population very quickly when an antibiotic is used.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce very rapidly (asexually, by binary fission), so a single surviving resistant bacterium can give rise to a large resistant population in hours; each offspring inherits the resistance allele.
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction / many generations quickly; B1 all offspring inherit resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each statement about antibiotics is true or false: (i) Antibiotics kill bacteria. (ii) Antibiotics are effective against all pathogens. (iii) Antibiotics should be taken until the course is finished. (iv) Antibiotics can be used to treat the common cold.
parts.answer: (i) true; (ii) false; (iii) true; (iv) false.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Antibodies and antibiotics are often confused. State one difference between them.
parts.answer: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes in the body; antibiotics are drugs (often made by microorganisms) taken to kill bacteria.
parts.working: B1 antibodies made by lymphocytes / white blood cells vs antibiotics are drugs taken into the body.

stem: The number of bacteria in samples from a patient with a throat infection (arbitrary units): day 0 – 48; day 3 – 12; day 5 – 25; day 7 – 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in bacteria between day 0 and day 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The patient stopped taking the antibiotic on day 3. Describe and explain the change in the number of bacteria from day 3 to day 7.
parts.answer: The number rose from 12 to 40 (arbitrary units); the bacteria that survived were not killed by the antibiotic (more resistant) and multiplied once the antibiotic was no longer present.
parts.working: B1 increase with data; B1 surviving bacteria multiply; B1 survivors likely more resistant / antibiotic no longer present.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hospital introduced compulsory hand cleaning with alcohol gel and stricter rules on prescribing antibiotics. MRSA infections per 10 000 patients: 2020 – 6.8; 2024 – 1.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in MRSA infections between 2020 and 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each of the two measures could have contributed to the decrease.
parts.answer: Hand washing / alcohol gel kills or removes MRSA from hands, so fewer bacteria are passed between patients; reduced prescribing lowers selection pressure, so resistant strains have less advantage and become less common.
parts.working: B1 hygiene removes / kills bacteria on hands; B1 so less transmission between patients; B1 fewer antibiotics → less selection for resistant bacteria; B1 resistant bacteria do not increase in proportion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person should not take antibiotics left over from a previous illness, or share them with a family member.
parts.answer: The illness may be viral, so the antibiotic will not work; it may be the wrong antibiotic / not enough for a full course / wrong dose; this exposes bacteria to low doses so resistant bacteria survive and multiply.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: illness may be viral; wrong antibiotic for that bacterium; incomplete course / wrong dose; increases resistance; may cause allergy / side effects (not the prescribed patient).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why antibiotics are sometimes called 'a precious resource'.
parts.answer: As resistance increases, fewer antibiotics work and very few new antibiotics are being developed.
parts.working: B1 resistance making them ineffective / few new ones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first antibiotic, penicillin, was obtained from a mould. State the kingdom to which moulds belong.
parts.answer: Fungi
parts.working: B1 fungi / fungus kingdom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to bacteria when they are exposed to an antibiotic to which they are not resistant.
parts.answer: They are killed or their growth (reproduction) is stopped.
parts.working: B1 killed / growth prevented.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a doctor may change to a different antibiotic if a patient's infection does not improve.
parts.answer: The bacteria may be resistant to the first antibiotic.
parts.working: B1 resistance.

stem: Equal volumes of a culture of a harmless bacterium were spread on agar plates with and without an antibiotic and incubated at 25 °C. Number of colonies: without antibiotic – mean 180; with antibiotic – 17, 20, 17.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of colonies on plates with antibiotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of colonies that survived on antibiotic plates compared with plates without antibiotic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the colonies growing on the antibiotic plates show about those bacteria.
parts.answer: They are resistant to the antibiotic.
parts.working: B1 resistant.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Data for four countries – antibiotic doses per 1000 people per day and % of E. coli infections resistant to one antibiotic: Q – 10, 9 %; R – 18, 20 %; S – 25, 29 %; T – 32, 41 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown in the data.
parts.answer: Countries with higher antibiotic use have a higher percentage of resistant E. coli; e.g. country T (32 doses) 41 % against country Q (10 doses) 9 % – a positive correlation.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 data quote with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that 'antibiotic use is the only cause of resistance'. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The data show a correlation but do not prove cause; other factors could affect resistance, e.g. use in farm animals, hospital hygiene, sanitation, travel; only four countries were studied; but it is consistent with selection of resistant bacteria by antibiotic use.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: correlation not proof of causation; other factors named (livestock use / hygiene / sanitation / spread between countries); small sample of countries; supported by mechanism of selection.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is treated with antibiotics for at least six months. Suggest why the treatment takes so long.
parts.answer: TB bacteria grow / reproduce slowly and some are hidden inside cells / tissues, so antibiotics take a long time to kill them all.
parts.working: B1 slow-growing bacteria / hard to reach.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Patients with TB are usually given three or four different antibiotics at the same time. Explain how this reduces the chance of resistant TB bacteria developing.
parts.answer: A bacterium is unlikely to be resistant to all the antibiotics at once; any bacterium resistant to one antibiotic is killed by another, so resistant strains do not survive to multiply.
parts.working: B1 unlikely to have resistance to all; B1 bacteria resistant to one killed by another.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best definition of a drug?
A any substance that kills bacteria
B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
C any substance made by a doctor
D any substance that is addictive
parts.answer: B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
parts.working: This is the general definition; antibiotics (A) are only one type of drug, and many drugs are neither prescribed nor addictive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why both a painkiller such as paracetamol and an antibiotic such as amoxicillin are drugs.
parts.answer: Both are substances taken into the body that modify or affect chemical reactions in the body.
parts.working: B1 taken into the body; B1 modify / affect chemical reactions in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference in what these two drugs are used for.
parts.answer: Paracetamol relieves symptoms (pain / fever) but does not kill the pathogen; amoxicillin kills bacteria, treating the cause of a bacterial infection.
parts.working: B1 painkiller relieves symptoms; B1 antibiotic kills bacteria / treats bacterial infection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A herbal tea is advertised as a cure for influenza. Using the definition of a drug, explain what would need to be true for the tea to be classed as a drug.
parts.answer: A substance in the tea would need to be taken into the body and modify or affect chemical reactions in the body.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into body; B1 affects / modifies chemical reactions in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it would not be useful for a patient with influenza to take an antibiotic instead.
parts.answer: Influenza is caused by a virus; antibiotics only act on bacteria, so they would not help (and could encourage resistance in bacteria in the body).
parts.working: B1 influenza is viral; B1 antibiotics do not affect viruses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how scientists could test fairly whether the tea reduces the length of the illness.
parts.answer: Compare two large groups of similar patients – one given the tea and one given a similar-tasting tea without the herb (placebo), without knowing which they get; record the number of days of illness and compare means.
parts.working: B1 large groups with a control / placebo group; B1 measure length of illness / compare means; accept blind trial.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A plant cell has an actual length of 0.04 mm. In a textbook photograph the image of the cell is 20 mm long. What is the magnification of the photograph?
A ×50
B ×500
C ×800
D ×5000
parts.working: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 20 ÷ 0.04 = 500 (both in mm). ×50 comes from misplacing the decimal point.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an electron micrograph a chloroplast is 30 mm long. The magnification is ×6000. What is the actual length of the chloroplast?
A 0.5 µm
B 5 µm
C 50 µm
D 180 µm
parts.answer: B 5 µm
parts.working: Convert the image to µm: 30 mm = 30 000 µm. Actual = 30 000 ÷ 6000 = 5 µm. 0.5 µm comes from using 3000 µm per 30 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A human red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. What is this diameter in millimetres?
A 0.075 mm
B 0.0075 mm
C 0.00075 mm
D 7500 mm
parts.working: 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 7.5 µm = 7.5 ÷ 1000 = 0.0075 mm. 0.075 mm results from dividing by 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a photomicrograph of root tip cells, a scale bar 25 mm long is labelled 10 µm. What is the magnification of the photomicrograph?
A ×250
B ×400
C ×2500
D ×25 000
parts.working: Scale bar image = 25 mm = 25 000 µm; actual = 10 µm. Magnification = 25 000 ÷ 10 = 2500. ×250 comes from converting 25 mm to 2500 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student draws a mango leaf from a photograph. On the drawing, the length of the leaf blade (line PQ, from leaf tip to the base of the blade) is 96 mm. The actual length of the leaf blade is 38 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Give your answer to two significant figures. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 magnification = length of drawing ÷ actual length; M1 96 ÷ 38 (= 2.526…); A1 ×2.5 (2 s.f., no units).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photograph shows a transverse section of an okra (bhindi) pod at a magnification of ×1.7. The line XY drawn across the widest part of the image of the section is 68 mm long.
Calculate the actual width of the okra pod in mm. Show your working.
parts.answer: 40 mm
parts.working: M1 actual size = image size ÷ magnification; M1 68 ÷ 1.7; A1 40 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why line XY should be measured in millimetres rather than centimetres.
parts.answer: mm gives a more precise reading / fewer decimal places / ruler graduated in mm
parts.working: B1 idea that measuring to the nearest mm is more precise (cm leads to rounding errors).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photograph of a green chilli has a magnification of ×0.8. On the photograph the chilli is 56 mm long, measured from the tip to the point where the stalk joins.
Calculate the actual length of the chilli in mm.
parts.answer: 70 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A student makes a large drawing of the chilli from the photograph. The same length on the drawing is 140 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the student's drawing compared with the real chilli. Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.working: M1 140 ÷ 70 (use of the actual length from (a), allow ecf); A1 ×2.0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the answer to (b) is not 140 ÷ 56.
parts.answer: 56 mm is the size of the photograph image, not the actual size; the photograph is itself magnified (×0.8)
parts.working: B1 magnification must compare the drawing with the actual object, not with another image.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photomicrograph of human cheek cells shows one cell with an image diameter of 45 mm. The actual diameter of the cell is 60 µm.
Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 convert 45 mm to 45 000 µm (or 60 µm to 0.06 mm) and divide; A1 ×750.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The nucleus of the same cell is 6 mm across in the photomicrograph. Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus in µm.
parts.answer: 8 µm
parts.working: M1 6000 µm ÷ 750 (ecf from (a)); A1 8 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rod-shaped bacterium is 2.5 µm long. It is drawn in a textbook at a magnification of ×12 000. Calculate the length of the drawing in mm.
parts.answer: 30 mm
parts.working: M1 image = actual × magnification = 2.5 × 12 000 = 30 000 µm; A1 30 mm (÷ 1000).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A yeast cell drawn at the same magnification is 96 mm long. How many times longer is the yeast cell than the bacterium?
parts.answer: 3.2 times
parts.working: M1 96 ÷ 30 (or actual 8 µm ÷ 2.5 µm); A1 3.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equation that links magnification, image size and actual size.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size
parts.working: B1 (any correct rearrangement accepted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 0.25 mm into micrometres (µm).
parts.answer: 250 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert 1800 µm into millimetres.
parts.answer: 1.8 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student views a thin strip of onion epidermis under a microscope. The diameter of the circular field of view is 2.0 mm. Along one diameter, 8 cells fit end to end exactly.
Calculate the mean length of one cell in µm.
parts.answer: 250 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why this method gives only an estimate of cell length.
parts.answer: cells are not all the same length / cells may not fit exactly / cells may not lie exactly along the diameter
parts.working: B1 any one valid idea.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A drawing of a neem leaflet is 152 mm long. The actual leaflet is 190 mm long.
Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what a magnification less than 1 tells you about the drawing.
parts.answer: the drawing is smaller than the real leaflet

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pollen grain from a cotton flower has an image diameter of 36 mm in a micrograph taken at ×800. Calculate its actual diameter in µm.
parts.answer: 45 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A pollen grain from a second species has an actual diameter of 40 µm. Calculate the diameter of its image, in mm, if photographed at the same magnification.
parts.answer: 32 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student traces the outline of a lotus leaf on centimetre-square grid paper. Inside the outline there are 42 complete squares and 18 squares that are partly covered. The student counts each part-covered square as half a square.
Estimate the area of the leaf in cm².
parts.answer: 51 cm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to (a) into mm².
parts.answer: 5100 mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the estimate of leaf area could be made more accurate.
parts.answer: use grid paper with smaller squares (e.g. mm squares)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photograph of a whole water-lily leaf has a line drawn across its widest part. On the photograph the line is 82 mm long. The actual width of the leaf is 164 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The sizes of four structures are:
mitochondrion 1.5 µm
nucleus of a liver cell 0.008 mm
bacterium 0.003 mm
red blood cell 7 µm
Convert all the sizes to µm.
parts.answer: mitochondrion 1.5 µm; nucleus 8 µm; bacterium 3 µm; red blood cell 7 µm
parts.working: B2 both conversions (0.008 mm = 8 µm, 0.003 mm = 3 µm) correct; B1 one correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the four structures in order of size, starting with the smallest.
parts.answer: mitochondrion, bacterium, red blood cell, nucleus
parts.working: B1 (ecf from (a)).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student draws a pigeon feather. Line AB on the drawing, from the tip of the feather to the end of the shaft, is 118 mm. The drawing has a magnification of ×3.5.
Calculate the actual length of the feather. Give your answer in mm to two significant figures.
parts.answer: 34 mm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification; M1 118 ÷ 3.5 (= 33.7…); A1 34 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both plant cells and animal cells but NOT in bacterial cells?
A cell membrane
B cell wall
C mitochondrion
D ribosome
parts.answer: C mitochondrion
parts.working: Bacteria have a cell membrane, a cell wall and ribosomes, but no mitochondria. Plant and animal cells both have mitochondria. Cell wall is wrong because animal cells lack one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which features are present in a bacterial cell?
1 cell wall
2 plasmids
3 nucleus
4 ribosomes
A 1, 2 and 4
B 1 and 3 only
C 2, 3 and 4
D 1 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: Bacteria have a cell wall, plasmids, ribosomes and circular DNA that is not enclosed in a nucleus. Any option including 3 is wrong; 1 and 4 only omits plasmids.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the cell structure that matches each description.
(i) the site of aerobic respiration
(ii) the site of protein synthesis
(iii) controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell
(iv) contains the chromosomes
parts.answer: (i) mitochondrion (ii) ribosome (iii) cell membrane (iv) nucleus
parts.working: B1 each. Do not accept cell wall for (iii).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three structural differences between a palisade mesophyll cell and a liver cell.
parts.answer: palisade cell has a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole; liver cell has none of these
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: cell wall (cellulose) present / absent; chloroplasts present / absent; large permanent vacuole (with cell sap) present / absent or only small vacuoles; regular shape / irregular shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Liver cells contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
parts.answer: liver cells have a high rate of metabolism, so they need a lot of energy released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria
parts.working: B1 mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration; B1 high metabolic rate / many energy-requiring reactions (e.g. protein synthesis, active transport) so much energy must be released. Do not credit 'produce energy'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Cells in the pancreas make and secrete large quantities of digestive enzymes. Electron micrographs of these cells show very many ribosomes and many mitochondria.
Explain how each of these features helps the cells to carry out their function.
parts.answer: enzymes are proteins; ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, so many ribosomes allow enzymes to be made quickly in large amounts; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing the energy needed for protein synthesis and for secreting the enzymes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: enzymes are proteins; ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis; many ribosomes = enzymes made quickly / in large quantities; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration; respiration releases energy; energy needed to join amino acids / for protein synthesis; energy needed for secretion of the enzymes out of the cell. Do not credit 'mitochondria produce energy'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two structures that are found in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell.
parts.answer: any two of: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two. (Not nucleus, not chloroplast, not mitochondrion.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one structure found in a bacterial cell that is not found in a plant cell.
parts.answer: plasmid

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the main genetic material of a bacterial cell differs from that of a plant cell.
parts.answer: bacterial DNA is a single circular chromosome / loop free in the cytoplasm, not enclosed in a nucleus
parts.working: B1 circular DNA; B1 not in a nucleus / no nuclear membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sentences about plant cells using suitable words.
The cell wall is made of ______ and stops the cell bursting. The large permanent vacuole contains ______. Chloroplasts absorb ______ energy for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: cellulose; cell sap; light
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows the mean number of mitochondria in four types of human cell.
cell type | mean number of mitochondria per cell
heart muscle cell | 5000
liver cell | 2000
skin cell (outer layer) | 300
mature red blood cell | 0
Calculate how many times more mitochondria a heart muscle cell has than a skin cell. Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.answer: 17 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in the number of mitochondria between heart muscle cells and skin cells.
parts.answer: heart muscle contracts continuously, needs much energy from aerobic respiration in mitochondria; skin cells are less active and need less energy
parts.working: B1 mitochondria are where aerobic respiration releases energy; B1 heart muscle contracts continuously / never rests; B1 so heart cells need much more energy than skin cells (skin cells have low metabolic activity).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a mature red blood cell can still release some energy even though it has no mitochondria.
parts.answer: it respires anaerobically (in the cytoplasm)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student peels a thin layer of epidermis from the inside of an onion bulb, places it on a slide in a drop of iodine solution and adds a coverslip. State why iodine solution is added.
parts.answer: to stain the cells / make the nucleus and cell outline visible

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two structures the student would see in the onion cells with a light microscope.
parts.answer: any two of: cell wall, nucleus, cytoplasm, vacuole
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student notices that the onion cells have no chloroplasts. Explain why.
parts.answer: the bulb grows underground / receives no light, so the cells do not photosynthesise and do not need chloroplasts
parts.working: B1 no light reaches these cells; B1 chloroplasts are for photosynthesis, which they do not carry out.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the coverslip should be lowered slowly at an angle.
parts.answer: to avoid trapping air bubbles

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence shows the levels of organisation from the smallest to the largest?
A cell → organ → tissue → organ system
B cell → tissue → organ → organ system
C tissue → cell → organ → organ system
D cell → tissue → organ system → organ
parts.answer: B cell → tissue → organ → organ system
parts.working: Similar cells form a tissue; tissues form an organ; organs working together form an organ system. Option A swaps tissue and organ.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each specialised cell, state one feature and explain how it helps the cell carry out its function.
(i) root hair cell
(ii) ciliated cell lining the trachea
(iii) palisade mesophyll cell
(iv) sperm cell
parts.answer: (i) long extension – large surface area for water and ion uptake; (ii) cilia – beat to move mucus up and out of the airway; (iii) many chloroplasts – absorb light for photosynthesis; (iv) flagellum / tail – swims to the egg (or many mitochondria – energy for swimming; enzymes in acrosome – digest jelly coat)
parts.working: 1 mark each for feature linked to function.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of these as a cell, a tissue, an organ or an organ system:
xylem; leaf; digestive system; neurone; heart
parts.answer: xylem – tissue; leaf – organ; digestive system – organ system; neurone – cell; heart – organ
parts.working: All five correct 3 marks; four correct 2 marks; two or three correct 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the stomach is described as an organ.
parts.answer: it is made of several different tissues (e.g. muscle, glandular / epithelial tissue) working together to perform a specific function (digestion)
parts.working: B1 group of different tissues; B1 working together for a specific function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape. State how this helps the cell carry out its function.
parts.answer: large surface area (to volume ratio) for fast diffusion of oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other features of red blood cells that help them transport oxygen.
parts.answer: contain haemoglobin; no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin); small and flexible to pass through capillaries
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme begins the digestion of protein in the stomach?
A amylase
B lipase
C maltase
D pepsin
parts.answer: D pepsin
parts.working: Pepsin is the protease secreted in the stomach and works at acidic pH. Amylase digests starch, not protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row shows the places where starch is digested and the product of amylase action?
A mouth and stomach; glucose
B mouth and small intestine; maltose
C stomach and small intestine; maltose
D mouth and small intestine; glucose
parts.answer: B mouth and small intestine; maltose
parts.working: Salivary amylase acts in the mouth and pancreatic amylase in the small intestine (duodenum); amylase produces maltose, which maltase then breaks down to glucose. Glucose is the product of maltase, not amylase; amylase does not act in the acid stomach.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.
Starch is broken down to ______ by the enzyme amylase. This sugar is then broken down to ______ by the enzyme ______, which is found on the membranes of the epithelium lining the small intestine. Proteins are broken down to ______ by proteases such as pepsin and ______.
parts.answer: maltose; glucose; maltase; amino acids; trypsin
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of the hydrochloric acid secreted in the stomach.
parts.answer: kills pathogens / harmful microorganisms in food; gives the acidic pH that is optimum for pepsin
parts.working: B1 kills bacteria / pathogens; B1 provides optimum (low) pH for enzymes (pepsin).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pepsin stops working when the stomach contents reach the duodenum. Explain why.
parts.answer: bile (alkaline) neutralises the acid so pH rises; pepsin is far from its optimum pH; the shape of its active site changes so substrate no longer fits
parts.working: B1 bile / alkaline secretion neutralises acid, pH rises; B1 pepsin has a low optimum pH; B1 active site changes shape / enzyme denatured / no enzyme–substrate complexes form.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student mixes salivary amylase with starch solution at different pH values at 37 °C. A drop of the mixture is tested with iodine solution every 15 s until it no longer turns blue-black. The results are:
pH | time for starch to disappear / s
4 | 300
6 | 75
7 | 60
8 | 100
10 | 600
The rate of reaction can be found as 1000 ÷ time. Calculate the rate at pH 7 and at pH 4. Give each answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the optimum pH of this amylase from these results.
parts.answer: pH 7

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the starch takes 600 s to disappear at pH 10.
parts.answer: pH far from the optimum changes the shape of the active site of amylase; fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form so digestion is slow
parts.working: B1 active site changes shape / some enzyme molecules denatured; B1 starch fits less often / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the substrate and the products of the enzyme lipase.
parts.answer: substrate: fats (lipids); products: fatty acids and glycerol
parts.working: B1 fat; B1 fatty acids and glycerol (both).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes lipase into the duodenum.
parts.answer: pancreas

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why proteins in a meal of chicken karahi must be digested before they can be used by body cells.
parts.answer: proteins are large insoluble molecules that cannot pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; they are broken down to small soluble amino acids that can be absorbed; cells then use the amino acids to build their own proteins
parts.working: B1 proteins are large / insoluble; B1 cannot be absorbed (cannot cross the epithelium / membranes); B1 amino acids are small and soluble so can be absorbed and then used to make new proteins.

stem:
A student fills a length of Visking (dialysis) tubing with a mixture of starch solution and amylase solution, ties both ends and places it in a boiling tube of distilled water at 37 °C. Every 10 minutes, samples of the water outside the tubing are tested with iodine solution and with Benedict's solution.
time / min | iodine test on water outside | Benedict's test on water outside
0 | orange-brown | blue
10 | orange-brown | green
20 | orange-brown | orange
30 | orange-brown | brick red

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results of the Benedict's test.
parts.answer: amylase digests starch to maltose / reducing sugar; maltose molecules are small enough to diffuse through the tubing; more sugar outside over time so colour goes from blue to brick red
parts.working: B1 starch digested to reducing sugar (maltose); B1 sugar is small and diffuses out through the tubing; B1 concentration outside increases with time (colour sequence).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the iodine test on the water outside stays orange-brown throughout.
parts.answer: starch molecules are too large to pass through the tubing

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this experiment.
parts.answer: repeat with boiled (denatured) amylase / with water instead of amylase

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some people with cystic fibrosis, thick mucus blocks the duct that carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum. Suggest and explain two effects of this on digestion.
parts.answer: less amylase, protease (trypsin) and lipase reach the duodenum, so starch, protein and fat are less digested; pancreatic juice is alkaline, so acid from the stomach is less neutralised and enzymes in the small intestine are not at their optimum pH
parts.working: Two effects, each with explanation (2 × 2): less fat digested because less lipase (fatty food passes out in faeces); less protein / starch digested because less trypsin / amylase; fewer nutrients absorbed so poor growth / weight loss; contents of duodenum stay acidic so intestinal enzymes work slowly.

stem:
Lipase is added to full-cream milk containing a few drops of an indicator that is pink above pH 8.3 and colourless below it. A little sodium carbonate solution is first added so the milk starts pink. The time taken for the pink colour to disappear is recorded at four temperatures.
temperature / °C | time for pink colour to disappear / s
15 | 420
25 | 210
35 | 110
55 | 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pink colour disappears.
parts.answer: lipase digests fat in the milk to fatty acids (and glycerol); the fatty acids lower the pH below 8.3
parts.working: B1 fats broken down to fatty acids; B1 acids lower the pH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the temperature at which lipase was most active in these results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 25 °C as 1000 ÷ time. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 4.8 (arbitrary units)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the effect of bile on fats in the small intestine?
A It breaks fats down into fatty acids and glycerol.
B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
C It absorbs fats into the lacteals.
D It produces lipase to digest fats.
parts.answer: B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
parts.working: Bile emulsifies fat, breaking large drops into small droplets and increasing their surface area for lipase. It contains no enzymes, so A is wrong: that is the action of lipase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of human tooth used for:
(i) biting off pieces of food
(ii) grinding and chewing food
parts.answer: (i) incisors (ii) molars (accept premolars)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how chewing food helps chemical digestion.
parts.answer: chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymes to act on, so digestion is faster
parts.working: B1 increases surface area; B1 for enzymes / faster chemical digestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where bile is made and where it is stored.
parts.answer: made in the liver; stored in the gall bladder
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which bile helps the digestion of fats in the small intestine.
parts.answer: emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase; it is alkaline and neutralises stomach acid, giving a suitable pH for enzymes in the small intestine
parts.working: B1 emulsification; B1 larger surface area for lipase so faster digestion; B1 bile is alkaline / neutralises hydrochloric acid; B1 optimum pH for enzymes in the small intestine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient has her gall bladder removed. Her liver continues to make bile, which now trickles slowly and continuously into the duodenum. Explain why the doctor advises her to avoid large fatty meals.
parts.answer: without a store there is no large release of bile when a fatty meal arrives; fat is poorly emulsified, so surface area is small; lipase digests the fat slowly / incompletely, causing discomfort or fatty faeces
parts.working: B1 bile cannot be released in large amounts at meal times; B1 less emulsification / small surface area of fat; B1 fat digestion by lipase is slow / incomplete.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the stomach carries out physical digestion.
parts.answer: muscles in the stomach wall contract to churn the food, mixing it with gastric juice and breaking it into smaller pieces
parts.working: B1 muscle contractions / churning; B1 breaks food up / mixes with juices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cube of boiled potato with sides of 1 cm is cut into 8 equal cubes, each with sides of 0.5 cm. Calculate the total surface area before and after cutting.
parts.answer: before 6 cm²; after 12 cm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (b) to explain why physical digestion speeds up chemical digestion.
parts.answer: the surface area doubles, so more food is exposed to enzymes at once

stem:
A student investigates the effect of bile salts on fat digestion. Two test-tubes each contain 5 cm³ of vegetable oil mixed with 5 cm³ of a dilute alkaline solution containing an indicator. Tube A also has 1 cm³ of bile salt solution; tube B has 1 cm³ of distilled water. Lipase is added to both tubes at 35 °C and the time for the indicator to change colour (showing a fall in pH) is recorded.
tube A (with bile salts): 4 min
tube B (without bile salts): 11 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in time when bile salts are present. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is faster in tube A.
parts.answer: bile salts emulsify the oil into small droplets; larger surface area for lipase so fatty acids form faster
parts.working: B1 emulsification; B1 larger surface area for lipase / more enzyme–substrate collisions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1 cm³ of distilled water was added to tube B.
parts.answer: to keep the total volume (and so concentrations) the same in both tubes

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Into which structure in a villus are most fatty acids and glycerol absorbed?
A blood capillary
B lacteal
C hepatic portal vein
D artery
parts.answer: B lacteal
parts.working: Fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lacteal, a lymphatic vessel at the centre of the villus. Glucose and amino acids enter the blood capillaries instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of villi that increase the rate of absorption of digested food.
parts.answer: microvilli give a large surface area; wall only one cell thick (short diffusion distance); dense capillary network maintains a concentration gradient; lacteal for fat absorption
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In coeliac disease, eating gluten damages the lining of the small intestine and the villi become flattened. In one patient the absorptive surface area fell from 32 m² to 4 m². Calculate the percentage decrease in surface area. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why an untreated patient with coeliac disease may lose body mass even though they eat normally.
parts.answer: smaller surface area means less glucose, amino acids and fats absorbed into the blood; less energy and fewer nutrients available, so body stores are used
parts.working: B1 less absorption of digested food; B1 less energy / materials, so fat or protein stores are used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define assimilation.
parts.answer: the movement of digested food molecules into the cells of the body where they are used, becoming part of the cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: After absorption, glucose and amino acids travel to the liver. Describe what happens to them in the body after absorption.
parts.answer: carried in the hepatic portal vein to the liver; glucose used in respiration to release energy or stored as glycogen in liver and muscles; amino acids used to make proteins (e.g. enzymes, plasma proteins); excess amino acids deaminated in the liver to form urea
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: hepatic portal vein; glucose used for respiration; excess glucose converted to glycogen (stored in liver / muscles); amino acids used to build proteins; excess amino acids deaminated / urea formed in liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where most water is absorbed in the alimentary canal.
parts.answer: small intestine

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Each day about 9.0 dm³ of water (from food, drinks and digestive juices) enters the small intestine. The small intestine absorbs 85 % of this water. The colon absorbs 90 % of the water that reaches it.
Calculate the volume of water lost in the faeces each day, in cm³.
parts.answer: 135 cm³
parts.working: M1 water reaching colon = 9.0 × 0.15 = 1.35 dm³; M1 water left = 1.35 × 0.10 = 0.135 dm³; A1 135 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the term for passing out of food that has not been digested or absorbed, as faeces, through the anus?
A ingestion
B digestion
C egestion
D excretion
parts.answer: C egestion
parts.working: This is egestion. Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste (e.g. urea, CO₂); undigested food was never part of body cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State one function of each organ in digestion.
(i) salivary glands
(ii) stomach
(iii) pancreas
(iv) liver
(v) large intestine (colon)
parts.answer: (i) secrete saliva containing amylase; (ii) secretes pepsin / hydrochloric acid, churns food; (iii) secretes amylase, trypsin and lipase into the duodenum; (iv) makes bile; (v) absorbs water
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define digestion.
parts.answer: the breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules (using mechanical and chemical processes)
parts.working: B1 large / insoluble to small / soluble; B1 so they can be absorbed (or mention of mechanical and chemical).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Write the following in the order food passes through them:
ileum, stomach, rectum, oesophagus, duodenum, colon
parts.answer: oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, ileum, colon, rectum
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair swapped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student eats a meal of rice and daal (lentils). Rice is mainly starch and daal contains much protein. Describe what happens to the starch and protein from the meal as it passes from the mouth to the end of the ileum.
parts.answer: mouth: chewing, salivary amylase starts starch → maltose; stomach: acid stops amylase, pepsin begins protein digestion, churning; duodenum: pancreatic amylase and trypsin continue; bile neutralises acid; maltase on epithelium makes glucose; proteases make amino acids; glucose and amino acids absorbed by villi into capillaries in the ileum
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: chewing increases surface area; salivary amylase in mouth; starch to maltose; stomach acid denatures / stops amylase; pepsin digests protein in stomach; pancreatic juice into duodenum with amylase and trypsin; bile / alkaline juice neutralises acid; maltase converts maltose to glucose (on membranes of epithelium); protein digested to amino acids; absorption of glucose and amino acids in the ileum into blood capillaries of villi.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each statement to one process: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation or egestion.
(i) amino acids are used by a muscle cell to make new proteins
(ii) a child takes a bite of a samosa
(iii) glucose moves from the ileum into the blood
(iv) fibre leaves the body through the anus
(v) starch is broken down to maltose in the mouth
parts.answer: (i) assimilation (ii) ingestion (iii) absorption (iv) egestion (v) digestion
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly matches a nutrient with the disease caused by its deficiency?
A vitamin C – rickets
B vitamin D – scurvy
C vitamin D – rickets
D iron – scurvy
parts.answer: C vitamin D – rickets
parts.working: Lack of vitamin D (and calcium) causes rickets; lack of vitamin C causes scurvy. A and B swap the two vitamins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hostel student eats mostly white rice and bread with very little fruit, vegetables or meat. Suggest two nutrients that may be lacking in this diet and state a good source of each.
parts.answer: e.g. vitamin C – citrus fruits / guava; iron – red meat / spinach; fibre – vegetables / whole grains; protein – meat / pulses; calcium – milk
parts.working: 1 mark each for nutrient with a matching source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the body needs (i) iron and (ii) dietary fibre.
parts.answer: (i) iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells; (ii) fibre helps food move through the gut / prevents constipation
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 100 g of guava contains 228 mg of vitamin C. A teenager needs 65 mg of vitamin C each day. Calculate the mass of guava, in g, that provides the daily need. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the deficiency disease caused by a long-term lack of vitamin C.
parts.answer: scurvy

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why rickets is more common in children who rarely go outdoors and drink little milk.
parts.answer: little sunlight on skin so less vitamin D made; little calcium (from milk) and vitamin D needed to absorb calcium, so bones are soft / weak
parts.working: B1 vitamin D made in skin in sunlight / milk supplies calcium (and vitamin D); B1 calcium needed for strong bones, vitamin D helps calcium absorption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a balanced diet.
parts.answer: a diet containing all the nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water) in the correct proportions
parts.working: B1 all nutrient groups; B1 in the correct amounts / proportions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the body needs water.
parts.answer: solvent for transport (e.g. in blood plasma); medium for chemical reactions; cooling by sweating; removal of waste in urine
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A lactic acid only
B carbon dioxide and water
C ethanol and carbon dioxide
D lactic acid and carbon dioxide
parts.answer: C ethanol and carbon dioxide
parts.working: Yeast respires anaerobically to ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is the product in human muscle; carbon dioxide and water are the products of aerobic respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After vigorous exercise, what happens to the lactic acid that has built up in the muscles?
A It is converted to glucose in the muscles and stored.
B It is carried in the blood to the liver and broken down by aerobic respiration.
C It is excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
D It is converted to ethanol in the liver.
parts.answer: B It is carried in the blood to the liver and broken down by aerobic respiration.
parts.working: Lactic acid is transported in the blood to the liver, where it is broken down by aerobic respiration, using the extra oxygen taken in (the oxygen debt). It is not mainly excreted by the kidneys.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement correctly compares anaerobic respiration with aerobic respiration?
A Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule.
B Anaerobic respiration takes place only in mitochondria.
C Anaerobic respiration releases more energy per glucose molecule.
D Anaerobic respiration uses oxygen but produces no carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: A Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule.
parts.working: Glucose is only partly broken down in anaerobic respiration, so much less energy is released per glucose molecule. It takes place in the cytoplasm, not mitochondria.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the balanced chemical equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₂H₅OH + CO₂
B C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
C C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
D C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃
parts.answer: B C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
parts.working: One glucose gives two ethanol and two carbon dioxide: atoms balance (C 6, H 12, O 6). Option A is unbalanced; C is aerobic respiration; D is lactic acid in muscle (not yeast).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.
