author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two hens' eggs had their shells dissolved by soaking in vinegar, leaving only a thin membrane around each egg. They were weighed, one was placed in distilled water and one in concentrated sugar syrup for 24 hours, then reweighed.
Egg in distilled water: initial mass 72.4 g, final mass 94.1 g
Egg in sugar syrup: initial mass 70.8 g, final mass 51.6 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass for each egg. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Egg in water: +30.0 %; egg in syrup: −27.1 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: The membrane under the shell behaves like a cell membrane. Explain the results.
parts.answer: The membrane is partially permeable. Water has a higher water potential than the egg contents, so water entered the first egg by osmosis; the syrup has a lower water potential than the egg contents, so water left the second egg by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark each: partially permeable membrane; water entered egg in water (higher water potential outside); water left egg in syrup (lower water potential outside).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the shell was dissolved before the experiment.
parts.answer: So that the change in mass is due to water crossing the membrane only / the shell does not limit or interfere with the movement of water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the water potential of the soil water with that of the root hair cell sap when the plant is absorbing water.
parts.answer: The soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a high concentration of sugars and ions in the vacuole of a root hair cell helps the plant to take up water.
parts.answer: The solutes lower the water potential of the cell sap below that of the soil water, maintaining a water potential gradient so water enters by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: lowers water potential of cell; 1 mark: water moves in by osmosis down the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A gardener adds far too much dry fertiliser around the roots of a chilli plant. After two days the leaves are wilted. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: The fertiliser dissolves in the soil water and lowers its water potential below that of the root hair cells; water leaves the roots by osmosis (or stops entering); less water reaches the leaves and leaf cells lose turgor, so the plant wilts.
parts.working: 1 mark each: soil water potential lowered / now lower than cells; water lost from roots by osmosis; leaf cells flaccid / plant wilts.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes active transport?
A movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration using energy from respiration
B movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration using energy from respiration
C movement of water from a lower to a higher concentration of solute without using energy
D movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration without using energy
parts.answer: B movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration using energy from respiration
parts.working: Active transport moves particles against a concentration gradient (lower → higher) through a membrane, using energy released by respiration. A is down the gradient; D omits the energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process depends on active transport?
A uptake of nitrate ions from soil into root hair cells
B loss of water vapour through stomata
C movement of oxygen from alveoli into the blood
D entry of water into root hair cells
parts.answer: A uptake of nitrate ions from soil into root hair cells
parts.working: Nitrate ions are usually more concentrated inside root hair cells than in soil water, so they are taken up against the gradient by active transport using carrier proteins. Oxygen moves by diffusion (C) and water enters by osmosis (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rice seedlings were grown in two trays of the same nutrient solution. Air was bubbled through tray P; tray Q was left still and became low in oxygen. After a week the roots in tray Q contained far fewer potassium ions. What is the best explanation?
A Less oxygen reduced aerobic respiration in the root cells, so less energy was available for active transport of potassium ions.
B Less oxygen reduced the diffusion of potassium ions because oxygen carries the ions into the cells.
C Without bubbling, the potassium ions could not move by osmosis into the roots.
D Low oxygen made the solution more concentrated, so potassium ions moved out of the roots by diffusion.
parts.answer: A Less oxygen reduced aerobic respiration in the root cells, so less energy was available for active transport of potassium ions.
parts.working: Ion uptake by roots is mainly active transport, which needs energy from aerobic respiration; low oxygen limits respiration. B is wrong because oxygen does not carry ions, C because osmosis is the movement of water, not ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process by which root hair cells take up mineral ions when the concentration in the soil is lower than in the cell.
parts.answer: Active transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this process needs energy, and where the energy comes from.
parts.answer: The ions are moved against their concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration); the energy is released by respiration in the cell (in mitochondria).
parts.working: 1 mark: against concentration gradient; 1 mark: energy from respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of protein carriers in the cell membrane in this process.
parts.answer: Carrier proteins bind the specific ions and change shape, using energy, to move them across the membrane into the cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: carrier protein binds/picks up the ion (specific); 1 mark: changes shape to move ion across membrane using energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why root hair cells contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: To carry out a lot of aerobic respiration to release the energy needed for active transport of ions.

stem:
The concentrations of three ions in the cell sap of a freshwater alga and in the pond water around it were measured (in mmol/dm³).
Ion | pond water | cell sap
potassium | 0.6 | 54.0
chloride | 1.2 | 90.0
sodium | 2.4 | 30.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated potassium ions are in the cell sap than in the pond water.
parts.answer: 90 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the data show that the alga takes up potassium and chloride ions by active transport.
parts.answer: The ions are far more concentrated inside the cells than in the pond water, so they must have moved in against their concentration gradient, which requires active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentration inside much higher than outside (quote figures); 1 mark: movement against concentration gradient = active transport.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When a poison that stops respiration was added to the pond water, the concentration of potassium ions in the cells slowly fell. Explain this observation.
parts.answer: Without respiration no energy is released for active transport, so uptake stops; potassium ions then leak out / diffuse out down their concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: no energy for active transport; 1 mark: ions diffuse out down the gradient.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Equal masses of carrot discs were kept in an aerated solution of potassium ions for 4 hours at different temperatures. The ions absorbed were measured in arbitrary units.
Temperature (°C): 5, 15, 25, 35, 45
Ions absorbed (units): 0.8, 2.0, 4.2, 6.0, 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: The carrot discs at 35 °C absorbed 6.0 units of ions in 4 hours. Calculate the mean rate of uptake in units per hour.
parts.answer: 1.5 units per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the results between 5 °C and 35 °C.
parts.answer: Uptake increases as temperature rises (0.8 to 6.0 units); higher temperature increases the rate of respiration (enzyme activity), so more energy is released for active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: description with data; 1 mark: more respiration / enzymes more active; 1 mark: more energy for active transport.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why uptake was much lower at 45 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes for respiration and/or the carrier proteins were denatured at high temperature, so less energy was released / carriers could not transport ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: denaturing of enzymes / carrier proteins; 1 mark: less respiration / less active transport.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables, other than time, that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: size/mass/surface area of discs; concentration of ion solution; volume of solution; oxygen supply (aeration); age/type of carrot.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a meal, glucose is absorbed into the epithelial cells of the villi even when the glucose concentration in these cells is higher than in the lumen of the small intestine. Name the process.
parts.answer: Active transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other place in the human body where glucose is moved by this process.
parts.answer: The (proximal convoluted) tubules of the kidney nephrons (reabsorption of glucose).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the epithelial cells of the villi have large numbers of mitochondria and microvilli.
parts.answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing the energy needed for active transport; microvilli increase the surface area of the membrane, so more carrier proteins / faster absorption.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria → respiration → energy; 1 mark: energy for active transport; 1 mark: microvilli give larger surface area for absorption.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the comparison of three transport processes. For each process state: (i) whether it needs energy from respiration, (ii) the direction of movement in relation to the concentration gradient, (iii) whether it needs a membrane.
Processes: diffusion, osmosis, active transport.
parts.answer: Diffusion: no energy from respiration (uses kinetic energy of particles); down the concentration gradient; no membrane needed. Osmosis: no energy from respiration; water moves from higher to lower water potential (down its gradient); needs a partially permeable membrane. Active transport: needs energy from respiration; against the concentration gradient (lower to higher); needs a membrane with carrier proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct pair of entries, six marks in total: diffusion energy + direction; diffusion membrane; osmosis energy + direction; osmosis partially permeable membrane; active transport energy; active transport against gradient + carrier proteins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A root cell takes up sodium ions by active transport. Suggest why the rate of uptake stops increasing at high external sodium ion concentrations, even with plenty of oxygen.
parts.answer: All the carrier proteins are in use (saturated), so the number of carriers limits the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: carrier proteins all occupied / limited number of carriers; 1 mark: carriers become the limiting factor.

stem: A brown seaweed growing off the coast of Balochistan contains iodide ions at a much higher concentration in its cells than in the seawater around it (0.4 µmol/dm³). Over 48 hours, the iodide concentration in its cells rose from 9600 µmol/dm³ to 12 000 µmol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in iodide concentration in the seaweed cells, in µmol/dm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 50 µmol/dm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process the seaweed uses to absorb iodide ions, and state two things the process needs.
parts.answer: Active transport; it needs energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the cell membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport; 1 mark: energy (from respiration); 1 mark: (protein) carriers in the membrane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seaweed absorbs iodide ions more slowly when the seawater is very cold.
parts.answer: Respiration is slower at low temperature because enzymes work more slowly, so less energy is available for active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: slower respiration / enzyme activity; 1 mark: less energy for active transport.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where does the energy for diffusion come from?
A respiration in the cell
B the kinetic energy of the random movement of molecules and ions
C ATP made in the mitochondria
D light energy absorbed by chlorophyll
parts.answer: B the kinetic energy of the random movement of molecules and ions
parts.working: Diffusion is passive: the energy comes from the kinetic energy of random movement of particles. A and C describe active transport, which needs energy from respiration.

stem:
Cubes of pink agar (containing an alkali and an indicator) were cut with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm and placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. The indicator turns colourless when acid reaches it.
Side length (cm) | time to become completely colourless (min)
1 | 3.5
2 | 13.0
3 | 29.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube.
parts.answer: 1 cm cube: surface area 6 cm², volume 1 cm³, ratio 6:1; 2 cm cube: 24 cm², 8 cm³, ratio 3:1; 3 cm cube: 54 cm², 27 cm³, ratio 2:1
parts.working: 1 mark each: SA = 6 × side², V = side³. 6/1; 24/8 = 3; 54/27 = 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between surface area to volume ratio and the time for the cube to become colourless.
parts.answer: The smaller the surface area to volume ratio, the longer the time to become colourless.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the results.
parts.answer: In smaller cubes there is more surface for the acid to diffuse in through, relative to the volume, and a shorter distance to the centre, so the acid reaches all parts faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area relative to volume; 1 mark: shorter diffusion distance to centre.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a large multicellular animal needs a transport system.
parts.answer: Its surface area to volume ratio is small and the distances to cells inside are large, so diffusion alone through the body surface would be too slow to supply cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: small SA:V / long distances; 1 mark: diffusion too slow, so a transport system (blood) is needed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define diffusion.
parts.answer: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration (down a concentration gradient), as a result of their random movement.
parts.working: 1 mark: net movement from higher to lower concentration / down gradient; 1 mark: due to random movement of particles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood.
parts.answer: The oxygen concentration in the alveoli is higher than in the blood arriving at the lungs, so oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher concentration in alveoli than blood; 1 mark: diffusion down gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two features of the alveoli that increase the rate of diffusion.
parts.answer: Any two of: large surface area; thin walls (short diffusion distance); good blood supply (maintains gradient); moist surface; good ventilation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem:
A student placed one crystal of potassium manganate(VII) in the centre of each of three Petri dishes of still water at 10 °C, 30 °C and 50 °C. After 15 minutes the distance the purple colour had spread from the crystal was measured.
Temperature (°C): 10, 30, 50
Distance (mm): 12, 21, 33

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of spread of the purple colour at 30 °C, in mm per minute. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 1.4 mm/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the results.
parts.answer: Higher temperature gives the particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster at random; the net movement down the concentration gradient is faster, so the colour spreads further in 15 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark: description (higher temperature, greater distance, quote data); 1 mark: more kinetic energy / faster random movement; 1 mark: faster diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to measure the distance the colour has spread, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: The edge of the colour is not sharp / fades gradually, so the end point is a matter of judgement. Improvement: compare against a colour standard / use a white tile and grid behind the dish / have the same person judge each time.
parts.working: 1 mark: difficulty; 1 mark: matching improvement.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the Petri dishes must not be moved during the experiment.
parts.answer: Moving the water would mix the dye by currents (convection/stirring), not by diffusion alone.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: During the day carbon dioxide diffuses from the air into a leaf. Describe the concentration gradient that causes this.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide in the mesophyll cells, so the concentration in the air spaces is lower than in the outside air; CO₂ diffuses in through the stomata down this gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentration lower inside leaf because used in photosynthesis; 1 mark: diffuses in through stomata from higher to lower concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain three factors that increase the rate of diffusion of a gas into a cell.
parts.answer: Any three of: larger surface area – more area for particles to cross; steeper concentration gradient – more net movement; higher temperature – more kinetic energy; shorter distance – particles have less far to travel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for factor with explanation, any three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The smell of frying pakoras reaches people across a room even when there is no wind. Explain how.
parts.answer: Molecules of the smell move at random and spread from a high concentration near the pan to the lower concentration across the room – net movement by diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: random movement of molecules; 1 mark: from higher to lower concentration (diffusion).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is transpiration?
A the uptake of water by root hair cells
B the loss of water vapour from leaves
C the movement of sucrose through the phloem
D the evaporation of water from the soil surface
parts.answer: B the loss of water vapour from leaves
parts.working: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves (water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffuses out through the stomata). A is water uptake; C is translocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Under which set of conditions will a well-watered maize plant with open stomata lose water vapour fastest?
A 15 °C, humid air, still air
B 15 °C, dry air, windy
C 35 °C, humid air, still air
D 35 °C, dry air, windy
parts.answer: D 35 °C, dry air, windy
parts.working: High temperature increases evaporation and diffusion; dry air gives a steep water vapour gradient; wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the gradient steep. C has a high temperature but humid, still air reduces the gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potometer is used to estimate the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Why does it not measure the rate of transpiration exactly?
A Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells, so uptake is not exactly equal to loss.
B Water vapour lost from the leaves is absorbed back into the capillary tube.
C The potometer measures the movement of sucrose instead of water.
D Water can only enter the shoot by osmosis when the stomata are closed.
parts.answer: A Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells, so uptake is not exactly equal to loss.
parts.working: A potometer measures water uptake. A small proportion of the water absorbed is used (e.g. in photosynthesis) or stays in cells to keep them turgid, so uptake is only approximately equal to water lost. B, C and D are not true.

stem: A leafy shoot of a guava plant was set up in a potometer. The air bubble in the capillary tube moved 36 mm in 5 minutes in still air. A fan was then switched on and the bubble moved 62 mm in 5 minutes. The internal radius of the capillary tube is 0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water taken up in still air in 5 minutes. Use the formula volume = πr²l, where r is the internal radius of the tube and l the distance moved. Give your answer in mm³ to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 28.3 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in still air in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 5.7 mm³/min
parts.working: 28.27 ÷ 5 = 5.7 mm³/min (allow follow-through).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the distance moved when the fan was switched on. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the fan increased the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: Moving air removes water vapour from around the leaf surface, keeping a steep water vapour concentration (diffusion) gradient between the air spaces and the outside air; more water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, so more water is pulled up the xylem (transpiration pull) and taken up from the potometer.
parts.working: 1 mark each: wind removes water vapour near the leaf; steeper diffusion gradient; faster loss through stomata / more transpiration pull.

parts.label: e
parts.text: State two precautions when setting up a potometer.
parts.answer: Cut the shoot under water; make all joints airtight (e.g. with petroleum jelly); dry the leaves; let the shoot settle for a few minutes before taking readings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway taken by water from the soil to the air around a leaf. Name the cells or tissues it passes through.
parts.answer: Water enters root hair cells (by osmosis), passes through the root cortex cells to the xylem, moves up the xylem in the root and stem into the leaf veins, passes into mesophyll cells, evaporates from their surfaces into the air spaces and diffuses out through the stomata.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four in correct order: root hair cell; root cortex; xylem (root → stem → leaf); mesophyll cells; evaporation into air spaces; diffusion out through stomata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to the loss of water vapour from leaves.
parts.answer: Transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves up the xylem of a tall tree such as a shisham tree.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cells and diffuses out of the leaf; this creates a transpiration pull (tension) on the water in the xylem; water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion), so a continuous column of water is pulled up from the roots; the xylem vessels are narrow, continuous, hollow tubes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: evaporation/transpiration from leaf; creates transpiration pull / tension; cohesion between water molecules; continuous column of water; pulled up through xylem (continuous hollow tubes) from roots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the trunk of a tree becomes very slightly narrower in diameter at midday than at night.
parts.answer: At midday the transpiration rate is highest, so the tension in the xylem is greatest; the walls of the xylem are pulled inwards, slightly reducing the diameter.
parts.working: 1 mark: high transpiration at midday; 1 mark: greater tension/pull on xylem walls draws them inwards.

stem:
Four similar leafy shoots of a bean plant were treated as follows and hung up in the same room for 48 hours.
A: no petroleum jelly; B: jelly on upper leaf surfaces; C: jelly on lower leaf surfaces; D: jelly on both surfaces.
Shoot | initial mass (g) | mass after 48 h (g)
A | 25.0 | 21.2
B | 24.6 | 21.3
C | 25.4 | 24.6
D | 24.8 | 24.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in mass for each shoot. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.working: (initial − final) ÷ initial × 100. 3 marks all four correct; 2 marks three correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What do the results suggest about where the stomata are found on these leaves? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Most stomata are on the lower surface: covering the lower surface (C) reduced mass loss far more than covering the upper surface (B), whose loss was almost the same as uncovered shoot A; the jelly blocks the stomata so water vapour cannot diffuse out.
parts.working: 1 mark: most stomata on lower surface; 1 mark: comparison using data B vs C (or A vs C); 1 mark: jelly blocks stomata / prevents diffusion of water vapour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why shoot D still lost a small amount of mass.
parts.answer: Water vapour was lost through the stem or through the jelly / cuticle, or the jelly did not cover the leaves completely.
parts.working: B1 for any valid suggestion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be made more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat with several shoots for each treatment and calculate mean percentages.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases when the temperature rises.
parts.answer: Water molecules gain more kinetic energy, so more water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells; water vapour diffuses faster out through the stomata; warm air can also hold more water vapour, so the diffusion gradient is steeper.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: more kinetic energy; faster evaporation from mesophyll surfaces; faster diffusion of water vapour through stomata; steeper gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration is lower on a humid day.
parts.answer: Humid air contains more water vapour, so the concentration gradient of water vapour between the air spaces in the leaf and the air outside is smaller; less water vapour diffuses out.
parts.working: 1 mark: more water vapour in the air outside; 1 mark: smaller diffusion gradient, slower diffusion out of stomata.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the feature of the leaf interior that provides a large surface for evaporation.
parts.answer: The large internal surface area of the mesophyll cells facing the interconnecting air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an investigation to find out how wind speed affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. You are provided with a potometer, an electric fan and normal laboratory apparatus.
In your plan, include: what you will vary and how; what you will measure; the variables you will keep constant; how you will make the results reliable.
parts.answer: Set up a potometer with a leafy shoot cut under water and airtight joints; vary wind speed by placing the fan at different distances (e.g. 25, 50, 75, 100 cm) or using fan speed settings, plus a no-fan control; measure the distance the bubble moves in a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) and calculate the rate; keep the same shoot, temperature, light intensity and humidity constant; allow 5 minutes to settle at each speed; repeat three times at each speed and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: independent variable – wind speed changed by fan distance/setting with at least 4 values; dependent variable – distance moved by bubble (or volume) in a stated time; rate = distance ÷ time; two controlled variables (e.g. temperature, light intensity, same shoot/leaf area, humidity); acclimatisation time before readings; reset the bubble with the reservoir; repeats and mean; safety/precaution such as airtight seals or cutting under water.

stem:
A potted cotton plant was weighed every 2 hours during a sunny day in Faisalabad, and the rate of water loss was calculated.
Time: 06:00, 08:00, 10:00, 12:00, 14:00, 16:00, 18:00
Rate of water loss (g per hour): 0.4, 1.6, 3.2, 4.1, 3.6, 1.8, 0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time at which the rate of water loss was highest.
parts.answer: 12:00 (4.1 g per hour).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss for the seven readings. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.17 g per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the rate was low at 06:00.
parts.answer: Low temperature; low light so stomata were (partly) closed; higher humidity in early morning.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the most suitable type of graph to display these results and how the axes should be arranged.
parts.answer: A line graph with time on the x-axis and rate of water loss (g per hour) on the y-axis.
parts.working: 1 mark: line graph; 1 mark: time on x-axis, rate on y-axis with units.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: On a hot afternoon in Multan the leaves of a pumpkin plant droop, even though the soil is moist. By evening they have recovered. Explain why the leaves droop.
parts.answer: The rate of transpiration is greater than the rate of water uptake by the roots; the leaf cells lose water and become flaccid (lose turgor pressure); so the leaves are no longer supported and wilt.
parts.working: 1 mark each: water loss faster than uptake; cells lose turgor / become flaccid; loss of support → wilting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to the plant of wilting.
parts.answer: The leaves hang down so less surface faces the sun / less heat absorbed, reducing further water loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the leaves recover in the evening.
parts.answer: Lower temperature and light, so transpiration falls (stomata close); water uptake now exceeds loss so cells take in water by osmosis and become turgid again.
parts.working: 1 mark: less transpiration in evening; 1 mark: cells regain water / become turgid.

stem:
A researcher measured the rate of water loss from a leafy shoot of a mulberry tree in still air and in moving air.
Still air: 2.4 g per hour
Moving air: 4.2 g per hour

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water loss in moving air compared with still air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The researcher then covered the shoot with a clear plastic bag in moving air, and the rate fell to 0.6 g per hour. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Water vapour collects inside the bag, so the air around the leaf becomes very humid / saturated; the bag also prevents wind removing water vapour; the diffusion gradient between leaf air spaces and the air is very small, so little water vapour diffuses out.
parts.working: 1 mark each: humidity in bag rises; wind cannot remove water vapour; small diffusion gradient → slow loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plants in very windy places, such as the northern mountain passes, often have small leaves.
parts.answer: Smaller leaf surface area means fewer stomata exposed and less water vapour lost, which reduces the risk of wilting when wind increases transpiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller surface area / fewer stomata; 1 mark: reduces water loss by transpiration.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink when it absorbs water. A student clipped one dry square of cobalt chloride paper to the upper surface and one to the lower surface of a leaf on a hibiscus plant, and timed how long each took to turn pink.
Upper surface: 240 s
Lower surface: 40 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster the paper on the lower surface changed colour than the paper on the upper surface.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the results show about the two leaf surfaces.
parts.answer: The lower surface loses water vapour faster, so it has more stomata than the upper surface.
parts.working: 1 mark: more water lost from lower surface; 1 mark: more stomata on lower surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cobalt chloride paper must be kept dry and handled with forceps.
parts.answer: Any moisture from the air or from fingers would turn the paper pink before the experiment starts, giving a false result.
parts.working: 1 mark: paper is sensitive to any water; 1 mark: fingers/air moisture would change colour → invalid result.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to improve the reliability of the results.
parts.answer: Repeat on several leaves of the same plant and calculate means.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substances are transported in the phloem?
A water and mineral ions
B sucrose and amino acids
C starch and glucose
D oxygen and carbon dioxide
parts.answer: B sucrose and amino acids
parts.working: Phloem translocates sucrose and amino acids from sources to sinks. Water and mineral ions are carried in the xylem (A). Starch is insoluble and is not transported.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In early spring, before any leaves have grown, the buds of a potato plant start to grow using food stored in the tuber. During this time, which statement is correct?
A The tuber is a source and the growing shoots are sinks.
B The tuber is a sink and the growing shoots are sources.
C The tuber and the shoots are both sinks.
D Sucrose moves from the shoots to the tuber in the xylem.
parts.answer: A The tuber is a source and the growing shoots are sinks.
parts.working: Stored starch in the tuber is converted to sucrose and sent in the phloem to the growing shoots, so the tuber is a source and the shoots are sinks. In summer the tuber becomes a sink (B describes summer, not spring). Sucrose moves in phloem, not xylem (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define translocation.
parts.answer: The movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources to sinks.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement of sucrose and amino acids; 1 mark: in phloem from source(s) to sink(s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a source and a sink, and give one example of each in a flowering plant.
parts.answer: Source: a part of the plant that releases sucrose or amino acids, e.g. a photosynthesising leaf (or a storage organ when its store is used). Sink: a part that uses or stores sucrose or amino acids, e.g. root, growing shoot tip, developing fruit or seed, storage organ.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of source; 1 mark: example; 1 mark: definition of sink; 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer removed a complete ring of bark (including the phloem) from one branch of a mango tree, without damaging the xylem. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swelled. Explain why.
parts.answer: Removing the bark removed the phloem, so sucrose made in the leaves could not be translocated past the ring down the branch; sucrose and other substances built up above the ring, causing swelling (extra growth).
parts.working: 1 mark each: phloem removed / cut; sucrose from leaves cannot pass the ring; accumulates above ring → swelling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves on the ringed branch did not wilt.
parts.answer: The xylem was not damaged, so water and mineral ions could still travel up to the leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem intact; 1 mark: water still reaches leaves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fruits on the ringed branch grew larger than fruits on other branches.
parts.answer: Sucrose made by the leaves of that branch could not move down to the roots or trunk, so more was available to the fruits (sinks) on that branch.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose kept in that branch; 1 mark: more sucrose to the fruits / fruits as sinks receive more.

stem: One mature leaf of a young bean plant was enclosed in a clear bag containing carbon dioxide made with radioactive carbon. The plant was left in light for 6 hours, then parts of the plant were tested for radioactivity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue in which the radioactive substance was found in the stem.
parts.answer: Phloem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the radioactive substance most likely to be carried in this tissue, and explain how it was formed.
parts.answer: Sucrose; the leaf used the radioactive carbon dioxide in photosynthesis to make glucose, which was converted to sucrose for transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose; 1 mark: from radioactive CO₂ fixed in photosynthesis → glucose → sucrose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Radioactivity was found both in the young leaves at the top of the plant and in the roots. Explain why the substance moved both upwards and downwards.
parts.answer: Translocation moves sucrose from a source (the mature leaf) to sinks; sinks are found both above (growing shoot tip / young leaves) and below (roots); so phloem can carry substances in either direction depending on where the sinks are.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mature leaf is a source; young leaves and roots are sinks; phloem transports in both directions, to wherever sinks are.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why no radioactivity was found in the mature leaves below the treated leaf.
parts.answer: These mature leaves are themselves sources (photosynthesising), not sinks, so they do not import sucrose.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aphids feed by pushing a fine mouthpart (stylet) into a plant stem. The liquid they drink contains a high concentration of sugar. Name the tissue the stylet enters and the sugar it contains.
parts.answer: Phloem; sucrose.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aphid colonies on a young tomato plant cause the fruits to stay small. Explain why.
parts.answer: The aphids remove sucrose (and amino acids) from the phloem, so less reaches the fruits, which are sinks; less energy/raw material for growth.
parts.working: 1 mark: aphids take sucrose/amino acids from phloem; 1 mark: less reaches fruits (sinks) for growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why aphids are often found feeding on the young growing tips of plants.
parts.answer: The phloem there carries sucrose and amino acids towards the growing tip (a sink), so the sap is rich in nutrients / tissues are soft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In sugarcane, sucrose is stored in the stem. Describe how sucrose made in a leaf reaches the stem.
parts.answer: Glucose is made by photosynthesis in the mesophyll cells and converted to sucrose; sucrose enters the phloem in the leaf veins; it is translocated through the phloem to the stem, which acts as a sink (store).
parts.working: 1 mark each: made in leaf by photosynthesis (glucose → sucrose); loaded into phloem; translocated to stem (sink).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plants transport carbohydrate as sucrose rather than as starch.
parts.answer: Sucrose is soluble so it can be carried in solution in the phloem sap; starch is insoluble and cannot be transported.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose soluble; 1 mark: starch insoluble so cannot move in phloem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why sugarcane fields need a supply of nitrate ions as well as sunlight.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids (and proteins) for growth.

stem: Radioactive carbon dioxide was supplied to a leaf near the top of a sunflower plant. A detector found that the radioactive sugar had travelled 72 cm down the stem in 1.5 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean speed of translocation in cm per hour.
parts.answer: 48 cm per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to mm per minute.
parts.answer: 8 mm per minute
parts.working: M1: 480 mm per hour; A1: 480 ÷ 60 = 8 mm/min.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The experiment was repeated at night in darkness. The radioactivity travelled only 30 cm in 1.5 hours. Suggest why translocation was slower.
parts.answer: Less photosynthesis in darkness, so less sucrose produced in the leaf / smaller concentration difference between source and sink; lower temperature at night slows the process.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid suggestions; one must refer to less sucrose from the source.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one hazard of using radioactive substances and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: ionising radiation can damage cells / DNA. Precaution: wear gloves, use forceps, keep exposure time short, dispose of material safely.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pea plant is forming pods with developing seeds. State whether the developing seeds are a source or a sink, and explain why.
parts.answer: Sink; they receive sucrose and amino acids from the leaves through the phloem and use them for growth or store them.
parts.working: 1 mark: sink; 1 mark: receive (import) sucrose/amino acids via phloem for growth or storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the insoluble carbohydrate that the developing seeds make from sucrose for storage.
parts.answer: Starch.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When one of these seeds germinates, its stored food supplies the growing shoot and root before the new leaves can photosynthesise. Explain whether the seed's food store is now a source or a sink.
parts.answer: Source; the stored starch is broken down to sugar, which is moved as sucrose in the phloem to the growing shoot and root (the sinks).
parts.working: 1 mark: source; 1 mark: starch broken down and sucrose translocated to growing shoot/root (sinks).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a function of xylem?
A transport of sucrose and amino acids
B transport of water and mineral ions and support
C absorption of light for photosynthesis
D gas exchange with the atmosphere
parts.answer: B transport of water and mineral ions and support
parts.working: Xylem transports water and mineral ions and its lignified walls help support the plant. Sucrose and amino acids travel in phloem (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the positions of xylem and phloem in a transverse section of a young dicotyledonous stem.
parts.answer: Vascular bundles in a ring near the outside of the stem; in each bundle the xylem is towards the inside (centre) and the phloem towards the outside.
parts.working: 1 mark: bundles in a ring; 1 mark: xylem inner, phloem outer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the positions of xylem and phloem in a transverse section of a root.
parts.answer: Xylem in the centre of the root (in a star or X shape); phloem in groups between the arms of the xylem.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem central; 1 mark: phloem between xylem arms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In a leaf vein, state which tissue is nearer the upper surface.
parts.answer: Xylem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain three ways in which the structure of xylem vessels is related to their function.
parts.answer: No cross walls (end walls broken down) – a continuous tube so water flows without obstruction; no cell contents (dead, hollow) – leaves a clear lumen for water; thick walls strengthened with lignin – support the plant and stop vessels collapsing under tension; narrow tubes – help maintain a continuous water column.
parts.working: For each of three features: 1 mark feature, 1 mark explanation. Features: no cross walls; no cytoplasm / hollow / dead; lignified thick walls; narrow continuous tubes; pits allow sideways movement.

stem: A celery stalk with leaves was stood in water containing red dye for 2 hours. A thin transverse slice was then cut. Red dots could be seen arranged in a ring near the outside of the slice. A student drew the slice; the width of the drawing is 84 mm and the actual width of the slice is 14 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue that was stained red and explain why.
parts.answer: Xylem; the dye solution was drawn up the stalk in the xylem with the water by transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem; 1 mark: water (and dye) carried up in xylem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
parts.working: M1: magnification = drawing size ÷ actual size = 84 ÷ 14; A1: ×6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dye moved up faster in the celery stalk that still had its leaves than in a stalk with the leaves removed.
parts.answer: Leaves carry out transpiration; the loss of water vapour from leaves creates the transpiration pull that draws water and dye up the xylem; without leaves there is little pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: leaves transpire; 1 mark: transpiration pull drives movement up xylem.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two features of a good biological drawing of this section.
parts.answer: Any two of: clear continuous outlines with no shading; correct proportions; large (uses most of the space); labelled with ruled label lines that do not cross.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says 'xylem vessels are living cells that pump water up the stem'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Mature xylem vessels are dead – they have no cytoplasm or cell contents; they cannot pump; water is pulled up by transpiration pull (with cohesion between water molecules), not pumped.
parts.working: 1 mark each: xylem vessels are dead / hollow; no contents to do work / no pumping; water moved by transpiration pull and cohesion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lignin in xylem walls is important for a tall tree.
parts.answer: Lignin makes the walls strong and rigid, giving support to the stem/trunk and stopping the vessels collapsing inwards under the tension of the transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: support/strength for the plant; 1 mark: prevents collapse under tension.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between the contents of xylem and phloem.
parts.answer: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries sucrose and amino acids (in solution).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is it an advantage for a root hair cell to have a long, thin extension?
A It increases the surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions.
B It contains chloroplasts for photosynthesis in the soil.
C It reduces the distance that sucrose has to travel to the leaves.
D It lets the root hair cell take in water by active transport.
parts.answer: A It increases the surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions.
parts.working: The extension greatly increases the surface area in contact with soil water, so more water (by osmosis) and ions (by active transport) can be absorbed. Root hair cells have no chloroplasts (B), and water enters by osmosis, not active transport (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water enters a root hair cell from the soil.
parts.answer: By osmosis: the soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap, so water moves in through the partially permeable cell membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: osmosis; 1 mark: from higher water potential (soil) to lower (cell) through partially permeable membrane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the route taken by water from the root hair cell to the leaf.
parts.answer: Through the root cortex cells; into the xylem in the centre of the root; up the xylem in the stem to the leaf; into mesophyll cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three in order: root cortex; xylem; stem xylem to leaf; mesophyll cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chilli seedlings were pulled from a nursery bed and replanted in a field. Many of them wilted for several days. Explain why.
parts.answer: Pulling up the seedlings damaged or tore off many root hairs; the surface area for water absorption was reduced; transpiration from the leaves continued, so water loss was greater than uptake and the cells lost turgor.
parts.working: 1 mark each: root hairs damaged/lost; less surface area for absorption; water loss by transpiration exceeds uptake → wilting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two things the farmer could do to reduce wilting after transplanting.
parts.answer: Lift seedlings with soil around the roots; transplant in the evening or on a cool, cloudy day; remove some leaves; water the field well; give shade for the first few days.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two, each linked to protecting root hairs or reducing transpiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seedlings recover after about a week.
parts.answer: New root hairs grow, restoring the surface area for water uptake.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substances are all present in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule of a healthy person?
A glucose, protein and urea
B glucose, salts and urea
C protein, red blood cells and water
D red blood cells, salts and water
parts.answer: B glucose, salts and urea
parts.working: Small molecules and ions (water, glucose, salts, urea) are filtered from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule. Proteins and red blood cells are too large to pass through the filter, so A, C and D are wrong; A is the main distractor because glucose and urea are filtered but protein is not.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where in the kidney does filtration of blood take place?
A from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule
B from the loop of Henle into the collecting duct
C from the collecting duct into the ureter
D from the renal vein into the renal artery
parts.answer: A from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule
parts.working: Blood at high pressure in the glomerulus is filtered into the Bowman's capsule. The collecting duct carries urine towards the ureter (C) but no filtration occurs there.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is completely reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule of a healthy person?
A urea
B glucose
C protein
D water
parts.answer: B glucose
parts.working: All the filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (by active transport). Protein is not filtered at all, so it cannot be reabsorbed (C); water is reabsorbed in several regions and not completely (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The concentration of urea in a person's blood plasma is 0.25 g/dm³ and in their urine is 18.0 g/dm³. How many times more concentrated is urea in the urine than in the plasma?
A 4.5
B 17.75
C 72
D 450
parts.working: 18.0 ÷ 0.25 = 72. The urea is concentrated because most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed while urea is not. 17.75 is the difference, not the ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the structures that urine passes through from a kidney to the outside of the body.
parts.answer: Ureter → bladder → urethra.
parts.working: 2 marks all three in correct order; 1 mark for three names in the wrong order or two in correct order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings blood to the kidney and the vessel that takes blood away.
parts.answer: Renal artery brings blood; renal vein takes it away.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define excretion.
parts.answer: The removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements from the body.
parts.working: 1 mark: removal of waste products of metabolism (e.g. urea, CO₂); 1 mark: and substances in excess of requirements.

stem:
The table shows the concentrations of some substances in the blood plasma, in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule and in the urine of a healthy person (g/dm³).
Substance | plasma | filtrate | urine
protein | 80.0 | 0.0 | 0.0
glucose | 1.0 | 1.0 | 0.0
urea | 0.3 | 0.3 | 20.0
salts | 7.2 | 7.2 | 15.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is no protein in the filtrate.
parts.answer: Protein molecules are too large to pass through the filter (the walls of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule), so they stay in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: protein molecules too large; 1 mark: cannot pass through glomerulus / capsule wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why glucose is present in the filtrate but absent from the urine.
parts.answer: Glucose molecules are small enough to be filtered; all of the glucose is reabsorbed into the blood (in the proximal convoluted tubule).
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose filtered (small molecule); 1 mark: all reabsorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the filtrate. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 67 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of urea increases as the filtrate passes along the nephron.
parts.answer: Most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed into the blood, but urea is not (or only a little), so the same amount of urea is in a much smaller volume.
parts.working: 1 mark: water reabsorbed; 1 mark: urea not reabsorbed / stays in tubule.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an adult, about 180 dm³ of filtrate is formed in the kidneys each day, but only about 1.5 dm³ of urine is produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the filtered water that is reabsorbed into the blood. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that so much of the filtered water is reabsorbed.
parts.answer: Otherwise the body would lose huge volumes of water each day and quickly become dehydrated; reabsorption keeps the water content (water potential) of the blood constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: prevents dehydration / huge water loss; 1 mark: keeps blood water content/water potential constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: On a very hot day a farm worker in Jacobabad sweats heavily and drinks little water. Describe and explain how the volume and concentration of the worker's urine change.
parts.answer: Smaller volume of urine; more concentrated (darker); because water is lost in sweat, the kidneys reabsorb more water from the filtrate back into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller volume; 1 mark: more concentrated; 1 mark: more water reabsorbed in the kidney to conserve water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the parts of a nephron that filtrate passes through after leaving the Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: Proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct.
parts.working: 3 marks all four in correct order; 2 marks three in order; 1 mark two in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the part of the nephron where all the glucose is reabsorbed.
parts.answer: Proximal convoluted tubule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two substances, other than glucose, that are reabsorbed from the filtrate.
parts.answer: Water and salts (ions); also amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A teacher prepared three samples of artificial 'urine' (1, 2 and 3) to represent samples from three patients. A student tested each with Benedict's solution and with biuret solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student would test each sample for glucose and what a positive result would look like.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the sample; heat in a water-bath at about 80 °C for a few minutes; a positive result is a colour change from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red.
parts.working: 1 mark: Benedict's solution; 1 mark: heat in water-bath; 1 mark: blue → green/yellow/orange/brick-red.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sample 2 gave an orange-red colour with Benedict's solution. Suggest what this indicates about the person.
parts.answer: Glucose is present in the urine, which suggests the person may have diabetes (type 1) – blood glucose is too high and not all is reabsorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose present; 1 mark: possible diabetes / high blood glucose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sample 3 gave a purple colour with biuret solution. Suggest what this shows and why it is a cause for concern.
parts.answer: Protein is present in the urine; protein is normally too large to be filtered, so the filter in the kidneys may be damaged (kidney disease).
parts.working: 1 mark: protein present; 1 mark: suggests damage to glomeruli/kidney filtration.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one safety precaution when carrying out these tests.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection / gloves; use a water-bath not a direct flame; handle hot tubes with a holder.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the excretory product removed by the lungs and the process that produces it.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide; (aerobic) respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances removed from the blood by the kidneys.
parts.answer: Urea, excess water, excess (salts) ions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organ where urea is made.
parts.answer: Liver.

stem:
A volunteer emptied their bladder and then drank 1 dm³ of water. Urine was collected every 30 minutes for 3 hours. On another day the same volunteer drank 1 dm³ of salt solution and the experiment was repeated.
Time period (min) | urine after water (cm³) | urine after salt solution (cm³)
0–30 | 40 | 40
30–60 | 250 | 55
60–90 | 310 | 60
90–120 | 140 | 50
120–150 | 60 | 45
150–180 | 45 | 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of urine produced in 3 hours after drinking (i) water and (ii) salt solution.
parts.answer: (i) 845 cm³; (ii) 290 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark each: sum of the six readings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the differences between the two sets of results.
parts.answer: After water, urine output rose to a peak of 310 cm³ at 60–90 min then fell; after salt solution the output stayed low (40–60 cm³) throughout; total volume about three times greater after water.
parts.working: 1 mark: water gives much larger volume / peak at 60–90 min; 1 mark: salt gives small, steady volume, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the results after drinking water.
parts.answer: Water absorbed from the gut raised the water content (water potential) of the blood; the kidneys reabsorbed less water from the filtrate; so a large volume of dilute urine was produced, returning blood water content to normal.
parts.working: 1 mark each: blood water content/water potential increased; less water reabsorbed in kidney; large volume of dilute urine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the volunteer emptied their bladder at the start of the experiment.
parts.answer: So that only urine produced during the experiment was collected and measured.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why red blood cells and plasma proteins are not found in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: They are too large to pass through the walls of the glomerulus capillaries and the Bowman's capsule, so they remain in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: too large; 1 mark: cannot pass through glomerulus/capsule walls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why blood in the glomerulus is at high pressure and why this is important.
parts.answer: The vessel leaving the glomerulus is narrower than the one entering it (and the renal artery comes directly from the aorta); the high pressure forces small molecules and water out of the blood into the capsule (filtration).
parts.working: 1 mark: cause – narrower exit vessel / close to aorta; 1 mark: pressure forces fluid out → filtration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region of the kidney in which the glomeruli are found.
parts.answer: Cortex.

stem:
The table shows whether glucose was found in the urine of a person at different blood glucose concentrations.
Blood glucose (mmol/dm³): 5, 8, 10, 12, 15
Glucose in urine: none, none, none, small amount, large amount

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between blood glucose concentration and glucose in the urine.
parts.answer: No glucose appears in the urine until the blood glucose concentration rises above about 10 mmol/dm³; above this, the amount of glucose in the urine increases as blood glucose increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: none up to 10 mmol/dm³; 1 mark: increasing glucose in urine above 10 / at 12 and 15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for these results in terms of how the nephron handles glucose.
parts.answer: All glucose in the blood is filtered into the nephron; reabsorption of glucose is by active transport with carrier proteins, which have a maximum rate; above about 10 mmol/dm³ more glucose is filtered than can be reabsorbed, so the excess stays in the filtrate and appears in urine.
parts.working: 1 mark each: glucose filtered in proportion to blood concentration; reabsorption by active transport / carriers limited; excess not reabsorbed → in urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person with untreated type 1 diabetes often produces large volumes of urine and feels very thirsty.
parts.answer: Glucose left in the filtrate lowers its water potential, so less water is reabsorbed by osmosis; large volumes of urine lose water, so the person becomes dehydrated and thirsty.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose in filtrate reduces water reabsorption (osmosis); 1 mark: more water lost → thirst.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A longitudinal section of a kidney shows an outer region, an inner region and a hollow space that leads into a tube. Name these three parts.
parts.answer: Cortex (outer); medulla (inner); pelvis leading to the ureter.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cortex; medulla; ureter (accept renal pelvis/ureter for the space and tube).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which parts of the nephrons lie in the medulla.
parts.answer: The loops of Henle (and collecting ducts).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each kidney contains about one million nephrons. Suggest why so many are needed.
parts.answer: To give a very large surface area / capacity for filtering the large volume of blood (about 180 dm³ filtrate per day) and for reabsorption.
parts.working: 1 mark: large total area for filtration/reabsorption; 1 mark: large volume of blood processed.

stem:
Six students measured the total volume of urine they produced in one 24-hour period.
Student: A, B, C, D, E, F
Volume (cm³): 1450, 1620, 980, 1800, 1350, 1520

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume of urine produced per student. Give your answer to the nearest cm³.
parts.answer: 1453 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Student C produced the smallest volume. Suggest two reasons for this.
parts.answer: Drank less water; did more exercise or was in a hot place so lost more water in sweat; ate salty food.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one variable that should be controlled to compare students fairly.
parts.answer: Volume of water drunk; amount of exercise; temperature of surroundings; the 24-hour period used.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria. Explain why.
parts.answer: These cells reabsorb glucose (and some ions) by active transport, against a concentration gradient; active transport needs energy; the energy is released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reabsorption of glucose/ions by active transport; requires energy; mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: These cells also have microvilli on the surface facing the filtrate. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Microvilli increase the surface area for reabsorption.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what would happen to the glucose content of urine if a poison stopped respiration in these cells.
parts.answer: Glucose would appear in the urine, because without energy it could not be reabsorbed by active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose in urine; 1 mark: no energy → no active transport.

stem: In a healthy adult, the kidneys produce filtrate at a rate of about 125 cm³ per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of filtrate produced in one day, in dm³.
parts.answer: 180 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The filtrate contains glucose at 1.0 g/dm³. Calculate the mass of glucose filtered each day and state how much of it is normally lost in the urine.
parts.answer: 180 g filtered; none (0 g) is lost in urine
parts.working: 1 mark: 180 × 1.0 = 180 g; 1 mark: 0 g – all reabsorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the body must reabsorb this glucose.
parts.answer: Glucose is needed for respiration to release energy; losing 180 g a day would waste a large energy source / blood glucose would fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose used in respiration / energy; 1 mark: loss would be wasteful / would lower blood glucose.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain two differences between the composition of blood in the renal artery and in the renal vein of a healthy person.
parts.answer: Urea concentration is lower in the renal vein, because urea is filtered out and not reabsorbed (removed in urine). Oxygen concentration is lower (and carbon dioxide higher) in the renal vein, because kidney cells use oxygen in respiration, especially for active transport. (Also: less water / fewer excess ions in the renal vein because they are removed in urine.)
parts.working: For each of two differences: 1 mark for the difference with direction, 1 mark for the explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the kidneys receive about a fifth of the blood pumped by the heart at rest, although they make up less than 1 % of body mass.
parts.answer: The whole blood volume must be filtered many times a day to remove urea and keep water and ion content constant; a large blood flow keeps filtration and removal of waste fast.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood needs to be filtered frequently / large volume processed; 1 mark: to keep removing urea / regulate water and ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which organ is urea formed?
A kidney
B liver
C bladder
D pancreas
parts.answer: B liver
parts.working: Urea is made in the liver from the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids (deamination). The kidney removes urea from the blood but does not make it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is deamination?
A the breakdown of proteins into amino acids in the small intestine
B the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea
C the filtration of urea from the blood in the kidney
D the joining of amino acids to make proteins in the liver
parts.answer: B the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea
parts.working: Deamination occurs in the liver: the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids is removed and converted to urea. A describes digestion; D describes protein synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person eats a meal rich in protein. One hour later, in which blood vessel will the concentration of urea be highest?
A hepatic portal vein
B hepatic vein
C renal vein
D pulmonary artery
parts.answer: B hepatic vein
parts.working: Urea is made in the liver and released into the blood leaving it, so the hepatic vein carries blood with the highest urea concentration. The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut to the liver, before urea is added; the renal vein has had urea removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why excess amino acids cannot be kept in the body for later use.
parts.answer: Amino acids cannot be stored in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the liver.
parts.answer: They are deaminated: the nitrogen-containing part is removed and converted into urea; the remaining part can be used in respiration for energy (or converted to carbohydrate / glycogen or fat).
parts.working: 1 mark: deamination; 1 mark: nitrogen-containing part → urea; 1 mark: rest used for respiration / energy / converted and stored.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how urea leaves the liver.
parts.answer: Dissolved in the blood plasma (in the hepatic vein).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route taken by a urea molecule from the liver to the kidney. Name the blood vessels and the chambers of the heart it passes through.
parts.answer: Hepatic vein → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → renal artery → kidney.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: hepatic vein and vena cava; right side of heart and pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary vein and left side of heart; aorta and renal artery. Order must be correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the vessel that carries urea out of the kidney to the bladder.
parts.answer: Ureter (urea dissolved in urine).

stem:
A dietitian measured the mass of urea excreted per day by one adult on three different diets.
Protein eaten (g per day): 40, 80, 120
Urea excreted (g per day): 9.5, 18.8, 28.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in urea excreted when protein intake rose from 40 g to 120 g per day. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of urea excreted per gram of protein eaten on the 120 g diet. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.24 g urea per g protein

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the relationship shown in the table.
parts.answer: More protein eaten → more amino acids absorbed than the body needs; the excess amino acids cannot be stored and are deaminated in the liver; so more urea is formed and excreted by the kidneys.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more amino acids absorbed than needed; excess deaminated in liver; more urea made → more excreted (urea roughly proportional to protein).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why some urea is still excreted on a diet with very little protein.
parts.answer: Body proteins are continually broken down / some amino acids are always deaminated, e.g. from the turnover of cells.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why urea must be removed from the body.
parts.answer: Urea is toxic; if it builds up in the blood it can damage cells / tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: toxic; 1 mark: build-up would harm cells / change water potential of blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some people with kidney failure have to limit the amount of protein they eat. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Less protein means fewer excess amino acids to deaminate, so less urea is made, which the damaged kidneys cannot remove properly.
parts.working: 1 mark: less protein → less deamination → less urea; 1 mark: kidneys cannot remove urea efficiently, so it would build up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After digestion, amino acids are taken to the liver in the hepatic portal vein. State two uses of these amino acids in the liver or the body, other than forming urea.
parts.answer: Making proteins, e.g. plasma proteins such as fibrinogen; making enzymes; growth and repair of cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the term used for the movement of digested food molecules into cells, where they are used and become part of the cells.
parts.answer: Assimilation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the liver does with excess glucose after a meal.
parts.answer: Converts it into glycogen and stores it.

stem:
The enzyme urease breaks down urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. A student mixed 5 cm³ of three urine samples (A, B and C) each with 1 cm³ of urease solution and three drops of phenol red indicator at 30 °C. Phenol red is yellow in acidic or neutral solution and turns pink in alkaline solution. The time for each mixture to turn pink was recorded.
Sample A: 45 s; sample B: 120 s; sample C: 80 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction for each sample, using rate = 1000 ÷ time. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: A: 22.2; B: 8.3; C: 12.5 (arbitrary units)
parts.working: 2 marks all three correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which sample contained the most urea and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Sample A; it changed colour fastest, so ammonia (alkali) was produced fastest because there was most urea for the enzyme to act on.
parts.working: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: shortest time / fastest rate because more substrate (urea) → more ammonia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the indicator changed colour.
parts.answer: Urease breaks down urea into ammonia (and carbon dioxide); ammonia makes the solution alkaline, turning phenol red from yellow to pink.
parts.working: 1 mark: urea → ammonia; 1 mark: alkaline → colour change.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State three variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of urine sample; volume/concentration of urease; volume of indicator; temperature; pH at start.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the concentrations of glucose and urea in the blood of the hepatic portal vein and of the hepatic vein one hour after a meal of rice and chicken.
parts.answer: Glucose: higher in the hepatic portal vein than in the hepatic vein. Urea: lower in the hepatic portal vein than in the hepatic vein.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a).
parts.answer: The hepatic portal vein brings glucose and amino acids absorbed from the small intestine; the liver removes excess glucose and stores it as glycogen; the liver deaminates excess amino acids and adds urea to the blood leaving in the hepatic vein.
parts.working: 1 mark each: portal vein carries absorbed food; excess glucose stored as glycogen; urea produced by deamination added to hepatic vein blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient has severe liver damage. Tests show that the concentration of urea in their blood is lower than normal but the concentration of amino acids is higher than normal. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: The damaged liver cannot deaminate amino acids efficiently; so amino acids build up in the blood; and less urea is formed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reduced deamination by liver; amino acids accumulate; less urea produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the patient's urine contains less urea than normal even though their kidneys are healthy.
parts.answer: Less urea is made by the liver, so less is filtered into the urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Doctors advise this patient to eat only a moderate amount of protein. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Excess amino acids cannot be dealt with properly by the damaged liver, so eating less protein reduces the amount of excess amino acids (and nitrogenous waste) building up.
parts.working: 1 mark: liver cannot process excess amino acids; 1 mark: less protein reduces the build-up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lion eats mainly meat. A goat eats mainly grass and leaves. Suggest which animal produces more urea per kilogram of body mass. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The lion; meat is rich in protein, so it absorbs more amino acids than it needs; the excess is deaminated in the liver, forming more urea.
parts.working: 1 mark: lion; 1 mark: high-protein diet / more excess amino acids; 1 mark: deamination → more urea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that removes urea from the blood in both animals.
parts.answer: Kidney.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the food chain  mango leaves → caterpillar → myna bird → hawk, what do the arrows show?
A the direction in which energy is transferred
B which organism is the largest
C the direction in which carbon dioxide moves
D the order in which the organisms arrived in the habitat
parts.answer: A the direction in which energy is transferred
parts.working: Arrows in a food chain point from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it, showing the transfer of energy. They do not show size (B).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a pond food web, algae are eaten by water fleas and by tadpoles; water fleas are eaten by small fish; tadpoles are eaten by water beetles; small fish and water beetles are eaten by herons. Herons also eat tadpoles. At which trophic levels does the heron feed?
A second only
B third only
C third and fourth
D fourth and fifth
parts.answer: C third and fourth
parts.working: Algae (1st) → tadpole (2nd) → heron gives heron at the 3rd level; algae → water flea → small fish → heron or algae → tadpole → water beetle → heron gives the 4th level. The heron is a secondary and a tertiary consumer, so 'third only' is incomplete.

stem:
A food web in a freshwater lake in Sindh is described below.
Algae are eaten by snails and by mosquito larvae.
Mosquito larvae are eaten by small fish.
Snails are eaten by ducks.
Small fish are eaten by kingfishers and herons.
Herons also eat ducks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the producer in this food web.
parts.answer: Algae (water plants).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one primary consumer and one secondary consumer.
parts.answer: Primary: snail or mosquito larva. Secondary: small fish (also duck, which eats snails).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the principal source of energy for this food web.
parts.answer: The Sun (light energy).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Fishermen remove most of the small fish from the lake. Suggest and explain two effects on other organisms in the web.
parts.answer: Any two, each with a reason: kingfishers decrease because they lose their only food; mosquito larvae increase because fewer are eaten by small fish; herons eat more ducks, so the duck population falls (and snails may then increase); algae decrease because the larger number of mosquito larvae eat more of them.
parts.working: For each of two effects: 1 mark effect, 1 mark matching explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why only a small proportion of the energy in one trophic level is transferred to the next.
parts.answer: Not all of the organism is eaten (e.g. roots, bones); not all that is eaten is digested and absorbed – some is lost in faeces; much energy is used in respiration and lost as heat (movement, keeping warm); energy remains in dead organisms and waste, passing to decomposers; energy is lost in excretory products such as urea.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
parts.answer: So much energy is lost at each transfer that after four or five levels there is too little energy left to support another population of animals.
parts.working: 1 mark: energy lost at each level; 1 mark: too little left to support a further level.

stem: In a mangrove ecosystem, dead mangrove leaves fall into the water. Crabs and bacteria feed on the leaves. Shrimps and small fish feed on the bacteria and on small pieces of leaf. Large fish such as groupers eat the crabs, shrimps and small fish.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what would happen to the energy in the dead leaves of the mangroves if there were no crabs or decomposers.
parts.answer: The energy would stay locked in the dead leaves; it would not be passed on to other organisms in the food web (and nutrients would not be recycled).
parts.working: 1 mark: energy not transferred / stays in dead material; 1 mark: other organisms (e.g. shrimps, fish) lose a food source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mangrove forests along the coast near Karachi have been cut down. Suggest and explain the effect on the number of large fish caught offshore.
parts.answer: Fewer mangroves → less dead leaf material for crabs and shrimps (and less nursery habitat for young fish) → fewer small fish/shrimps for large fish to eat → fewer large fish caught.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer producers / less leaf litter; fewer primary/secondary consumers; fewer large fish because less food (or loss of breeding habitat).

parts.label: c
