parts.text: Suggest why the crab is described as both a decomposer-feeder (detritivore) and a primary consumer in this web.
parts.answer: It feeds on dead plant material (leaves), which came from producers, so it gets energy from producers at the second trophic level.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms producer and consumer.
parts.answer: Producer: an organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually using energy from sunlight, through photosynthesis. Consumer: an organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term decomposer and state its role in an ecosystem.
parts.answer: An organism that gets its energy from dead or waste organic material; it breaks this down and releases nutrients (e.g. ammonium, carbon dioxide) back into the environment for recycling.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition; 1 mark: recycles nutrients / releases CO₂ and mineral ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why energy is described as flowing through an ecosystem whereas nutrients such as carbon are described as cycling.
parts.answer: Energy enters as light and is eventually lost as heat, so it cannot be reused; carbon atoms are passed between organisms and the environment and used again and again.
parts.working: 1 mark: energy enters from Sun and leaves as heat (not recycled); 1 mark: nutrients recycled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Snow leopards are top carnivores in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan. They feed on ibex and markhor, which eat grasses and shrubs. Explain, in terms of energy flow, why each snow leopard needs a very large hunting area.
parts.answer: Energy is lost at each transfer between trophic levels (heat from respiration, waste, parts not eaten); so only a small fraction of the energy fixed by the plants reaches the snow leopard (third trophic level); plant growth in cold mountains is low, so a large area of plants and many prey animals are needed to supply enough energy for one leopard.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: energy lost at each transfer; little energy reaches the top level; many prey / large area of producers needed per leopard; low productivity of mountain vegetation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to suggest why top carnivores are often among the first animals to become endangered when their habitat is reduced.
parts.answer: Their populations are already small because little energy reaches them; losing habitat removes prey and hunting area, so the population quickly becomes too small to survive.
parts.working: 1 mark: small populations at top trophic level; 1 mark: habitat loss reduces prey / area below what is needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the trophic level of the snow leopard in this food chain.
parts.answer: Third trophic level (secondary consumer).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a sigmoid population growth curve of bacteria in a flask, which phase comes immediately after the lag phase?
A death phase
B stationary phase
C exponential (log) phase
D a second lag phase
parts.answer: C exponential (log) phase
parts.working: The order is lag → exponential (log) → stationary → death. The stationary phase follows the exponential phase, not the lag phase, and the death phase comes last.

stem:
Yeast cells were added to a flask of glucose solution at 25 °C. Samples were counted every 2 hours.
Time (h): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14
Number of yeast cells (thousands per mm³): 2, 3, 8, 25, 60, 92, 98, 97

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in yeast numbers between 4 and 8 hours, in thousand cells per mm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 13 thousand cells per mm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the phases of growth shown between 0–2 hours and between 10–14 hours.
parts.answer: 0–2 h: lag phase; 10–14 h: stationary phase.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the population stopped increasing after 12 hours.
parts.answer: Glucose (food) was being used up; toxic waste products such as ethanol built up; the birth (reproduction) rate became equal to the death rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: limited food/glucose; accumulation of toxic waste (ethanol, CO₂); competition; reproduction rate = death rate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the population if counting continued for several more days. Give a reason.
parts.answer: The population would decrease (death phase) because food runs out and toxic waste increases, so death rate exceeds reproduction rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease / death phase; 1 mark: reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student estimated the number of dandelion plants on a school field of area 1200 m². She placed ten quadrats, each 0.25 m², on the field and counted the dandelions in each.
Counts: 3, 0, 5, 2, 4, 1, 6, 2, 3, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat.
parts.answer: 3.0 dandelions per quadrat

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelions per m².
parts.answer: 12 per m²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of dandelions on the field.
parts.answer: about 14 400 dandelions

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the student should decide where to place the quadrats.
parts.answer: Place them at random, e.g. use random numbers as coordinates on a grid of measuring tapes laid along two edges of the field; this avoids bias in choosing where to sample.
parts.working: 1 mark: random placement using random numbers/coordinates; 1 mark: avoids bias / representative sample.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest two ways the estimate could be made more reliable.
parts.answer: Use more quadrats; repeat on different days; use a larger quadrat; have clear rules for counting plants on the edge of the quadrat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four factors that affect the rate of growth of a population.
parts.answer: Food supply; competition; predation; disease (also availability of space, nesting sites, water).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The human population of the world grew slowly for thousands of years and then increased very rapidly in the last 200 years. Suggest two reasons for the rapid increase.
parts.answer: Better medical care / vaccines / antibiotics reducing death rate (especially infant mortality); improved food supply through modern agriculture; clean water and sanitation reducing disease.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After heavy rains, desert locusts in Balochistan and Sindh can increase from a few thousand to millions within months. Suggest two reasons for this rapid increase.
parts.answer: Plenty of fresh plant food after rain; moist soil for egg laying; few predators relative to locust numbers; locusts reproduce quickly with many eggs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the phase of a population growth curve that describes this rapid increase and explain what is happening to birth and death rates.
parts.answer: Exponential (log) phase; the birth (reproduction) rate is much greater than the death rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: exponential/log phase; 1 mark: birth rate greatly exceeds death rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three factors that eventually cause the swarm to decline.
parts.answer: Food runs out (vegetation eaten / dries up); increased predation by birds; disease spreading in crowded conditions; competition for food; insecticide spraying.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a population that has reached the stationary phase, compare the birth rate with the death rate.
parts.answer: The birth rate equals the death rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a predator–prey relationship affects the number of prey in a population of rabbits.
parts.answer: When predators (e.g. foxes) increase, more rabbits are eaten, so the rabbit population falls; with fewer rabbits, predators have less food and their numbers fall; then the rabbit population can increase again (numbers rise and fall in cycles).
parts.working: 1 mark each: more predators → fewer prey; fewer prey → fewer predators; prey numbers then rise again (cycle).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by a limiting factor for a population.
parts.answer: A factor that is in short supply and so restricts the growth of the population (e.g. food, space).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organisms in the root nodules of pea plants convert nitrogen gas into compounds the plant can use?
A nitrifying bacteria
B denitrifying bacteria
C nitrogen-fixing bacteria
D decomposing fungi
parts.answer: C nitrogen-fixing bacteria
parts.working: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium/nitrogen compounds. Nitrifying bacteria (A) live in the soil and convert ammonium ions to nitrate ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In waterlogged soil, which process is increased and makes the soil less fertile?
A denitrification of nitrate ions to nitrogen gas
B nitrification of ammonium ions to nitrate ions
C nitrogen fixation by lightning
D absorption of nitrate ions by root hairs
parts.answer: A denitrification of nitrate ions to nitrogen gas
parts.working: Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen; denitrifying bacteria thrive in anaerobic conditions and convert nitrate ions to nitrogen gas, which is lost from the soil. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so nitrification (B) decreases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how nitrogen in the proteins of dead leaves becomes nitrate ions in the soil. Name the types of organism involved.
parts.answer: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the proteins in dead leaves; they release ammonium ions (ammonification); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium ions into nitrite ions; and then into nitrate ions.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decomposers break down proteins / amino acids; ammonium ions released; nitrifying bacteria; ammonium → nitrite → nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how plants absorb nitrate ions and what they use them for.
parts.answer: By active transport into root hair cells; to make amino acids and then proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport through root hairs; 1 mark: amino acids / proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many farmers in Punjab grow a legume crop such as berseem clover or chickpea between wheat crops. Explain how this improves the yield of the next wheat crop.
parts.answer: Legumes have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria; these convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonium / nitrogen compounds used to make amino acids; when the legume roots and leftover plant parts are ploughed in, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria release nitrate ions into the soil; wheat absorbs the nitrate to make proteins, so it grows better.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: root nodules; nitrogen-fixing bacteria; N₂ → ammonium/nitrogen compounds; decomposition and nitrification add nitrate to soil; wheat uses nitrate for amino acids/proteins → growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of this method over using large amounts of nitrate fertiliser.
parts.answer: Cheaper; less nitrate washed (leached) into rivers, so less eutrophication; adds organic matter to the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two, or 2 marks for one fully explained point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ploughing and aerating soil increases the concentration of nitrate ions in it.
parts.answer: Ploughing lets oxygen into the soil; nitrifying bacteria need oxygen (aerobic) to convert ammonium ions into nitrate ions; and denitrifying bacteria, which work in anaerobic conditions, are less active.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more oxygen; nitrifying bacteria aerobic, more nitrification; less denitrification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one way, other than by bacteria, in which nitrogen gas in the air is fixed.
parts.answer: Lightning (or the industrial Haber process to make fertiliser).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in a plant protein can become part of a goat's muscle and later reach the soil.
parts.answer: The goat eats the plant; the protein is digested to amino acids, which are absorbed and assimilated into goat proteins (muscle); excess amino acids are deaminated and the nitrogen leaves in urea/urine, or when the goat dies decomposers break down its proteins, releasing ammonium ions to the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark each: feeding and digestion to amino acids; assimilation into goat protein; return via urea/excretion or death and decomposition to ammonium.

stem:
Researchers measured the nitrate concentration in the soil of two plots at the end of a season. One plot grew chickpeas; the other grew wheat only.
Chickpea plot: 42 mg nitrate per kg soil
Wheat-only plot: 28 mg nitrate per kg soil

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the nitrate concentration in the plot that grew chickpeas was greater than in the plot that grew wheat only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: Chickpeas are legumes with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules; the nitrogen compounds from their roots and remains were converted to nitrate by decomposers and nitrifying bacteria.
parts.working: 1 mark: nitrogen-fixing bacteria in nodules; 1 mark: decomposition / nitrification adds nitrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should have been the same for both plots to make the comparison valid.
parts.answer: Soil type; amount of fertiliser added; watering / rainfall; time of year sampled; depth of soil sampling.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the researchers could make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Take several soil samples from different places in each plot (and/or use several plots of each type) and calculate a mean.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A single neem tree supports 3000 caterpillars, which are eaten by 20 birds. What shape is the pyramid of numbers for this food chain?
A a normal pyramid, wide at the base and narrowing to the top
B narrow at the base, widest in the middle and narrower at the top
C widest at the top and narrowest at the base
D all three levels the same width
parts.answer: B narrow at the base, widest in the middle and narrower at the top
parts.working: One tree (narrow base), 3000 caterpillars (widest bar) and 20 birds (narrower). A pyramid of biomass for the same chain would have the normal shape (A), because the tree has a very large mass.

stem:
Energy in each trophic level of a grassland in kJ per m² per year:
Producers (grasses): 25 000
Primary consumers (grasshoppers): 2500
Secondary consumers (frogs): 200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from producers to primary consumers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from primary consumers to secondary consumers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to the energy that is not passed on from the primary consumers to the secondary consumers.
parts.answer: Used in respiration and lost as heat; lost in faeces (undigested food) and excretory products such as urea; parts not eaten / dead bodies pass to decomposers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For the food chain  rose bush → aphids → ladybirds, describe the shapes of the pyramid of numbers and the pyramid of biomass.
parts.answer: Pyramid of numbers: narrow base (one bush), very wide second bar (thousands of aphids), narrower top (ladybirds). Pyramid of biomass: normal pyramid – largest at the base (bush), smaller for aphids, smallest for ladybirds.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of biomass gives a more useful picture of the feeding relationships than a pyramid of numbers.
parts.answer: It takes account of the size (mass) of the organisms; one large producer is shown as large, so it shows how much living material is available at each level.
parts.working: 1 mark: accounts for size/mass of individuals; 1 mark: shows amount of material/energy available at each level.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of energy is never inverted.
parts.answer: Energy is lost at every transfer (respiration, heat, waste), so each level must contain less energy than the level below it.
parts.working: 1 mark: energy lost at each transfer; 1 mark: each level has less energy than the one it feeds on.

stem: A field of maize contains 50 000 kJ of energy in parts that humans can eat. If this maize is fed to cattle, only 4 % of the energy ends up in beef that humans eat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy that reaches humans as beef.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy humans would get by eating the maize directly.
parts.answer: 25 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why so little of the energy in the maize ends up in the beef.
parts.answer: Cattle use most of the energy in respiration for movement and to keep warm, which is lost as heat; some energy is lost in faeces and urine / methane; some energy is in parts of the cow that are not eaten (bones, skin).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ecologists sampled a small area of grassland and measured the dry biomass at each trophic level (g per m²).
Producers: 820
Primary consumers: 74
Secondary consumers: 9.2
Tertiary consumers: 1.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the biomass of primary consumers that is present as secondary consumers. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of producer biomass that is present as primary consumers. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the samples were dried before weighing.
parts.answer: The water content of organisms varies (e.g. with recent rain or drinking), so fresh mass is unreliable; dry mass measures only the organic material / biomass.
parts.working: 1 mark: water content varies; 1 mark: dry mass gives a fair comparison of biomass.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one disadvantage of measuring dry biomass.
parts.answer: The organisms must be killed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Grass in a field receives energy from the Sun. A herd of goats eats grass containing 18 000 kJ of energy, and 1620 kJ of this becomes goat biomass. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the trophic level of the goats.
parts.answer: Second trophic level (primary consumers).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why most of the energy in the grass did not become goat biomass.
parts.answer: Lost as heat from respiration / lost in faeces (cellulose not digested) / used for movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and two processes that add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Removes: photosynthesis. Adds: any two of respiration (by plants, animals and decomposers), combustion of fossil fuels or wood, decomposition.
parts.working: 1 mark: photosynthesis; 1 mark each for two adding processes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how carbon in a dead tree trunk can return to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Decomposers (fungi and bacteria) feed on the dead wood and respire, releasing carbon dioxide; or the wood is burnt (combustion).
parts.working: 1 mark: decomposers; 1 mark: respiration releases CO₂ (or combustion).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how carbon from plants that died millions of years ago is now being added to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: The plants were not fully decomposed and were fossilised to form coal, oil or gas; burning these fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: fossilisation into fossil fuels; 1 mark: combustion releases CO₂.

stem: A monitoring station in the northern hemisphere recorded the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air during one year. The highest reading, 424.6 ppm, was in May. The lowest, 418.9 ppm, was in September.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the highest and lowest carbon dioxide concentrations recorded during the year.
parts.answer: 5.7 ppm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the carbon dioxide concentration falls between May and September.
parts.answer: In the northern summer, longer days, more light and warmth mean more photosynthesis by plants (more leaves on trees); photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide faster than respiration (and decomposition) releases it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: summer conditions / more leaves; more photosynthesis; rate of CO₂ uptake exceeds release by respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The May reading in the following year was 427.1 ppm. Suggest two human activities that explain the year-on-year increase.
parts.answer: Combustion of fossil fuels (vehicles, power stations, industry); deforestation – fewer trees to photosynthesise, and burning of the cleared wood.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which term describes all the populations of different species living together in one area?
A habitat
B community
C ecosystem
D population
parts.answer: B community
parts.working: A community is all of the populations of different species in an ecosystem. An ecosystem (C) is the community together with its non-living environment, interacting with each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use examples from the Thar Desert to explain the meaning of each term: population, community, ecosystem.
parts.answer: Population: a group of organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time, e.g. all the chinkara gazelles in one part of the desert. Community: all the populations of different species there, e.g. gazelles, desert foxes, lizards, khejri trees and grasses together. Ecosystem: the community and its environment (sand, water, climate) interacting together.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct definition with a suitable example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two non-living (abiotic) factors in the desert ecosystem that affect the organisms living there.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature; rainfall / water availability; light intensity; wind; soil type / sand.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the water cycle, naming the processes by which water moves between living organisms, the land, the sea and the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from seas, lakes and soil; plants lose water vapour by transpiration; water vapour cools and condenses to form clouds; it falls as precipitation (rain or snow); water runs off into rivers and seas or soaks into the soil, where it is absorbed by roots.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: evaporation; transpiration; condensation; precipitation; run-off / infiltration and uptake by plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how cutting down a large area of forest in the northern hills could affect local rainfall.
parts.answer: Less transpiration from trees, so less water vapour enters the air; fewer clouds form, so local rainfall decreases.
parts.working: 1 mark: less transpiration; 1 mark: less water vapour/condensation → less rainfall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to test four separate food samples for (i) starch, (ii) reducing sugar, (iii) protein and (iv) fat. For each nutrient, name the reagent used and state the colour seen when the nutrient is present.
parts.answer: Starch: iodine solution → blue-black. Reducing sugar: Benedict's solution (heated) → green / yellow / orange / brick-red. Protein: biuret solution → purple (violet). Fat: ethanol (then water) → milky white emulsion.
parts.working: 1 mark per nutrient for the correct reagent AND the correct positive colour (4 × B1). Accept 'cloudy white' for the emulsion test; do not accept 'pink' for biuret.

stem: A student in Multan squeezes a ripe mango to obtain some juice. She wants to find out whether the juice contains reducing sugar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should carry out the Benedict's test on a sample of the juice.
parts.answer: Put about 2 cm³ of juice in a test-tube, add an equal volume of Benedict's solution, heat in a hot water-bath (about 80 °C) for a few minutes and record the colour.
parts.working: B1 add Benedict's solution to the juice; B1 heat in a (hot / boiling) water-bath; B1 heat for a stated time (e.g. 2–5 minutes) / observe colour change. Do not credit 'heat over a Bunsen flame' alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The juice turned from blue to brick-red. State what this shows.
parts.answer: The juice contains a reducing sugar (a large amount).
parts.working: B1 reducing sugar present; accept 'high concentration of reducing sugar'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution the student should take during this test.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection (goggles) / point the test-tube away from people / use a test-tube holder.
parts.working: B1 any one sensible precaution linked to heating.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A food sample is heated with Benedict's solution. Which final colour shows that the sample contains the most reducing sugar?
A blue
B green
C yellow
D brick-red
parts.answer: D brick-red
parts.working: Brick-red shows the highest concentration of reducing sugar; blue means none. Green and yellow show smaller amounts.

stem: A student places a few drops of iodine solution on each of two samples on a white tile: the cloudy water left after boiling rice, and a solution of table sugar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour the student would see if starch is present.
parts.answer: Blue-black.
parts.working: B1 blue-black; accept 'black' or 'dark blue'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student adds iodine solution to the sugar solution. State the colour seen and what this shows.
parts.answer: Stays orange-brown (yellow-brown); starch is absent.
parts.working: B1 orange / brown / yellow-brown colour; B1 no starch.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student uses a separate clean dropper for each sample.
parts.answer: To avoid contaminating one sample with another (which could give a false result).
parts.working: B1 idea of contamination / cross-contamination.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A breakfast in Lahore consists of a paratha fried in ghee, a boiled egg and a glass of lassi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the emulsion test could be used to show that the paratha contains fat.
parts.answer: Crush / cut the paratha and shake it with ethanol; pour the ethanol (liquid) into a tube of water; a milky white emulsion shows fat.
parts.working: B1 shake (crushed) food with ethanol; B1 add the ethanol to water (or add water); B1 cloudy / milky white = fat present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the reagent used to show that the egg contains protein and state the positive result.
parts.answer: Biuret solution; the colour changes from blue to purple.
parts.working: B1 biuret; B1 purple / violet / lilac.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student mixes some grated cheese with water to make a cheese solution for a protein test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the biuret test is carried out on the cheese solution.
parts.answer: Add (a few drops of) dilute sodium hydroxide and then (dilute) copper(II) sulfate solution — or add biuret solution — and shake; no heating.
parts.working: B1 add biuret reagent / sodium hydroxide + copper sulfate; B1 shake / mix and observe (no heating needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student also sets up a tube containing distilled water instead of cheese solution, and adds the same reagents. Explain why.
parts.answer: It is a control; it shows the colour of a negative result (blue), so any purple in the test tube must be due to protein in the cheese.
parts.working: B1 control / comparison; B1 shows the colour without protein / shows the reagent alone does not turn purple.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student heats 2 cm³ of each of five glucose solutions with 2 cm³ of Benedict's solution for 5 minutes in a boiling water-bath. She does the same with 2 cm³ of guava juice.
Glucose concentration / % : colour after 5 minutes
0 : blue
0.5 : green
1.0 : yellow
2.0 : orange
4.0 : brick-red
guava juice : yellow-orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table, estimate the concentration of glucose in the juice.
parts.answer: Between 1 % and 2 % (more than 1 %, less than 2 %).
parts.working: B1 range 1–2 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two variables that must be kept the same for every tube.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume of solution / volume of Benedict's solution / temperature of water-bath / heating time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two controlled variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change to the method that would give a more precise estimate.
parts.answer: Make more glucose standards at smaller intervals between 1 % and 2 % (e.g. 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8 %) / use a colorimeter instead of judging colour by eye.
parts.working: B1 any one valid improvement.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the student kept all the tubes in the same water-bath and recorded the colour after the same time.
parts.answer: Colour depends on temperature and time of heating; keeping them the same makes it a fair comparison so colour depends only on glucose concentration.
parts.working: B1 time / temperature affect the colour reached; B1 fair test / only glucose concentration varies.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
DCPIP is a blue solution that is decolourised by vitamin C. A student finds the volume of each liquid that must be added, drop by drop, to decolourise 1.0 cm³ of DCPIP.
Vitamin C solution, 1.0 mg/cm³ : 2.5 cm³
Fresh lemon juice : 4.0 cm³
Lemon juice boiled for 10 minutes : 6.4 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of vitamin C needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of the DCPIP solution.
parts.answer: 2.5 mg
parts.working: 1.0 mg/cm³ × 2.5 cm³ = 2.5 mg (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of vitamin C, in mg/cm³, in (i) the fresh lemon juice and (ii) the boiled lemon juice. Give (ii) to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: (i) 0.625 mg/cm³; (ii) 0.39 mg/cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in vitamin C concentration caused by boiling.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why a larger volume of boiled juice was needed.
parts.answer: Boiling destroys (breaks down) some of the vitamin C, so the juice has less vitamin C per cm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wants to show that roasted groundnuts (peanuts) contain fat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the test-tube used for the emulsion test must be dry when the crushed nuts are first shaken with ethanol.
parts.answer: Fat does not dissolve in water; any water present would form the emulsion too early / stop the fat dissolving in the ethanol, so the result would be unclear.
parts.working: B1 fat dissolves in ethanol (not in water); B1 water would interfere / give a false or unclear result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a milky white colour appears when the ethanol is poured into water.
parts.answer: The fat that was dissolved in ethanol comes out of solution because fat is insoluble in water; tiny droplets of fat are suspended (an emulsion), which scatter light and look cloudy.
parts.working: B1 fat insoluble in water / comes out of solution; B1 forms tiny droplets / emulsion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the ethanol should not be heated with a Bunsen burner.
parts.answer: Ethanol is flammable.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A food is tested. Results: iodine solution stays orange-brown; Benedict's solution stays blue after heating; biuret solution turns purple; the ethanol emulsion test gives a milky white layer. Which nutrients does the food contain?
A starch and protein
B protein and fat
C reducing sugar and fat
D starch only
parts.answer: B protein and fat
parts.working: Purple biuret = protein; milky emulsion = fat. Iodine orange-brown means no starch (so A and D are wrong) and Benedict's blue means no reducing sugar (so C is wrong).

stem: Two shops in Peshawar sell honey. A student wants to compare the amount of reducing sugar in each honey after diluting each with water in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Benedict's test is described as semi-quantitative. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: It gives an approximate idea of how much reducing sugar is present (by the colour reached), but not an exact concentration.
parts.working: B1 shows relative amount / range; B1 not an exact value (colours judged by eye).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the results of Benedict's tests on two honey samples could be made more quantitative.
parts.answer: Any two of: use a colorimeter to measure the colour; filter, dry and weigh the red precipitate; time how long each sample takes to change colour; compare with a range of glucose standards of known concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compares the amount of reducing sugar in apple, orange and pomegranate juice using the Benedict's test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: type of fruit juice. Dependent: colour of the Benedict's solution after heating (amount of reducing sugar).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of juice; volume of Benedict's solution; temperature of water-bath; time of heating; dilution of juice; size of test-tube.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why each juice should be tested three times.
parts.answer: To check the results are repeatable / to identify anomalous results.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student adds orange juice drop by drop from a dropping pipette to 1 cm³ of blue DCPIP solution, shaking after each drop, and counts the drops needed to decolourise it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to decide exactly when the DCPIP has been decolourised by orange juice.
parts.answer: The juice is coloured itself (orange), so the end-point colour is hard to judge / the colour fades gradually.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two other sources of error in the method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: e.g. size of drops varies → use a burette or graduated syringe; tube not shaken evenly → shake after every drop the same way; judging the colour → compare against a white background / a reference tube of decolourised DCPIP; juice left standing loses vitamin C → test immediately after squeezing.
parts.working: For each of two errors: B1 error, B1 matching improvement. Generic 'repeat it' alone scores 0.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A length of Visking tubing (a partially permeable membrane) is filled with a mixture of starch suspension and glucose solution. The tubing is rinsed and placed in a tube of distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the results of an iodine test and a Benedict's test on the water outside the tubing after 30 minutes. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Iodine: stays orange-brown — no starch, because starch molecules are too large to pass through the tubing. Benedict's: green/yellow/orange/red — reducing sugar present, because glucose molecules are small enough to diffuse out through the tubing.
parts.working: B1 iodine negative; B1 starch molecules too large; B1 Benedict's positive; B1 glucose small, diffuses through (partially permeable) tubing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what this model shows about digestion in the small intestine.
parts.answer: Large insoluble molecules like starch must be broken down into small soluble molecules (e.g. glucose) before they can be absorbed through the gut wall into the blood.
parts.working: B1 large molecules cannot be absorbed; B1 must be digested into small soluble molecules first.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the vitamin C content of freshly squeezed orange juice with orange juice that has been kept in an open glass at room temperature for 24 hours. Include the apparatus, method, variables to control, how results are recorded and how a conclusion is reached.
parts.answer: DCPIP titration: same volume of DCPIP; add each juice drop by drop from a burette/syringe until decolourised; record volume; repeat three times; less volume = more vitamin C.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: use DCPIP (blue, decolourised by vitamin C); fixed volume of DCPIP (e.g. 1 cm³) in a test-tube; add juice from burette / graduated pipette / syringe drop by drop, shaking; record volume of juice when blue colour disappears; same oranges / same juice divided into two portions; same temperature / same concentration of DCPIP; repeat at least three times and calculate a mean; a smaller volume of juice needed means more vitamin C; table with headings 'volume of juice / cm³' for each juice; safety: eye protection.

stem:
A student times how long it takes for Benedict's solution to show the first colour change (from blue to green) when heated with glucose solutions in a water-bath at 90 °C.
Glucose concentration / % : time / s
0.2 : 150
0.4 : 95
0.6 : 70
0.8 : 52
1.0 : 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in the results.
parts.answer: As glucose concentration increases, the time for the first colour change decreases (falling more slowly at higher concentrations).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of sugar-cane juice, diluted in the same way, took 80 s to show the first colour change. Assuming the change is linear between the two nearest readings, estimate the glucose concentration of the diluted juice. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why judging the 'first colour change' is a source of error and suggest how to reduce it.
parts.answer: The change is gradual and judged by eye, so it is subjective; compare against a reference tube / white background or use a colorimeter.
parts.working: B1 subjective / gradual; B1 improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Maize grains are soaked and left to germinate. A student crushes samples on day 0 and day 4 and tests them.
Day 0: iodine test blue-black; Benedict's test green.
Day 4: iodine test pale blue-black; Benedict's test brick-red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the results between day 0 and day 4.
parts.answer: Starch content decreases (blue-black becomes paler / orange-brown); reducing sugar increases (Benedict's goes from blue/green to orange/brick-red).
parts.working: B1 starch decreases; B1 reducing sugar increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain these changes.
parts.answer: Amylase (enzyme) becomes active in the germinating seed; it breaks down stored starch into maltose / reducing sugars; the sugars are soluble and are used in respiration to release energy for growth of the embryo.
parts.working: B1 enzyme / amylase; B1 starch → reducing sugar (maltose); B1 sugar used for respiration / energy / growth.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The same volume of DCPIP solution is decolourised by 2 cm³ of juice X but needs 8 cm³ of juice Y. Which statement is correct?
A Juice Y contains four times the concentration of vitamin C of juice X.
B Juice X contains four times the concentration of vitamin C of juice Y.
C Juice X contains twice the concentration of vitamin C of juice Y.
D Both juices contain the same mass of vitamin C per cm³.
parts.answer: B Juice X contains four times the concentration of vitamin C of juice Y.
parts.working: The same mass of vitamin C is needed each time. X supplies it in 2 cm³ and Y in 8 cm³, so X is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 times more concentrated. A is the common error of assuming a larger volume means more vitamin C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
parts.answer: Two strands coiled together to form a double helix; each strand contains chemicals called bases; bases on the two strands are joined in pairs (A with T, C with G).
parts.working: B1 two strands; B1 double helix; B1 bases pair / bonds between bases hold strands together; accept named pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One strand of a short piece of DNA has the base sequence A T G C C T A G. Write the sequence of bases on the complementary strand.
parts.answer: T A C G G A T C
parts.working: B1 all correct.

stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA from the cells of a goat is analysed. 22 % of the bases are adenine (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the percentage of thymine in this DNA. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 22 %; A always pairs with T, so there is the same amount of each.
parts.working: B1 22 %; B1 A pairs with T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cytosine in this DNA.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pairs of bases join together in a DNA molecule?
A A with C, and G with T
B A with G, and C with T
C A with T, and C with G
D A with A, and C with C
parts.answer: C A with T, and C with G
parts.working: Adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine. B pairs bases wrongly.

stem: A section of double-stranded DNA from a wheat plant contains 600 base pairs. 180 of the bases in this section are cytosine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of thymine bases in this section.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine bases in this section. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

author: HomiLabs

stem: One strand of a short piece of DNA has the sequence A T T G C A G C T A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the base sequence of the complementary strand.
parts.answer: T A A C G T C G A T

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the double-stranded piece, state the total number of adenine bases and the total number of guanine bases.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine in the double-stranded piece.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The base composition of DNA from two sources was measured.
Sample : A % : T % : C % : G %
P : 30 : 30 : 20 : 20
Q : 25 : 33 : 20 : 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, in double-stranded DNA, the percentage of adenine is always equal to the percentage of thymine.
parts.answer: Every A on one strand is paired with a T on the other strand (complementary base pairing), so the numbers must be equal.
parts.working: B1 A pairs with T; B1 one-to-one across the two strands.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which sample, P or Q, comes from a virus that has only a single strand of DNA. Give a reason using the data.
parts.answer: Q; its percentage of A (25) is not equal to T (33) and C (20) is not equal to G (22), so the bases are not paired.
parts.working: B1 Q; B1 A ≠ T / C ≠ G in Q (or A = T and C = G in P).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the chemical elements found in (i) carbohydrates, (ii) fats and (iii) proteins.
parts.answer: (i) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen; (ii) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen; (iii) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (some also sulfur).
parts.working: B1 each; (iii) must include nitrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the smaller molecules that join to make (i) proteins and (ii) fats.
parts.answer: (i) amino acids; (ii) fatty acids and glycerol.
parts.working: B1 each; (ii) needs both.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which smaller molecules join together to form glycogen?
A amino acids
B fatty acids and glycerol
C glucose
D sucrose
parts.answer: C glucose
parts.working: Glycogen, like starch and cellulose, is a chain of glucose molecules. Sucrose is a sugar made of two units and is not the building block.

stem: Water makes up about 60 % of the mass of an adult human body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water is important as a solvent in the human body. Give three examples.
parts.answer: Any three of: digested food molecules dissolve in water so they can be absorbed; plasma (mainly water) transports dissolved glucose, ions, hormones and CO₂; urea and other wastes are excreted dissolved in water (urine); enzyme reactions take place in solution in cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three examples linked to dissolving.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made from the same small molecule. Name it.
parts.answer: Glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each of starch, glycogen and cellulose, state whether it is found in plants or animals and give one role.
parts.answer: Starch: plants — energy store. Glycogen: animals (liver, muscles) — energy store. Cellulose: plants — forms cell walls.
parts.working: B1 each for correct location AND role.

stem: A scientist analyses two substances taken from the cells of a cow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Substance X contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur. Suggest which group of biological molecules X belongs to. Explain.
parts.answer: Protein; only proteins (of these groups) contain nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur).
parts.working: B1 protein; B1 reason about N / S.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Substance Y contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. It is insoluble in water, is stored in liver cells, and when broken down releases glucose. Identify Y and explain why being insoluble is useful for a storage molecule.
parts.answer: Glycogen; insoluble so it does not dissolve in cytoplasm / does not affect water movement by osmosis / cannot diffuse out of the cell.
parts.working: B1 glycogen; B1 does not affect osmosis / water potential; B1 stays in the cell / does not move out.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says 'proteins and carbohydrates contain exactly the same elements'. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Proteins also contain nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur); carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the order of amino acids in a protein can affect the way an enzyme works.
parts.answer: The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds and so the shape of the protein; the shape of the active site depends on this; a different order gives a different-shaped active site, so the substrate may not fit (not complementary) and the enzyme does not work.
parts.working: B1 sequence determines folding / shape; B1 active site shape; B1 substrate fits / complementary — changed order means it may not fit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fish has a single circulation and a mammal has a double circulation. Explain the difference between these two systems.
parts.answer: Single: blood passes through the heart once for each complete circuit of the body (heart → gills → body → heart). Double: blood passes through the heart twice for each circuit (once to the lungs, once to the rest of the body).
parts.working: B1 single = once through heart per circuit; B1 double = twice (pulmonary and systemic circuits).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a double circulation.
parts.answer: Blood can be pumped to the body at a higher pressure (after returning from the lungs), so oxygenated blood reaches tissues faster.
parts.working: B1; accept keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these structures in the order in which a red blood cell passes through them, starting at the vena cava:
left atrium, aorta, right ventricle, lungs, pulmonary vein, right atrium, left ventricle, pulmonary artery
parts.answer: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta
parts.working: B3 all correct; B2 one structure out of place; B1 the right side (RA → RV → pulmonary artery) or the left side correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in this pathway the blood becomes oxygenated.
parts.answer: In the lungs (capillaries around the alveoli).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood into the left atrium?
A aorta
B pulmonary artery
C pulmonary vein
D vena cava
parts.answer: C pulmonary vein
parts.working: The pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle.
parts.answer: The left ventricle pumps blood all round the body, which needs a higher pressure; the right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs (low pressure protects lung capillaries). Thicker wall = more muscle = stronger contraction.
parts.working: B1 left pumps to whole body / further; B1 needs higher pressure / more muscle for stronger contraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the septum.
parts.answer: Separates oxygenated blood (left side) from deoxygenated blood (right side), so they do not mix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the valves between the atria and the ventricles and state their function.
parts.answer: Atrioventricular valves (bicuspid on the left, tricuspid on the right); they prevent blood flowing back into the atria when the ventricles contract.
parts.working: B1 name; B1 prevent backflow into the atria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the semilunar valves at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery help the heart to work efficiently.
parts.answer: They close when the ventricles relax, so blood in the arteries cannot flow back into the ventricles; this keeps blood moving in one direction.
parts.working: B1 close when ventricles relax / pressure in artery higher; B1 prevent backflow into ventricles / one-way flow.

stem:
Five students at a school in Rawalpindi measure their pulse rate at rest and immediately after two minutes of skipping.
Student : resting / beats per min : after exercise / beats per min
1 : 72 : 128
2 : 68 : 120
3 : 75 : 134
4 : 70 : 126
5 : 65 : 117

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean resting pulse rate and the mean pulse rate after exercise.
parts.answer: Resting 70 beats/min; after exercise 125 beats/min
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean pulse rate. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: type of exercise; duration / intensity of exercise; time the pulse is counted for; time after exercise when pulse is measured; resting time before the first reading.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student counts her pulse for 15 seconds at one-minute intervals after running. Her resting rate is 72 beats per minute.
Time after running / min : beats in 15 s
0 : 31
1 : 27
2 : 24
3 : 21
4 : 30
5 : 18
6 : 18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each count into a pulse rate in beats per minute.
parts.working: Multiply each 15-second count by 4 (M1); all correct (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest one reason for it.
parts.answer: 4 minutes (120 beats/min); e.g. the student miscounted / moved or talked / lost the pulse / counted for longer than 15 s.
parts.working: B1 4 min reading; B1 plausible reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the results, state how long it took for the pulse rate to return to its resting value (72 beats/min).
parts.answer: 5 minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why counting for 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 is less accurate than counting for a full minute.
parts.answer: Any counting error is multiplied by 4 (a miss of one beat gives an error of 4 beats/min).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate increases during a game of football.
parts.answer: Muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose; faster heart rate delivers more blood (oxygen, glucose) to muscles; and removes more carbon dioxide (and heat) from them.
parts.working: B1 more respiration in muscles / more energy needed; B1 more oxygen and glucose delivered; B1 more carbon dioxide removed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the hormone that increases heart rate before the match begins.
parts.answer: Adrenaline.

stem:
Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute.
cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume
A trained athlete from Karachi has a resting heart rate of 52 beats/min and a stroke volume of 96 cm³. A student who does not train has a resting heart rate of 75 beats/min and a stroke volume of 66 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cardiac output of each person in dm³ per minute. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Athlete: 4.99 dm³/min; other student: 4.95 dm³/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the athlete has a lower resting heart rate but almost the same cardiac output.
parts.answer: Training has made the heart muscle stronger / larger, so each beat pumps more blood (larger stroke volume); fewer beats are needed to deliver the same volume of blood.
parts.working: B1 stronger / larger heart muscle; B1 larger stroke volume so fewer beats needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A doctor at a clinic in Hyderabad wants to check the heart of a patient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the activity of the heart can be monitored.
parts.answer: Measuring pulse rate (at wrist or neck); listening to the sounds of the valves closing with a stethoscope; electrocardiogram (ECG).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Some babies are born with a hole in the septum between the left and right ventricles. In some of these babies, deoxygenated blood passes through the hole from the right ventricle into the left ventricle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this affects the oxygen concentration of the blood in the aorta.
parts.answer: Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle mixes with oxygenated blood in the left ventricle; so blood in the aorta has a lower oxygen concentration than normal.
parts.working: B1 mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood; B1 lower oxygen in aorta / to body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two symptoms a baby with this condition might show.
parts.answer: Any two of: tiredness / lack of energy; breathlessness; slow growth / poor feeding; bluish skin or lips.
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to less oxygen reaching tissues.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row describes the valves while the ventricles are contracting and pumping blood out of the heart?
A atrioventricular valves open; semilunar valves open
B atrioventricular valves open; semilunar valves closed
C atrioventricular valves closed; semilunar valves open
D atrioventricular valves closed; semilunar valves closed
parts.answer: C atrioventricular valves closed; semilunar valves open
parts.working: As the ventricles contract the atrioventricular valves close to stop backflow into the atria, and the semilunar valves are pushed open so blood leaves through the arteries. B gives the opposite.

stem:
The table shows the pressure in the left ventricle and in the aorta during one heartbeat.
Time / s : left ventricle / kPa : aorta / kPa
0.0 : 1 : 11
0.1 : 8 : 10
0.2 : 16 : 15
0.3 : 15 : 14.5
0.4 : 9 : 13
0.5 : 2 : 12
0.6 : 1 : 11.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table, state the times at which the semilunar valve in the aorta is open. Explain how you decided.
parts.answer: 0.2 s and 0.3 s; this is when the pressure in the left ventricle is higher than the pressure in the aorta.
parts.working: B1 both times; B1 ventricle pressure greater than aortic pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the maximum and minimum pressure in the aorta.
parts.answer: 5 kPa

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pressure in the aorta never falls as low as the pressure in the left ventricle.
parts.answer: The semilunar valve closes so blood cannot flow back into the ventricle; the elastic wall of the aorta recoils, keeping pressure up between beats.
parts.working: B1 valve closes / prevents backflow; B1 elastic recoil of artery wall.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the part of the heart described by each statement.
(i) the chamber that pumps blood to the lungs
(ii) the chamber that receives blood from the vena cava
(iii) the wall of muscle that separates the left and right sides
(iv) the chamber with the thickest wall
parts.answer: (i) right ventricle; (ii) right atrium; (iii) septum; (iv) left ventricle
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the length of time spent exercising affects a person's heart rate. Include what you would measure, how you would make it a fair test, how you would record the results and how you would reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Measure resting pulse; do the same exercise (e.g. step-ups at a fixed rate) for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 minutes; measure pulse immediately afterwards for 1 minute; rest until pulse returns to resting before the next trial; repeat and calculate means; plot pulse against time.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: measure resting pulse first; independent variable – exercise times (at least 4 values); same type and intensity of exercise (e.g. step height and rate set by a metronome); measure pulse at wrist/neck for 60 s (or with a pulse monitor) immediately after; rest until pulse returns to resting rate between trials; same person / same conditions (same time of day, no food or drink); repeat each time and calculate a mean; table: exercise time / min against pulse rate / beats per min; conclusion from graph trend; safety: stop if dizzy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence shows the path of blood in the circulation of a fish?
A heart → gills → body → heart
B heart → body → gills → heart
C heart → gills → heart → body → heart
D heart → lungs → heart → body → heart
parts.answer: A heart → gills → body → heart
parts.working: A fish has a single circulation: blood goes from the heart to the gills, then directly to the body and back to the heart. C and D describe a double circulation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare arteries, veins and capillaries by stating for each: the relative thickness of the wall, the size of the lumen, and whether valves are present.
parts.answer: Arteries: thick muscular elastic wall, narrow lumen, no valves (except at base of aorta/pulmonary artery). Veins: thin wall, wide (large) lumen, valves present. Capillaries: wall one cell thick, very narrow lumen, no valves.
parts.working: B1 per vessel with all three features correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a capillary is related to its function.
parts.answer: Wall is one cell thick so diffusion distance is short; substances (oxygen, glucose) diffuse quickly into tissues / narrow lumen brings red cells close to tissue cells.
parts.working: B1 thin wall / one cell thick; B1 short diffusion distance / exchange of materials.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function.
parts.answer: Thick muscular and elastic wall withstands high pressure from the heart; elastic tissue stretches and recoils to maintain pressure / smooth flow.
parts.working: B1 thick wall withstands high pressure; B1 elastic recoil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why veins have valves.
parts.answer: Blood in veins is at low pressure; valves prevent backflow (keep blood moving towards the heart).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel carries blood from the small intestine to the liver?
A hepatic artery
B hepatic portal vein
C hepatic vein
D renal vein
parts.answer: B hepatic portal vein
parts.working: The hepatic portal vein carries blood rich in absorbed food from the gut to the liver. The hepatic vein carries blood away from the liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the blood vessel that:
(i) carries blood to a kidney
(ii) carries blood away from the liver
(iii) carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs
(iv) carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the body
parts.answer: (i) renal artery; (ii) hepatic vein; (iii) pulmonary artery; (iv) aorta
parts.working: B1 each.

stem:
The mean blood pressure was measured in different vessels of a person at rest.
Vessel : mean pressure / kPa
aorta : 13
large arteries : 12
arterioles : 7
capillaries : 3
large veins : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in pressure between the aorta and the capillaries. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Blood pressure in large veins is very low. Explain how blood in the leg veins is still returned to the heart.
parts.answer: Valves in veins prevent backflow; contraction of skeletal muscles around the veins squeezes them and pushes blood towards the heart; wide lumen gives little resistance to flow.
parts.working: B1 valves prevent backflow; B1 skeletal muscle contraction squeezes veins; B1 wide lumen / low resistance.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rings of the same width were cut from an artery and a vein from a goat (from a butcher). Each ring was hung from a hook, its length measured, a 50 g mass hung on it, and the length measured again. The mass was then removed.
Ring : length at start / mm : length with mass / mm : length after mass removed / mm
artery : 20 : 26 : 20.5
vein : 20 : 33 : 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in length of each ring when the mass was added.
parts.answer: Artery: 30 %; vein: 65 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the results, compare the elasticity of the two rings and explain why this property of the artery wall is useful.
parts.answer: The artery ring stretched less and returned almost to its original length (20.5 mm), so its wall is elastic; the vein ring stayed stretched (30 mm), so it is much less elastic. Elastic recoil of the artery wall helps keep blood pressure up and blood flowing smoothly between heartbeats.
parts.working: B1 artery recoils almost fully / more elastic than vein, with data; B1 recoil maintains pressure / evens out flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to make this investigation more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat with several rings from each vessel (from more animals) and calculate means.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each of the following blood components: (i) red blood cells, (ii) phagocytes, (iii) lymphocytes, (iv) platelets.
parts.answer: (i) transport oxygen (using haemoglobin); (ii) engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis); (iii) produce antibodies; (iv) help blood to clot.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances transported dissolved in plasma.
parts.answer: Any two of: glucose, amino acids, carbon dioxide, urea, hormones, ions (salts), water, plasma proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A boy cuts his knee while playing cricket.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens in the blood to form a clot when the skin is cut.
parts.answer: Platelets are involved; soluble fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh of fibres that traps red blood cells, forming a clot.
parts.working: B1 fibrinogen → fibrin; B1 soluble to insoluble; B1 mesh traps blood cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of blood clotting.
parts.answer: Prevents loss of blood; prevents entry of pathogens.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which part of the blood carries carbon dioxide, urea and hormones?
A plasma
B platelets
C red blood cells
D white blood cells
parts.answer: A plasma
parts.working: These substances are carried dissolved in the plasma. Red blood cells mainly carry oxygen.

stem:
Red blood cell counts were measured for two healthy adults of the same age.
Person living in Karachi (sea level): 5.0 million per mm³
Person living in Murree (about 2300 m above sea level): 5.9 million per mm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference in red blood cell count of the person living in Murree compared with the person living in Karachi.
parts.answer: 18 % higher

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: Air at high altitude contains less oxygen (lower pressure); more red blood cells / haemoglobin carry more oxygen to the tissues.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen at altitude; B1 more red cells increase oxygen transport.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a blood smear, 200 white blood cells were counted: 136 phagocytes, 56 lymphocytes and 8 other white cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of white blood cells that were lymphocytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a phagocyte and a lymphocyte can be distinguished when seen under a microscope.
parts.answer: Phagocyte: lobed (multi-lobed) nucleus and granular cytoplasm; lymphocyte: large round nucleus filling most of the cell, little cytoplasm.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A week later the person develops a bacterial infection. Suggest how the numbers of each type of white blood cell change and explain why.
parts.answer: Both increase; more phagocytes to engulf and digest the bacteria; more lymphocytes to make antibodies against the bacterial antigens.
parts.working: B1 increase; B1 phagocytes engulf/digest; B1 lymphocytes produce (specific) antibodies.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dengue fever is common in Pakistan after the monsoon. In one patient the platelet count fell from 250 000 per mm³ to 40 000 per mm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in platelet count.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why doctors watch for bleeding and bruising in this patient.
parts.answer: Platelets are needed for blood clotting; with fewer platelets, blood clots slowly / less well, so small damaged vessels keep bleeding.
parts.working: B1 platelets needed for clotting; B1 so clotting is slower and bleeding continues.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the coronary arteries.
parts.answer: Supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood (oxygen and glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a blockage in a coronary artery can cause a heart attack.
parts.answer: Fatty deposits (cholesterol) build up in the artery wall and narrow it / a clot forms; less blood, oxygen and glucose reach part of the heart muscle; that muscle cannot respire aerobically, so it stops contracting / dies.
parts.working: B1 fatty deposit / clot blocks artery; B1 less oxygen (and glucose) to heart muscle; B1 less respiration / muscle cells die / cannot contract.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two risk factors for coronary heart disease that a person can change.
parts.answer: Any two of: diet high in saturated fat / salt; smoking; lack of exercise; stress; obesity.
parts.working: 1 mark each; not age, sex or genes.

stem:
A study followed men aged 45–60 for ten years.
Group : deaths from coronary heart disease per 100 000 men per year
non-smokers : 120
smoke 1–14 cigarettes per day : 210
smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day : 390

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for heavy smokers than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 3.25 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the data show about smoking and coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Death rate increases as the number of cigarettes smoked increases; heavy smokers have over three times the death rate of non-smokers.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 quoting figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why these data alone do not prove that smoking causes coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Other factors could be involved (diet, exercise, age, stress, genes); smokers may differ from non-smokers in these ways; correlation does not show cause.
parts.working: B1 other risk factors not controlled; B1 correlation ≠ causation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each part of the eye:
(i) cornea
(ii) iris
(iii) lens
(iv) retina
(v) optic nerve
parts.answer: (i) refracts (bends) light entering the eye; (ii) controls how much light enters (changes pupil size); (iii) focuses light onto the retina (fine focusing); (iv) contains light receptors (rods and cones); (v) carries nerve impulses from the retina to the brain.
parts.working: B1 each.

stem: A student leaves a dark cinema hall in Islamabad and walks out into bright sunlight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the changes in the iris when the student walks into the bright sunlight.
parts.answer: Circular muscles of the iris contract; radial muscles relax; pupil becomes smaller (constricts), so less light enters and the retina is protected from damage.
parts.working: B1 circular contract; B1 radial relax; B1 pupil smaller so less light enters / protects retina.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of response this is and why it is useful that it is automatic.
parts.answer: A reflex (involuntary) action; it is very fast and does not need thought, so the retina is protected immediately.
parts.working: B1 reflex; B1 fast / no conscious thought.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A girl looks up from a book she is reading to a bird far away. Which row shows the changes in her eyes when she focuses on the book again?
A ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments tighten; lens becomes thinner
B ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken; lens becomes fatter
C ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments tighten; lens becomes fatter
D ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments slacken; lens becomes thinner
parts.answer: B ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken; lens becomes fatter
parts.working: For a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the elastic lens becomes fatter (more convex) to refract light more. A describes focusing on a distant object.

stem: A man on a train is reading messages on his phone, then looks out of the window at hills several kilometres away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the eye that allow the man to focus on the distant hills after looking at his phone.
parts.answer: Ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments are pulled tight (tension increases); lens is pulled thinner / less convex.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lens must change shape for the image to be focused on the retina.
parts.answer: Light from a distant object needs less refraction (rays almost parallel); a thinner lens refracts light less, so the image is focused on the retina rather than in front of it.
parts.working: B1 distant object needs less refraction / bending; B1 thinner lens bends light less to focus on retina.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare rods and cones, stating for each the light conditions in which it works best, whether it detects colour, and where it is mainly found in the retina.
parts.answer: Rods: work in dim light; black and white only (no colour); found throughout the retina but not at the fovea. Cones: work in bright light; detect colour (three types); concentrated in the fovea.
parts.working: B1 rods light / colour; B1 rods distribution; B1 cones light / colour; B1 cones concentrated at fovea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to see the colours of objects at night.
parts.answer: Cones do not work in dim light; only rods respond, and rods do not detect colour.

stem:
A volunteer's pupil was photographed after two minutes at each light intensity and its diameter measured.
Light intensity / lux : pupil diameter / mm
50 : 6.4
200 : 4.8
500 : 3.6
1000 : 2.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in pupil diameter between 50 lux and 1000 lux.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between light intensity and pupil diameter.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, pupil diameter decreases (not in direct proportion).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the volunteer stayed at each light intensity for two minutes before the photograph was taken.
parts.answer: To allow time for the pupil to adjust fully / reach a steady size.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one variable, other than light intensity, that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Distance of the light from the eye / same eye measured / same volunteer / same direction of light / looking at the same object at the same distance.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes insulin and glucagon.
parts.answer: Pancreas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of insulin when blood glucose concentration rises after a meal.
parts.answer: Insulin is secreted into the blood; it causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen (storage), so the blood glucose concentration falls.
parts.working: B1 glucose taken up by liver / muscle; B1 converted to glycogen / blood glucose falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of glucagon on the liver.
parts.answer: Liver converts (breaks down) glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood.

stem: A 12-year-old boy in Quetta is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the cause of type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: The pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin, because the insulin-secreting cells are destroyed (by the body's immune system).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two symptoms of type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: Any two of: high blood glucose; glucose in the urine; thirst; frequent urination; tiredness; weight loss; blurred vision.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how type 1 diabetes is treated.
parts.answer: Regular injections of insulin (or insulin pump); monitoring blood glucose concentration; controlling diet (carbohydrate intake) and exercise.
parts.working: B1 insulin injections; B1 any other: monitor glucose / control diet / regular meals.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two people drank a glucose drink after fasting overnight. Their blood glucose concentration (mmol/dm³) was measured.
Time / min : person A : person B
0 : 5.0 : 6.2
30 : 7.8 : 12.4
60 : 6.4 : 12.9
120 : 5.2 : 11.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose concentration from 0 to 30 minutes for each person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which person has type 1 diabetes. Use the data to explain your answer.
parts.answer: Person B; glucose rises much higher (to 12.4) and is still high (11.0) after 120 minutes; no / little insulin is secreted, so glucose is not taken up by liver and muscle and converted to glycogen.
parts.working: B1 B; B1 data quoted (higher peak / stays high); B1 lack of insulin so glucose not converted to glycogen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the blood glucose of person A returns to normal by 120 minutes.
parts.answer: Rise in glucose detected by the pancreas; insulin secreted, causing liver and muscles to convert glucose to glycogen; this is negative feedback.
parts.working: B1 insulin released; B1 glucose stored as glycogen / negative feedback.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person eats a large plate of rice. Which events follow?
A Glucagon is secreted and the liver converts glycogen to glucose.
B Insulin is secreted and the liver converts glucose to glycogen.
C Insulin is secreted and the liver converts glycogen to glucose.
D Glucagon is secreted and the liver converts glucose to glycogen.
parts.answer: B Insulin is secreted and the liver converts glucose to glycogen.
parts.working: Digested starch raises blood glucose, so the pancreas secretes insulin, which makes the liver store glucose as glycogen. A describes the response to low blood glucose.

stem: Runners in a marathon in Lahore are running for more than three hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During a long-distance run, blood glucose concentration begins to fall. Explain how the body brings it back to normal.
parts.answer: Fall detected by the pancreas; less insulin and more glucagon secreted; glucagon travels in the blood to the liver; liver converts glycogen to glucose, which enters the blood; glucose rises back towards the set point — negative feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: pancreas detects fall; glucagon secreted (insulin reduced); liver breaks down glycogen to glucose; glucose released into blood; negative feedback / returns to set point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why adrenaline released at the start of the race also helps the runner.
parts.answer: Adrenaline raises blood glucose concentration (by glycogen breakdown) and increases heart rate, so more glucose and oxygen reach the muscles for respiration.
parts.working: B1 increases blood glucose; B1 more glucose / oxygen delivered to muscles for respiration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways the body responds when it is too hot.
parts.answer: Sweating; vasodilation (arterioles in the skin widen); (also less shivering / hair erector muscles relax).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways the body responds when it is too cold.
parts.answer: Shivering; vasoconstriction (arterioles in the skin narrow); (also hairs raised).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the brain that controls body temperature.
parts.answer: Hypothalamus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how vasodilation helps a person to lose heat on a hot day.
parts.answer: Arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen (dilate); more blood flows near the skin surface; more heat is lost from the blood to the surroundings by radiation.
parts.working: B1 arterioles dilate; B1 more blood to skin surface capillaries; B1 more heat lost (radiation / convection). Do not credit 'capillaries move'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the skin of a person looks pale when they are very cold.
parts.answer: Vasoconstriction: arterioles to the skin narrow, so less blood flows near the surface (reducing heat loss).
parts.working: B1 arterioles constrict; B1 less blood near skin surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sweating cools the body.
parts.answer: Water in sweat evaporates from the skin; evaporation uses heat energy from the skin, so the skin and blood are cooled.
parts.working: B1 evaporation of water; B1 takes heat (energy) from the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person feels hotter in Karachi in humid monsoon weather than in Jacobabad in dry heat at the same air temperature.
parts.answer: In humid air there is already a lot of water vapour, so sweat evaporates slowly; less heat is removed from the skin, so cooling is less effective.
parts.working: B1 less evaporation in humid air; B1 so less heat lost / less cooling.

stem:
Three identical test-tubes each contain 20 cm³ of water at 80 °C. One has no covering, one is wrapped in one layer of cotton wool and one in three layers. The temperature is recorded after 10 minutes.
Tube : temperature after 10 min / °C
no covering : 52
one layer of cotton wool : 60
three layers of cotton wool : 68

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of cooling, in °C per minute, for each tube.
parts.answer: no covering: 2.8 °C/min; one layer of cotton wool: 2 °C/min; three layers of cotton wool: 1.2 °C/min
parts.working: (80 − final temperature) ÷ 10 for each (M1); 2.8 and 2.0 (A1); 1.2 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these results relate to the layer of fat under the skin of a seal living in cold water.
