parts.answer: The covering acts as insulation, reducing heat loss — thicker layers cool more slowly; a thick fat layer under the skin insulates the seal and reduces heat loss to cold water.
parts.working: B1 more layers = less heat loss / insulation; B1 fat acts as insulator in the animal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any two of: starting temperature of water; volume of water; size / material of test-tube; room temperature; time interval.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the hypothalamus and negative feedback keep body temperature close to 37 °C when a person sits in a cold room.
parts.answer: Temperature receptors (in the hypothalamus / skin) detect a fall in blood temperature; hypothalamus sends nerve impulses to effectors; shivering (muscle contraction releases heat from respiration) and vasoconstriction (less heat lost); temperature rises back to the set point, then the responses stop — negative feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: receptors detect fall; hypothalamus coordinates / sends impulses; named effector response with explanation (shivering / vasoconstriction); return to set point / responses switched off = negative feedback.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that core body temperature stays close to 37 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes work best at about 37 °C (optimum); too high and they denature, too low and reactions such as respiration are too slow.
parts.working: B1 enzymes optimum; B1 denature at high / slow at low temperature.

stem: A potted plant is left on a windowsill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms (i) phototropism and (ii) gravitropism.
parts.answer: (i) a growth response of a plant to the direction of light; (ii) a growth response of a plant to gravity.
parts.working: B1 each; must refer to growth response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether a shoot shows positive or negative phototropism and positive or negative gravitropism.
parts.answer: Positive phototropism (grows towards light); negative gravitropism (grows away from gravity / upwards).
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to grow towards light coming from one side.
parts.answer: Auxin is made in the shoot tip; it diffuses down the shoot; auxin moves to / accumulates on the shaded side; auxin stimulates cell elongation, so cells on the shaded side grow longer and the shoot bends towards the light.
parts.working: 1 mark each: made in tip; diffuses down; more on shaded side; stimulates cell elongation on shaded side → bending.

stem:
Three groups of five oat seedlings were lit from one side for 6 hours. In group 1 the seedlings were untreated; in group 2 the tip of each shoot was covered with a foil cap; in group 3 the tip was cut off. The angle by which each shoot bent towards the light was measured.
Group : angles / °
untreated : 32, 28, 35, 30, 25
foil cap on tip : 2, 0, 1, 0, 2
tip removed : 0, 0, 1, 0, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean angle of curvature for each group.
parts.answer: untreated 30°; foil cap 1°; tip removed 0.2°
parts.working: M1 sum ÷ 5; A1 all three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the results show about where light is detected and where auxin is made.
parts.answer: Light is detected by the tip: covering the tip stops bending although the rest of the shoot is exposed; removing the tip stops bending, so the tip produces the substance (auxin) that causes bending.
parts.working: B1 tip detects light (foil result); B1 tip produces auxin / growth substance (tip-removed result); B1 comparison with untreated control.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why each group contained five seedlings.
parts.answer: To calculate a mean / reduce the effect of individual variation / identify anomalies.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potted bean seedling is placed on its side in the dark. Which statement explains why the shoot grows upwards?
A Auxin collects on the upper side, so cells on the upper side elongate more.
B Auxin collects on the lower side, so cells on the lower side elongate more.
C Auxin is destroyed by gravity on the lower side, so cells on the upper side elongate more.
D Auxin collects on the lower side and stops cells on the lower side from elongating.
parts.answer: B Auxin collects on the lower side, so cells on the lower side elongate more.
parts.working: In a horizontal shoot auxin accumulates on the lower side; it stimulates cell elongation there, so the lower side grows faster and the shoot curves upwards (negative gravitropism).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sequence of events at a synapse after an impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone.
parts.answer: Impulse arrives and vesicles move to the membrane; neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic gap; it diffuses across the gap; binds to receptor proteins on the next neurone, starting an impulse in it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: vesicles release neurotransmitter; into gap; diffuses across; binds to receptors → new impulse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why impulses can pass across a synapse in one direction only.
parts.answer: Neurotransmitter is released only from vesicles in the first (pre-synaptic) neurone; receptor proteins are found only on the membrane of the second neurone.
parts.working: B1 vesicles / neurotransmitter only on one side; B1 receptors only on the other side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A drug has a shape similar to the neurotransmitter and binds permanently to the receptor proteins without starting an impulse. Suggest and explain the effect of the drug.
parts.answer: Impulses are blocked / not passed on; the neurotransmitter cannot bind because the receptors are occupied, so no impulse is started in the second neurone.
parts.working: B1 transmission stops / reduced; B1 receptors blocked so neurotransmitter cannot bind.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What crosses the gap at a synapse?
A an electrical impulse
B neurotransmitter molecules
C receptor proteins
D vesicles
parts.answer: B neurotransmitter molecules
parts.working: Neurotransmitter is released from vesicles and diffuses across the gap. The electrical impulse itself cannot jump the gap.

stem: A girl accidentally touches a hot tawa (griddle) and pulls her hand away before she feels pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these in the order an impulse passes along a reflex arc, starting with the receptor:
motor neurone, effector (muscle), relay neurone, receptor, sensory neurone
parts.answer: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector (muscle)
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the relay neurone is found.
parts.answer: In the spinal cord (central nervous system).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of a reflex action.
parts.answer: It is very fast / automatic, so damage to the body is reduced.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measures his reaction time. A partner drops a metre ruler between his finger and thumb, and he catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls is recorded.
Trial : distance / cm
1 : 18
2 : 15
3 : 21
4 : 16
5 : 15
reaction time (s) = √(2d ÷ 9.8), where d is the distance in metres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance fallen.
parts.answer: 17 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the formula to calculate the reaction time for the mean distance. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is not a reflex action.
parts.answer: The response involves the brain and is a conscious decision (voluntary), so it is slower than a reflex.
parts.working: B1 involves brain / conscious; B1 voluntary / not automatic.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A patient has damage to the motor neurones that run from the spinal cord to the muscles of his left leg. The sensory neurones are not damaged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the patient can feel a pin prick on his foot but cannot move his foot away.
parts.answer: Receptors and sensory neurones still work, so impulses travel to the spinal cord and up to the brain (pain felt); but impulses cannot travel along the damaged motor neurones to the leg muscles (effectors), so no movement.
parts.working: B1 sensory pathway intact → brain; B1 motor neurones damaged; B1 impulse cannot reach effector / muscle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a voluntary action and a reflex action.
parts.answer: Voluntary: involves conscious thought / the brain decides, slower. Reflex: automatic, no conscious thought, faster.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term hormone.
parts.answer: A chemical substance produced by a gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs.
parts.working: B1 chemical made by gland; B1 carried in blood to target organ(s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gland that secretes each hormone: (i) adrenaline, (ii) testosterone, (iii) oestrogen.
parts.answer: (i) adrenal gland; (ii) testes; (iii) ovaries.
parts.working: B1 each.

stem: A cricket batter is about to face a very fast bowler in front of a large crowd in Lahore. His adrenal glands release adrenaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three effects of adrenaline on the body.
parts.answer: Any three of: increased heart rate (pulse); increased breathing rate; dilated pupils; increased blood glucose concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how one of these effects helps the batter to react to the ball.
parts.answer: e.g. higher heart rate / blood glucose supplies more oxygen and glucose to muscles; faster respiration releases more energy for muscle contraction.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen / glucose to muscles; B1 more respiration / energy for movement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare nervous control with hormonal control. Give three differences.
parts.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses / hormonal: chemicals; nervous: along neurones / hormonal: in the blood; nervous: very fast / hormonal: slower; nervous: short-lived effect / hormonal: longer-lasting; nervous: precise target / hormonal: may affect several organs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct comparison, max 3. Both sides needed for each mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why control of blood glucose is better done by hormones than by nerves.
parts.answer: The response needs to last a long time and affect organs throughout the body (liver, muscles); speed is not essential, and hormones in the blood reach all target cells.
parts.working: B1 long-lasting / continuous; B1 widespread targets / speed not needed.

stem: A thermostat in an air-conditioned office in Karachi switches the cooler on when the room rises above 24 °C and off when it falls back to 24 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define homeostasis.
parts.answer: The maintenance of a constant internal environment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the thermostat in the office as a model, explain the principle of negative feedback in the body.
parts.answer: A set point is maintained; a change away from the set point is detected (by receptors); a response (by effectors) reverses the change, returning it to the set point; once back at the set point the corrective response stops.
parts.working: B1 set point; B1 change detected; B1 response opposes / reverses the change (and is switched off when normal).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term genetic modification.
parts.answer: Changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three examples of genetic modification and state the benefit of each.
parts.answer: Any three of: bacteria given the human insulin gene → produce human insulin; crops resistant to herbicides → weeds can be sprayed without killing crop; crops resistant to insect pests → less insecticide, higher yield; crops with improved nutritional quality (e.g. rice with extra vitamin A) → reduce deficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark each for example + benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme is used to join a human gene into a bacterial plasmid?
A amylase
B DNA ligase
C protease
D restriction enzyme
parts.answer: B DNA ligase
parts.working: DNA ligase joins the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid together. A restriction enzyme cuts DNA; it does not join it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
parts.answer: Human insulin gene is cut out using a restriction enzyme, leaving sticky ends; a bacterial plasmid is cut with the same restriction enzyme; the gene and plasmid are joined with DNA ligase to form a recombinant plasmid; the recombinant plasmid is inserted into a bacterium; the bacteria multiply (in a fermenter) and express the gene, making human insulin, which is extracted and purified.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: restriction enzyme cuts out gene; sticky ends; plasmid cut with same enzyme; ligase joins; recombinant plasmid put into bacteria; bacteria reproduce / grown in fermenter and make insulin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'sticky ends'.
parts.answer: Short lengths of single-stranded DNA left at the cut ends after a staggered cut by a restriction enzyme; their exposed bases can pair with complementary bases.
parts.working: B1 single-stranded overhang; B1 unpaired bases that can pair with complementary bases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut both the human DNA and the plasmid.
parts.answer: The enzyme cuts at a specific base sequence and leaves the same sticky ends; so the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid are complementary and can pair up.
parts.working: B1 same sequence cut / same sticky ends; B1 complementary so they join.

stem: Many cotton farmers in Punjab grow cotton that has been genetically modified to contain a gene from a bacterium. The gene makes a protein that is toxic to caterpillars that feed on cotton.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to farmers and the environment of growing insect-resistant GM cotton.
parts.answer: Advantages: crop makes its own toxin so pests die; less insecticide sprayed (lower cost, less harm to farm workers and to non-target insects); higher yield / less damage. Disadvantages: GM seed is expensive and must be bought each season; pests may become resistant to the toxin; non-target insects may be harmed; reduced biodiversity in a monoculture; genes may spread to wild relatives.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark each, max 6, with at least 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages for full marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A farmer near Bahawalpur grew GM insect-resistant cotton in one field and non-GM cotton in a similar field in the same season.
Cotton type : yield / kg per hectare : number of insecticide sprays
GM : 2250 : 3
non-GM : 1800 : 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield of the GM cotton compared with the non-GM cotton.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of insecticide sprays. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the farmer should not conclude from these results alone that GM cotton is better on all farms.
parts.answer: Only one farm / one season — results may not be repeatable; other factors (soil, rainfall, pests that year) may differ between fields; cost of GM seed not included.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rice genetically modified to contain extra vitamin A precursor could improve health in some countries.
parts.answer: In places where people eat mainly rice, the diet may lack vitamin A; GM rice provides it, reducing vitamin A deficiency (e.g. poor night vision / blindness).
parts.working: B1 rice is a staple / main food; B1 reduces deficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some people prefer to increase vitamin A intake by eating a more varied diet (for example carrots and leafy vegetables) rather than growing GM rice.
parts.answer: Any one of: concerns about the safety or environmental effects of GM crops; a varied diet also provides other vitamins and minerals; cost of GM seed / dependence on seed companies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a plasmid is correct?
A It is a small circle of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main bacterial chromosome.
B It is a chromosome found in the nucleus of a human cell.
C It is an enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together.
D It is a protein coat that surrounds the genetic material of a virus.
parts.answer: A It is a small circle of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main bacterial chromosome.
parts.working: Plasmids are small circular loops of DNA in bacterial cytoplasm; they are used as vectors to carry genes into bacteria. C describes DNA ligase, and bacteria have no nucleus, so B is wrong.

stem: A maize variety has been genetically modified to be resistant to a herbicide (weedkiller).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing a herbicide-resistant GM crop helps a farmer.
parts.answer: The whole field can be sprayed with herbicide; weeds are killed but the crop is not, so there is less competition and a higher yield.
parts.working: B1 herbicide kills weeds but not crop; B1 less competition / higher yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two concerns people have about growing herbicide-resistant crops.
parts.answer: Any two of: the resistance gene could spread to wild plants / weeds (making 'superweeds'); more herbicide may be used; reduced biodiversity; possible effects on human health not fully known.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Under ideal conditions in a fermenter, a bacterium divides into two every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bacteria present after 4 hours, starting with one GM bacterium, if every cell divides once every 20 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the number of bacteria in a real fermenter after 4 hours is usually smaller than your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Any two of: not every cell divides every 20 minutes (some cells die); nutrients (e.g. glucose) start to run out; toxic waste products build up / pH changes; the bacteria need time to adjust to the new conditions before dividing quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before GM bacteria were used, insulin for people with diabetes was extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs. Suggest three advantages of using insulin made by GM bacteria.
parts.answer: Any three of: identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic or immune reactions; can be made in large quantities; cheaper / quicker to produce; consistent purity; acceptable to people who avoid pig or animal products for religious or ethical reasons; no risk of disease passed from animals.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why a gene taken from a human can still be used by a bacterium to make the same human protein.
parts.answer: The base sequence of the gene codes for the order of amino acids; the same base sequence codes for the same amino acids in all organisms, so the bacterium makes a protein with the same amino acid sequence.
parts.working: B1 gene / base sequence codes for amino acid sequence; B1 code is the same (universal) in bacteria and humans.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the human protein made by bacteria must be purified before it can be used as a medicine.
parts.answer: To remove bacterial cells, other bacterial proteins and toxins / nutrients from the fermenter that could cause harmful reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The steps below describe how a gene is transferred to bacteria. Put them in the correct order (write the letters).
P Recombinant plasmids are taken up by bacteria.
Q The gene and plasmid are joined using DNA ligase.
R The gene is cut out of human DNA with a restriction enzyme.
S The bacteria multiply and make the human protein.
T A plasmid is cut open with the same restriction enzyme.
parts.answer: R, T, Q, P, S
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair reversed (accept T before R).

stem: Fish have been genetically modified with an extra growth hormone gene. At a research farm the mean mass of GM fish at 12 months was 2.8 kg and of non-GM fish of the same species 1.2 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much greater, as a percentage, the mean mass of the GM fish was than the non-GM fish. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one benefit and one concern of farming such GM fish.
parts.answer: Benefit: more food produced in less time / cheaper protein. Concern: GM fish escaping and breeding with or out-competing wild fish / effects on ecosystems / unknown health effects.
parts.working: B1 benefit; B1 concern.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA only at the base sequence GAATTC. A linear piece of DNA has this sequence on one strand:
TTGAATTCAGCCGAATTCTTAGGCTAGAATTCCGA
How many fragments are produced when this DNA is cut completely by the enzyme?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 5
parts.answer: C 4
parts.working: GAATTC occurs 3 times, and each cut in a linear molecule adds one fragment: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer B (3) counts the cut sites, not the fragments.

stem: Wheat is the main crop in parts of Sindh and Balochistan where rainfall is low.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how genetically modified drought-tolerant wheat could help farmers in a region with low and unreliable rainfall.
parts.answer: Wheat survives / grows with less water, so yields are higher in dry years; more reliable food supply and income / less irrigation needed.
parts.working: B1 survives dry conditions; B1 higher / more reliable yield or less water used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why some people are against growing GM crops.
parts.answer: Any two of: genes could transfer to wild plants; possible unknown effects on health; reduced biodiversity; seeds are expensive and farmers depend on big companies; ethical objection to altering organisms.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four reasons why bacteria are useful in biotechnology.
parts.answer: Reproduce rapidly; can make complex molecules; few ethical concerns over their use and manipulation; have plasmids (can be genetically modified easily); can be grown in fermenters cheaply.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4.

stem: A baker in Peshawar mixes flour, water, sugar and yeast to make dough for naan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
parts.answer: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 ethanol; B1 carbon dioxide (with glucose as reactant).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dough rises when left in a warm place.
parts.answer: Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide gas; bubbles of gas are trapped in the dough, making it expand.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide produced; B1 gas trapped in dough.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the ethanol when the naan is baked.
parts.answer: It evaporates (because of the high temperature).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Equal samples of bread dough were placed in measuring cylinders at different temperatures. Each started at 50 cm³. The volume was read after 30 minutes.
Temperature / °C : volume after 30 min / cm³
20 : 62
30 : 84
40 : 98
60 : 51

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in volume, in cm³ per minute, at each temperature. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result at 60 °C.
parts.answer: Yeast enzymes are denatured (or yeast cells killed) at high temperature; so little or no respiration / carbon dioxide produced.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured; B1 little respiration / CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find the optimum temperature more accurately.
parts.answer: Repeat with smaller temperature intervals between 30 °C and 60 °C (e.g. 35, 40, 45, 50, 55 °C).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A factory in Swat makes apple juice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the enzyme pectinase is used in the production of fruit juice.
parts.answer: Pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls; cells break open more easily, so more juice is released; the juice is clearer (less cloudy).
parts.working: B1 breaks down pectin; B1 cell walls; B1 more juice / clearer juice.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Samples of 100 g of apple pulp were mixed with different volumes of pectinase and left at 40 °C for 20 minutes, then filtered.
Pectinase / cm³ : volume of juice / cm³
0.0 : 12
1.0 : 21
2.0 : 27, 29, 18, 28
3.0 : 30
4.0 : 30.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result for 2.0 cm³ of pectinase and calculate the mean volume of juice without it.
parts.answer: 18 cm³; mean = 28 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your mean, calculate the percentage increase in juice volume with 2.0 cm³ of pectinase compared with no pectinase. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the volume of juice hardly increases above 3.0 cm³ of pectinase.
parts.answer: All the pectin has already been broken down / another factor (amount of pulp or time) is now limiting.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any two of: mass of apple pulp; temperature; time; type of apple; total volume (add water to make volumes equal); filter paper / funnel type.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the enzyme lactase used to produce?
A biological washing powder
B clear fruit juice
C lactose-free milk
D ethanol for biofuel
parts.answer: C lactose-free milk
parts.working: Lactase breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose, so the milk can be drunk by people who are lactose intolerant. Clear fruit juice is made using pectinase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the enzymes in biological washing powders remove stains of curry and egg from clothes.
parts.answer: Lipases break down fats / oils in curry into fatty acids and glycerol; proteases break down proteins in egg into amino acids; the products are small and soluble, so they wash away in water.
parts.working: B1 lipase / fats; B1 protease / protein; B1 soluble products washed away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why biological washing powders are less effective in very hot water.
parts.answer: The enzymes are denatured at high temperatures; the shape of the active site changes so substrates no longer fit.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site changes shape / substrate does not fit.

stem:
Pieces of cloth stained with egg yolk were placed in a biological washing powder solution at different temperatures. The time for the stain to disappear was recorded.
Temperature / °C : time / s
20 : 600
30 : 300
40 : 160
50 : 240
60 : 900

parts.label: a
parts.text: The rate of stain removal can be calculated as 1 ÷ time. Calculate the rate at 40 °C, in s⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the temperature at which the washing powder worked best and explain the result at 60 °C.
parts.answer: 40 °C; at 60 °C the enzymes are (partly) denatured so the stain takes much longer to remove.
parts.working: B1 40 °C; B1 denatured at 60 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of making the end point of this experiment easier to judge.
parts.answer: Compare each cloth with a clean, unstained piece of the same cloth / use a light sensor or colorimeter / place cloth against a white background.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain why each of the following is controlled in an industrial fermenter producing insulin from GM bacteria:
(i) temperature
(ii) pH
(iii) oxygen supply
(iv) nutrient supply
parts.answer: (i) enzymes work best at an optimum temperature / too high denatures them; (ii) enzymes have an optimum pH; (iii) for aerobic respiration of the microorganisms; (iv) provides glucose for respiration and raw materials (e.g. amino acids / nitrogen) for growth and product.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fermenter is cleaned with steam before use.
parts.answer: To kill microorganisms (aseptic conditions); contaminating microorganisms would compete with the GM bacteria / reduce yield / contaminate the product.
parts.working: B1 kills microorganisms / sterilises; B1 contamination would reduce yield or spoil product.

stem:
Penicillin is made by a fungus grown in a fermenter.
Day : penicillin concentration / g per dm³
0 : 0
2 : 0.5
4 : 4.1
6 : 8.9
8 : 10.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of penicillin production between day 2 and day 6, in g/dm³ per day.
parts.answer: 2.1 g/dm³ per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: The fermenter has a water jacket through which cold water is pumped. Explain why.
parts.answer: The fungus respires and releases heat energy; cooling stops the temperature rising above the optimum, which would denature enzymes / kill the fungus.
parts.working: B1 respiration releases heat; B1 prevents temperature rising / denaturing enzymes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the production rate between day 6 and day 8 is lower than between day 2 and day 6.
parts.answer: Nutrients (e.g. glucose) run low; waste products build up / pH changes; so fewer cells are active.
parts.working: B1 nutrients used up; B1 waste builds up.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Yeast is used to produce a biofuel from sugar cane. Which product of yeast respiration is used as the fuel?
A carbon dioxide
B ethanol
C glucose
D lactic acid
parts.answer: B ethanol
parts.working: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces ethanol, which can be burned as a fuel. Lactic acid is made by anaerobic respiration in muscles, not yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of sugar affects the rate of carbon dioxide production by yeast. Include apparatus, method, variables to control, how results are recorded and how a conclusion is reached.
parts.answer: Yeast suspension + sugar solutions of different concentrations; collect CO₂ in a gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder or count bubbles for a fixed time; constant temperature water-bath; repeats; calculate rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: at least five sugar concentrations (e.g. 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 %); same volume and concentration of yeast suspension; same volume of sugar solution; water-bath at a fixed temperature (e.g. 35 °C, thermostatically controlled); allow time to equilibrate; measure CO₂ volume in a gas syringe (or count bubbles / measure balloon) over a fixed time; repeat three times and calculate mean; rate = volume ÷ time; table of concentration against volume of CO₂; graph and describe trend for conclusion.

stem: A farm grows 65 tonnes of sugar cane per hectare on 12 hectares. Each tonne of cane can yield 72 dm³ of ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of ethanol that could be produced from the farm's sugar cane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the sugar from cane is converted into ethanol.
parts.answer: Sugar solution is mixed with yeast in a fermenter without oxygen (anaerobic); yeast respires anaerobically to produce ethanol (and carbon dioxide); ethanol is separated (distilled).
parts.working: B1 yeast; B1 anaerobic respiration / fermentation produces ethanol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of using large areas of land to grow sugar cane for biofuel.
parts.answer: Less land for food crops / higher food prices / habitat destruction and loss of biodiversity / heavy water use.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The temperature inside a large fermenter rises unless it is cooled. What is the main cause of this rise?
A The stirrer rubs against the walls.
B The microorganisms release heat energy during respiration.
C Steam used to sterilise the fermenter stays inside.
D The nutrient solution reacts with the oxygen supplied.
parts.answer: B The microorganisms release heat energy during respiration.
parts.working: Respiration by the large population of microorganisms releases energy as heat, so a water jacket is needed. Steam is only used before the fermenter is filled, so C is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student measured the rate of an enzyme reaction at different temperatures.
temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
rate / arbitrary units: 4, 9, 17, 23, 11, 1
Which temperature is closest to the optimum temperature of this enzyme?
A 20 °C
B 30 °C
C 40 °C
D 50 °C
parts.answer: C 40 °C
parts.working: The rate is highest (23) at 40 °C, so the optimum is nearest 40 °C. 50 °C is wrong: the rate has already fallen because the enzyme is being denatured.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction fall when the temperature is raised well above the optimum?
A The enzyme molecules are killed by the heat.
B The substrate molecules move too fast to collide with the enzyme.
C The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.
D The enzyme is used up faster at high temperatures.
parts.answer: C The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.
parts.working: High temperature denatures the enzyme: the active site loses its shape and is no longer complementary to the substrate. Enzymes are proteins, not living things, so they cannot be 'killed' (A); faster movement actually increases collisions (B).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two protein-digesting enzymes, P and Q, were tested at different pH values. Enzyme P worked best at pH 2 and enzyme Q worked best at pH 8.
Which row shows where each enzyme is most likely to act in the human alimentary canal?
A P: mouth; Q: stomach
B P: stomach; Q: small intestine
C P: small intestine; Q: stomach
D P: stomach; Q: mouth
parts.answer: B P: stomach; Q: small intestine
parts.working: The stomach is acidic (hydrochloric acid, about pH 2), so P acts there; the small intestine (duodenum) is slightly alkaline, so Q acts there. Option D is wrong because protein digestion does not take place in the mouth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme from a human cell is tested at 10 °C, 25 °C and 37 °C. The rate increases as the temperature rises.
Explain why the rate increases between 10 °C and 37 °C.
parts.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate molecules move faster and collide more often, forming more enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: more kinetic energy; more (frequent / successful) collisions between enzyme and substrate; more enzyme–substrate complexes formed (per unit time) / more product per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the term used for the temperature at which an enzyme works fastest.
parts.answer: Optimum temperature
parts.working: B1 optimum (temperature).

stem:
Amylase was mixed with starch solution at five temperatures. A drop of the mixture was tested with iodine solution every 10 s until it no longer turned blue-black. The time taken was recorded.
temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
time for starch to disappear / s: 600, 300, 150, 90, 240, no end point after 900 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 40 °C and at 50 °C, using rate = 1000 ÷ time. Give each answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction shown by the results.
parts.answer: Rate increases from 10 °C to 40 °C (the time halves for each 10 °C rise from 10 °C to 30 °C); highest rate at 40 °C; rate decreases above 40 °C, to zero/no end point at 60 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: rate increases from 10 °C to 40 °C; maximum / optimum at (about) 40 °C; rate falls above 40 °C; quoting data with units (e.g. 600 s at 10 °C, 90 s at 40 °C).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the iodine never stopped turning blue-black at 60 °C.
parts.answer: The amylase was denatured; its active site changed shape so starch could no longer bind, so starch was not digested and remained.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: amylase denatured; active site shape changed / starch no longer fits / no enzyme–substrate complexes; so starch remains (iodine stays blue-black).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student put a protease solution in two tubes.
Tube A was kept at 2 °C for 30 minutes, then warmed to 37 °C and mixed with protein.
Tube B was kept at 80 °C for 30 minutes, then cooled to 37 °C and mixed with protein.
Tube A digested the protein normally. Tube B digested none of the protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for tube A and tube B.
parts.answer: Tube A: at 2 °C the enzyme had little kinetic energy, so there were few collisions and little activity; it was not denatured, so when warmed to 37 °C it worked normally. Tube B: at 80 °C the enzyme was denatured; the active site permanently changed shape, so substrate could not bind even after cooling.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: low temperature – low kinetic energy / few collisions (A); enzyme not denatured at low temperature, so activity returns on warming; high temperature denatures enzyme (B); active-site shape changed permanently / irreversibly, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form when cooled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seeds kept dry in a freezer in a seed bank can still germinate many years later, but seeds that have been boiled never germinate. Use your knowledge of enzymes to suggest why.
parts.answer: Freezing only makes the seeds' enzymes inactive (low kinetic energy) without denaturing them, so they work again when the seed is warmed; boiling denatures the enzymes irreversibly (active sites change shape), so the reactions needed for germination cannot take place.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: freezing slows / stops enzyme activity temporarily (not denatured, activity returns on warming); boiling denatures enzymes irreversibly / active site permanently changed, so no germination.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Potato contains catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. A student put 5.0 g of chopped potato into a flask with 10 cm³ of buffer solution and 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide. The oxygen was collected in an inverted measuring cylinder for 2 minutes. This was repeated with buffers of different pH.
pH: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11
volume of oxygen after 2 minutes / cm³: 4.5, 11.0, 18.5, 12.0, 3.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the pH at which catalase in potato worked best in this investigation.
parts.answer: pH 7
parts.working: B1 pH 7 (largest volume, 18.5 cm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: pH (of buffer). Dependent: volume of oxygen collected (in 2 minutes).
parts.working: B1 pH; B1 volume of oxygen (collected in 2 min) – 'amount' or 'oxygen' alone not credited.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same, and say how one of them could be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature, volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, mass/size/surface area of potato, time of collection. E.g. temperature controlled with a thermostatically controlled water-bath.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two controlled variables (B1 + B1); 1 mark for a matching method of control (e.g. thermostatically controlled water-bath; measure peroxide with a syringe; same mass of potato on a balance).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student added 1 cm³ of liver extract (contains catalase) to 5 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide mixed with 2 cm³ of buffer in a narrow tube, and measured the maximum height of foam produced. Each pH was tested three times.
pH 3: 4, 5, 4 mm
pH 5: 12, 14, 13 mm
pH 7: 30, 32, 31 mm
pH 9: 18, 8, 20 mm
pH 11: 6, 5, 7 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 8 mm at pH 9 (trial 2)
parts.working: B1 8 mm at pH 9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean height of foam at pH 3 (to 1 decimal place) and at pH 9 (leaving out the anomalous result).
parts.answer: pH 3: 4.3 mm; pH 9: 19.0 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the anomalous result may have occurred.
parts.answer: E.g. less liver used / hydrogen peroxide volume measured wrongly / foam height read late or early / tube not mixed.
parts.working: Any one sensible, specific reason linked to the method.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write a conclusion for this investigation.
parts.answer: Catalase activity (foam height) increases from pH 3 to pH 7, where it is greatest, and decreases from pH 7 to pH 11; optimum pH about 7.
parts.working: 1 mark for increase up to pH 7 / greatest at pH 7; 1 mark for decrease above pH 7. Must link pH to foam height / activity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an investigation to find the effect of temperature on the activity of lipase.
Lipase digests fat in milk into fatty acids and glycerol. Milk mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator is pink; the pink colour disappears when enough fatty acids have been produced.
In your plan, include the apparatus and the method, the variables you will control, and how you will make your results reliable.
parts.answer: Use milk + sodium carbonate + phenolphthalein in test-tubes at five or more temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C) in thermostatically controlled water-baths; equilibrate milk and lipase separately; mix, start timer, record time for pink colour to disappear; control volumes, concentrations, pH; repeat three times and calculate a mean; wear eye protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: 1. at least five temperatures stated / range; 2. temperature controlled with thermostatically controlled water-bath; 3. equilibrate milk mixture and lipase at the temperature before mixing; 4. measure time for pink colour to disappear (dependent variable), e.g. with a stopwatch; 5. two controlled variables with method, e.g. same volume of milk/lipase measured with syringe, same lipase concentration, same volume of sodium carbonate / indicator; 6. repeat each temperature (at least) three times and calculate mean / identify anomalies; 7. control tube with boiled lipase or water instead of lipase; 8. relevant safety, e.g. eye protection with sodium carbonate or care with hot water.

stem:
Agar containing milk protein is cloudy. Paper discs were soaked in protease solution made up in buffers of different pH and placed on the milk agar. After 24 hours at 30 °C, the diameter of the clear zone around each disc was measured. Three discs were used for each pH.
pH 4: 6, 7, 8 mm
pH 6: 14, 15, 16 mm
pH 8: 11, 12, 10 mm
pH 10: 3, 4, 2 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the clear zone at each pH.
parts.answer: pH 4: 7 mm; pH 6: 15 mm; pH 8: 11 mm; pH 10: 3 mm
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mean diameter between pH 6 and pH 8. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a clear zone forms around each disc.
parts.answer: Protease diffuses out of the disc into the agar and digests the milk protein into soluble amino acids, so the cloudy protein disappears.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: protease diffuses into the agar; digests / breaks down milk protein (into amino acids), removing the cloudiness.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the measurement of the clear zones more accurate.
parts.answer: Measure the diameter at two right angles and take the mean / use a ruler with mm divisions held under the dish against a dark background.
parts.working: Any one specific improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Biological washing powders contain enzymes, including proteases and lipases. The label on one powder says: 'Best results at 30–40 °C. Do not use above 60 °C.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the biological washing powder removes egg and blood stains well at 40 °C.
parts.answer: Stains contain protein; the protease in the powder digests the protein into soluble amino acids; 40 °C is close to the optimum temperature of the enzymes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: protease digests protein (in egg/blood) into (soluble) amino acids; 40 °C is near the optimum, so rate is high.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the powder works poorly if the clothes are washed at 90 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes are denatured at 90 °C; active site changes shape so the protein stains no longer fit / bind.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed / substrate cannot bind.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it can be cheaper for a family in Karachi to wash clothes with biological powder in cool tap water rather than with non-biological powder in hot water.
parts.answer: Less energy (electricity or gas) needed to heat the water.
parts.working: B1 saves energy / fuel for heating water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student investigates the effect of pH on the activity of amylase. Which variable must be kept constant?
A pH of the solution
B temperature of the mixture
C time taken for starch to be digested
D colour of the iodine solution
parts.answer: B temperature of the mixture
parts.working: Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it must be controlled. pH is the independent variable (A) and the time taken is the dependent variable (C).

stem: Some bacteria live in hot springs in northern Pakistan where the water is about 75 °C. An enzyme extracted from one of these bacteria has an optimum temperature of 75 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the enzyme from the hot-spring bacterium is not denatured at 75 °C, but a human enzyme would be.
parts.answer: The bacterial enzyme has a shape (bonds holding its 3-D shape) that remains stable at high temperature, so its active site keeps its shape; the human enzyme's shape changes above about 40–45 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for: bacterial enzyme's active site / shape stays the same at 75 °C; 1 mark for: human enzyme's active site changes shape / is denatured at this temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bacterial enzyme works more slowly at 37 °C than at 75 °C.
parts.answer: At 37 °C molecules have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: less kinetic energy; fewer collisions / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using an enzyme like this in an industrial process that runs at a high temperature.
parts.answer: It is not denatured, so it keeps working at high temperatures where reactions are faster / it can be used for longer.
parts.working: Any one: works at high temperature without denaturing; faster reaction; lasts longer / reused; fewer contaminating microorganisms grow at high temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Pectinase helps to release juice from fruit. A student mixed 20 g of crushed apple with 2 cm³ of pectinase at different temperatures, then filtered the mixture for 20 minutes.
temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
volume of juice / cm³: 6.0, 9.5, 14.0, 11.0, 4.5
A control with boiled pectinase at 40 °C gave 3.0 cm³ of juice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume from 20 °C to 40 °C. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some juice was produced in the control tube with boiled pectinase.
parts.answer: Juice drains from apple pieces by gravity / from cells already broken when the apple was cut, without enzyme action.
parts.working: B1 some juice released without enzyme, e.g. from cut cells / gravity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student placed the beakers of apple pulp and pectinase in water-baths and mixed them straight away. Identify one source of error in this method and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Error: the pulp and enzyme were not at the test temperature when mixed. Improvement: leave pulp and pectinase separately in the water-bath for 5–10 minutes before mixing.
parts.working: B1 error (no equilibration / temperature not reached); B1 matching improvement (equilibrate separately before mixing). Accept other matched pairs, e.g. temperature of water-bath varied – use thermostatically controlled water-bath.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the temperature range in which the optimum temperature lies, and describe how the investigation could be extended to find it more precisely.
parts.answer: Between 30 °C and 50 °C; test temperatures at smaller intervals, e.g. every 2 °C from 30 °C to 50 °C.
parts.working: B1 30–50 °C; B1 smaller intervals in this range.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.
'Each enzyme works best at a particular pH, called its ____ pH. If the pH is too high or too low, the shape of the ____ ____ changes. The substrate no longer ____ into it, so fewer enzyme–substrate ____ are formed. The enzyme is said to be ____.'
parts.answer: optimum; active site; fits; complexes; denatured
parts.working: 1 mark each: optimum; active site; fits (accept binds); complexes; denatured. (Active site counts as one mark.)

stem:
Yeast suspension (contains catalase) was added to hydrogen peroxide at five temperatures. The time taken to collect 10 cm³ of oxygen in a gas syringe was recorded.
temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55
time to collect 10 cm³ / s: 125, 64, 40, 52, 160

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen production at 25 °C and at 45 °C in cm³ per second. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concluded that the optimum temperature is 35 °C. Explain why this conclusion may not be correct and suggest what further work would show the optimum more precisely.
parts.answer: The optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 45 °C, because only 10 °C intervals were tested; repeat with temperatures at 2 °C (or smaller) intervals between 25 °C and 45 °C, with repeats.
parts.working: 1 mark: only 10 °C steps / large intervals; 1 mark: optimum lies between 25 °C and 45 °C; 1 mark: test more temperatures at smaller intervals in this range (with repeats).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why measuring the time to collect 10 cm³ of gas is better than collecting gas for a fixed long time, such as 10 minutes, at every temperature.
parts.answer: Over a long time the hydrogen peroxide may be used up at the faster temperatures, so the volumes would no longer show the rate / the cylinder could overflow.
parts.working: B1 substrate used up / cylinder overflows so later volumes do not reflect rate.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient with a fever has a body temperature of 40.5 °C. Suggest why a very high fever can be dangerous, in terms of enzymes.
parts.answer: Some enzymes may start to denature / active sites change shape, so metabolic reactions slow down.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes (begin to) denature / active site changes shape; 1 mark: metabolic reactions (e.g. respiration) slow / cells cannot function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage for humans to keep their body temperature close to 37 °C.
parts.answer: 37 °C is close to the optimum temperature of human enzymes, so reactions happen at a fast and constant rate; it is low enough that enzymes are not denatured.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: near optimum for enzymes; reactions fast / steady; enzymes not denatured (any two).

stem:
A student placed a tube of 5 cm³ starch solution and a tube of 1 cm³ amylase solution separately in a water-bath at 37 °C for 5 minutes, then mixed them and kept the mixture in the water-bath. Every 30 s, a drop of the mixture was added to a drop of iodine solution on a spotting tile.
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180
colour: blue-black, blue-black, blue-black, dark brown-black, brown-black, orange-brown, orange-brown

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time at which the starch had been fully digested.
parts.working: B1 150 s (first time the drop stays orange-brown).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the amylase and starch were placed in the water-bath separately for 5 minutes before they were mixed.
parts.answer: So both solutions reached the test temperature (37 °C) before the reaction started; otherwise the reaction would begin at a different temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: to reach the temperature of the water-bath (equilibrate); 1 mark: so the reaction occurs at the stated temperature from the start / fair test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour that iodine solution turns when starch is present.
parts.answer: Blue-black
parts.working: B1 blue-black.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one safety precaution needed in this experiment.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection (iodine solution is an irritant) / wipe up spills.
parts.working: Any one relevant precaution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about enzymes are correct?
1 Extreme pH can change the shape of the active site.
2 Enzymes are denatured at low temperatures such as 5 °C.
3 Different enzymes can have different optimum pH values.
A 1, 2 and 3
B 1 and 2 only
C 1 and 3 only
D 2 and 3 only
parts.answer: C 1 and 3 only
parts.working: Statement 2 is false: at low temperatures enzymes are inactive (few collisions) but not denatured. Statements 1 and 3 are true (e.g. pepsin about pH 2, salivary amylase about pH 7). Option A is the main distractor.

stem:
Slices of mango were kept for 5 days at two temperatures. The mass lost because of decay was measured.
kept at 4 °C (refrigerator): mass lost 3.2 g
kept at 30 °C (kitchen in summer): mass lost 14.4 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mass loss was at 30 °C than at 4 °C.
parts.answer: 4.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in mass loss, in terms of the enzymes of decomposers on the mango.
parts.answer: At 4 °C the decomposers' enzymes have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions and slower digestion and respiration; the decomposers grow and reproduce slowly. At 30 °C enzymes are near their optimum, so decay is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: decomposers (bacteria/fungi) use enzymes to digest the mango; low temperature – less kinetic energy / fewer enzyme–substrate collisions; enzymes not denatured but activity / growth / reproduction slower at 4 °C; nearer optimum at 30 °C (any three).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the rate of decay if the mango slices kept at 4 °C were moved to 30 °C. Give a reason.
parts.answer: The rate would increase to about the same as at 30 °C, because the enzymes were not denatured at 4 °C.
parts.working: B1 rate increases; B1 enzymes not denatured (activity returns).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which description of enzymes is correct?
A carbohydrates that act as biological catalysts
B proteins that act as biological catalysts
C proteins that are used up in the reactions they control
D fats that speed up reactions in cells
parts.answer: B proteins that act as biological catalysts
parts.working: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions and are not changed by them. C is wrong because enzymes are not used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme acts on only one substrate. Which feature explains this?
A The substrate has a shape complementary to the active site of the enzyme.
B The enzyme is denatured by all other substrates.
C The enzyme has many active sites of different shapes.
D The product has the same shape as the active site.
parts.answer: A The substrate has a shape complementary to the active site of the enzyme.
parts.working: Specificity: only a substrate whose shape is complementary to the active site can bind and form an enzyme–substrate complex. B is wrong: other molecules simply do not fit; they do not denature the enzyme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction.
parts.working: B1 speeds up reaction AND not changed / used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product formed when amylase acts on starch.
parts.answer: Maltose
parts.working: B1 maltose (accept simple reducing sugar).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why amylase cannot digest protein.
parts.answer: Enzymes are specific; protein is not complementary in shape to the active site of amylase, so it cannot bind.
parts.working: 1 mark: active site shape; 1 mark: protein not complementary / does not fit, so no enzyme–substrate complex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an enzyme molecule catalyses the breakdown of a substrate molecule. Use the terms active site and enzyme–substrate complex in your answer.
parts.answer: Enzyme and substrate collide; substrate fits into the complementary active site; an enzyme–substrate complex forms; substrate is broken into products; products leave the active site; enzyme is unchanged and can be used again.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: collision / random movement; substrate binds to active site (complementary shape); enzyme–substrate complex forms; products formed and released; enzyme unchanged / reused.

stem: Some people cannot digest lactose, the sugar in milk. A dairy company in Lahore makes lactose-free milk by adding the enzyme lactase, which breaks lactose into glucose and galactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why lactase breaks down lactose but not sucrose, even though both are disaccharides.
parts.answer: Lactase's active site is complementary only to lactose; sucrose has a different shape so cannot bind / form an enzyme–substrate complex.
parts.working: B1 active site complementary to lactose (specific); B1 sucrose different shape, does not fit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company adds a small amount of lactase to a large tank of milk. Explain why only a small amount of enzyme is needed.
parts.answer: Enzymes are not used up / are unchanged at the end of the reaction, so each enzyme molecule can break down many lactose molecules.
parts.working: B1 not used up / unchanged; B1 reused many times.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mutation in the gene for lactase changes one amino acid in the active site. Suggest how this could affect the enzyme.
parts.answer: The active site may change shape so lactose no longer fits; fewer or no enzyme–substrate complexes; lactose not broken down.
parts.working: 1 mark: active site shape changed; 1 mark: lactose no longer binds / enzyme does not work (or works more slowly).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four tubes each contained 5 cm³ of starch solution at 35 °C:
A: + 1 cm³ amylase
B: + 1 cm³ protease
C: + 1 cm³ amylase that had been boiled and cooled
D: + 1 cm³ water
After 15 minutes a drop from each tube was tested with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the result expected for each tube.
parts.answer: A: orange-brown (no starch); B: blue-black; C: blue-black; D: blue-black
parts.working: 2 marks for all four; 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results show about enzymes.
parts.answer: Only amylase digests starch, so enzymes are specific; boiled amylase does not work because it is denatured.
parts.working: B1 specificity – protease cannot digest starch; B1 boiling denatures amylase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why tube D is included.
parts.answer: Control: shows that starch does not break down without enzyme / that any change is due to the enzyme.
parts.working: B1 control idea, comparison.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the table by naming the missing substances.
Enzyme | substrate | product(s)
amylase | starch | (i) ____
protease | (ii) ____ | amino acids
lipase | fats and oils | (iii) ____
catalase | (iv) ____ | water and oxygen
parts.answer: (i) maltose / simple reducing sugars; (ii) protein; (iii) fatty acids and glycerol; (iv) hydrogen peroxide
parts.working: 1 mark each; (iii) needs both fatty acids and glycerol.

stem:
An enzyme was mixed with a fixed quantity of substrate at its optimum temperature. The mass of product was measured every minute.
time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
mass of product / mg: 0, 8, 16, 22, 26, 28, 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of reaction over the first 2 minutes in mg per minute.
parts.answer: 8 mg per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why no more product forms after 5 minutes.
parts.answer: All the substrate has been used up / converted to product, so there is nothing left for the enzyme to act on; the enzyme is not used up.
parts.working: B1 substrate used up; B1 enzyme still active / not used up (no enzyme–substrate complexes can form).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with twice the concentration of enzyme and the same amount of substrate. Predict the effect on the initial rate and on the final mass of product. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Initial rate higher (about double) because more active sites are available; final mass the same, 28 mg, because the amount of substrate is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: initial rate increases; 1 mark: more active sites / more enzyme–substrate complexes; 1 mark: final mass still 28 mg because same quantity of substrate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student mixed starch solution with amylase and left it at 35 °C for 15 minutes. She then tested a sample of the mixture with Benedict's solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should carry out the Benedict's test on the mixture.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the sample and heat in a hot water-bath (about 80 °C) for a few minutes.
parts.working: B1 add Benedict's solution; B1 heat in a (hot) water-bath.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mixture turned brick red. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Amylase broke down starch into maltose, a reducing sugar, which gives a positive Benedict's test.
parts.working: B1 amylase digested starch; B1 into maltose / reducing sugar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour you would expect if Benedict's test was done on the starch solution before amylase was added.
parts.answer: Blue (no colour change)
parts.working: B1 blue.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why enzymes are important to living organisms.
parts.answer: They speed up metabolic reactions (such as respiration and digestion) so that they happen fast enough at body temperature to keep the organism alive.
parts.working: 1 mark: speed up (metabolic) reactions / catalysts; 1 mark: fast enough at body temperature (low temperatures) to sustain life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A liver cell contains hundreds of different enzymes. Suggest why so many different enzymes are needed.
parts.answer: Each enzyme is specific to one substrate / reaction, and the cell carries out many different reactions.
parts.working: B1 enzymes specific / one substrate each; B1 many different reactions in the cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cells produce antibodies?
A lymphocytes
B phagocytes
C platelets
D red blood cells
parts.answer: A lymphocytes
parts.working: Lymphocytes make antibodies. Phagocytes (B) engulf and digest pathogens; they do not make antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of passive immunity?
A A child is given a polio vaccine by mouth.
B A baby receives antibodies in breast milk.
C A person recovers from chickenpox and does not catch it again.
D A nurse is injected with a weakened measles virus.
parts.answer: B A baby receives antibodies in breast milk.
parts.working: Passive immunity: antibodies made by another person are received. A, C and D all make the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells (active immunity).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does passive immunity give only short-term protection?
A The antibodies received are digested by phagocytes immediately.
B No memory cells are made by the person's own immune system.
C The antigens received are destroyed by the person's antibodies.
D Lymphocytes are killed by the antibodies received.
parts.answer: B No memory cells are made by the person's own immune system.
parts.working: In passive immunity the person's own lymphocytes are not stimulated, so no memory cells form; the received antibodies are gradually broken down. A is the main distractor – antibodies are not engulfed straight away, they last weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the human body stops pathogens from entering it.
parts.answer: Any three of: skin as a barrier; hairs in the nose trap particles; mucus traps pathogens in the airways; hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills pathogens; blood clotting seals wounds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three mechanical / chemical barriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.
parts.answer: Phagocyte
parts.working: B1 phagocyte.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how vaccination gives a child long-term protection against measles.
parts.answer: Vaccine contains weakened / harmless measles pathogen with its antigens; antigens stimulate lymphocytes; lymphocytes produce specific antibodies; memory cells are produced; on later infection memory cells give a faster, larger antibody response, destroying the pathogen before symptoms develop.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: weakened / dead pathogen or its antigens; antigens trigger an immune response; lymphocytes make antibodies; antibodies specific / complementary to the antigen; memory cells made; secondary response faster and greater (more antibodies); pathogen destroyed before disease develops; this is active immunity.

stem:
The concentration of antibodies against a virus was measured in a person's blood. The person was exposed to the virus on day 0 and again on day 30.
day: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 33, 37, 42, 50
antibody concentration / arbitrary units: 0, 2, 12, 20, 9, 3, 40, 160, 120, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the peak antibody concentration was after the second exposure than after the first.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to describe two differences between the responses to the first and second exposures.
parts.answer: Second response is faster: peak reached 7 days after exposure (day 37) instead of 15 days; second response is larger: peak 160 a.u. instead of 20 a.u. (also antibodies stay higher for longer).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two comparative differences, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference in the responses.
parts.answer: The first exposure produced memory cells; on second exposure memory cells recognise the antigen and divide quickly; so antibodies are produced more rapidly and in greater quantity.
parts.working: 1 mark each: memory cells formed after first exposure; memory cells recognise the (same) antigen; rapid production of many antibodies / lymphocytes divide rapidly.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between an antigen and an antibody.
parts.answer: An antigen is a molecule (on the surface of a pathogen) that triggers an immune response; an antibody is a protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
parts.working: B1 antigen – on pathogen / foreign, causes response; B1 antibody – protein made by lymphocytes / binds antigen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why an antibody against the measles virus does not protect against the cholera bacterium.
parts.answer: Antibodies are specific; the antibody's shape is complementary only to the measles antigen.
parts.working: B1 specificity / different antigen shapes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: Antibodies have a shape complementary to a specific antigen; they lock on to the antigens on the pathogen; this leads to direct destruction of the pathogen or marks it so that phagocytes engulf and digest it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: complementary / specific shape; bind / lock on to antigens; pathogen destroyed directly OR marked for phagocytes to engulf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student wrote: 'Antibodies engulf bacteria.' Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Antibodies are protein molecules, not cells; engulfing is done by phagocytes.
parts.working: B1 antibodies are molecules / phagocytes engulf.

stem: In a polio vaccination campaign in one district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 45 120 of the 48 000 children under five years old received the vaccine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of children in the district who were vaccinated. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why vaccinating a high percentage of children also protects the children who were not vaccinated.
parts.answer: Most people are immune, so the virus cannot pass from person to person; fewer infected people to spread it; chance of an unvaccinated child meeting an infected person is very low (herd immunity).
parts.working: 1 mark each: few people can be infected / carry the virus; transmission chain broken / spread reduced; unvaccinated child unlikely to come into contact with pathogen; idea of herd / community immunity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why health workers aim to vaccinate every child, even in a district where 94 % are already vaccinated.
parts.answer: Any remaining unvaccinated group allows the virus to survive and spread / outbreaks can start among the unvaccinated; aim to eradicate the disease.
parts.working: Any one sensible suggestion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the comparison.
(i) Source of antibodies in active immunity.
(ii) Source of antibodies in passive immunity.
(iii) Whether memory cells are made in passive immunity.
parts.answer: (i) the person's own lymphocytes; (ii) another individual, e.g. from the mother across the placenta or in breast milk, or an injection of antibodies; (iii) no
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage to a newborn baby to receive antibodies from its mother.
parts.answer: The baby's immune system has not met these pathogens; maternal antibodies give immediate protection while the baby's own immunity develops.
parts.working: B1 immediate protection / no time needed to make antibodies; B1 baby's immune system immature / not yet exposed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row describes active immunity produced by vaccination?
A antibodies made by the person: yes; memory cells made: yes
B antibodies made by the person: yes; memory cells made: no
C antibodies made by the person: no; memory cells made: yes
D antibodies made by the person: no; memory cells made: no
parts.answer: A antibodies made by the person: yes; memory cells made: yes
parts.working: In active immunity the person's own lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells, giving long-term protection. D describes passive immunity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how mucus and cilia in the trachea help to protect the body from pathogens.
parts.answer: Goblet cells make mucus, which traps pathogens and dust; cilia beat / move the mucus up to the throat; where it is swallowed (and pathogens killed by stomach acid).
parts.working: 1 mark each: mucus traps pathogens; cilia beat / waft; mucus moved upwards to throat / swallowed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why people whose cilia are damaged by smoke get more chest infections.
parts.answer: Mucus and trapped pathogens are not removed, so pathogens stay in the lungs and can multiply.
parts.working: B1 mucus / pathogens not removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how blood clotting acts as a defence against disease.
parts.answer: When skin is cut, platelets cause the soluble protein fibrinogen to be converted to insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh of fibres that traps red blood cells; the clot seals the wound and stops pathogens entering.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fibrinogen (soluble) changed to fibrin (insoluble); mesh / network traps cells; seals wound so pathogens cannot enter (also limits blood loss).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person whose blood does not clot properly is more likely to suffer infections after an injury.
parts.answer: Wound stays open for longer so more pathogens can enter.
parts.working: B1 open wound / entry point for pathogens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person who has had measles rarely catches it again, but people can catch influenza (flu) many times. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: Measles memory cells remain and recognise the same antigens on reinfection; the flu virus mutates and changes its antigens often; so memory cells / antibodies from earlier infections no longer fit the new antigens.
parts.working: 1 mark each: memory cells give long-term immunity to measles; flu virus changes antigens (mutation / new strains); existing antibodies / memory cells specific to old antigen shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a new flu vaccine is often needed each year.
parts.answer: New strains have different antigens, so the vaccine must contain the new antigens.
parts.working: B1 antigens change / new strains.

stem:
A student pressed a finger onto three sterile agar plates: (1) before washing, (2) after washing with water only, (3) after washing with soap and water. The plates were incubated for 3 days and the bacterial colonies were counted.
unwashed: 184 colonies
water only: 112 colonies
soap and water: 23 colonies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of colonies when hands were washed with soap and water, compared with unwashed hands. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a conclusion for this investigation.
parts.answer: Washing hands reduces the number of bacteria transferred; washing with soap and water reduces them much more (87.5 %) than water alone (39.1 %).
parts.working: B1 washing reduces colonies; B1 soap more effective than water alone (data optional).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two safety precautions the student should take with the plates after they have been touched.
parts.answer: Seal the lid with tape and do not open it; incubate at about 25 °C, not 37 °C (to avoid growing human pathogens); dispose of plates by autoclaving; wash hands afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the investigation should be repeated with several students.
parts.answer: Different people's hands carry different numbers of bacteria, so results from one person may not be representative; to find a mean / spot anomalies.
parts.working: B1 representative / identify anomalous results.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by active immunity.
parts.answer: Defence against a pathogen by the body making its own antibodies after infection or vaccination, with memory cells formed.
parts.working: B1 body makes its own antibodies; B1 after exposure to antigen (infection or vaccination) / memory cells formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways a person can gain active immunity.
parts.answer: By catching the disease (natural infection) and by vaccination.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem:
Country X increased the vaccination coverage for measles among young children.
2012: coverage 61 %, measles cases 8640
2022: coverage 91 %, measles cases 1210

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in measles cases between 2012 and 2022. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the rise in vaccination coverage caused the fall in cases.
parts.answer: More children have memory cells / immunity, so fewer can be infected; less transmission of the virus in the population.
parts.working: B1 more people immune (memory cells / antibodies); B1 spread reduced / herd immunity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why there were still measles cases in 2022.
parts.answer: Any two: 9 % of children unvaccinated; some children had only one dose; vaccine not effective in every child; infected travellers bring the virus in; babies too young to be vaccinated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible reasons.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A man in Hyderabad is bitten by a dog that may carry the rabies virus. On the first day, doctors inject him with ready-made rabies antibodies and also give the first dose of rabies vaccine. More vaccine doses are given over the next two weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the injection of ready-made antibodies is given on the first day.
parts.answer: It gives immediate (passive) protection, because the person's own lymphocytes would take days / weeks to make enough antibodies; rabies virus could reach the nervous system before that.
parts.working: B1 immediate protection / antibodies act at once; B1 own immune response too slow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the vaccine is also given.
parts.answer: The injected antibodies are broken down after a few weeks and no memory cells are made; the vaccine stimulates the person's own lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells, giving long-term (active) immunity.
parts.working: B1 passive immunity short-lived / no memory cells; B1 vaccine gives active immunity / memory cells.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.
'Pathogens have molecules called ____ on their surface. White blood cells called ____ make antibodies that fit these molecules. Some of these cells remain in the blood as ____ cells, which give long-term immunity. Other white blood cells, called ____, engulf and digest pathogens.'
parts.answer: antigens; lymphocytes; memory; phagocytes
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The cholera toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine. Which row describes the effect on water potential and water movement?
A water potential of gut contents: increases; water moves: into the cells lining the intestine
B water potential of gut contents: decreases; water moves: into the cells lining the intestine
C water potential of gut contents: increases; water moves: out of the cells into the gut
D water potential of gut contents: decreases; water moves: out of the cells into the gut
parts.answer: D water potential of gut contents: decreases; water moves: out of the cells into the gut
parts.working: Chloride ions lower the water potential of the gut contents, so water leaves the cells (and blood) by osmosis into the lumen, causing watery diarrhoea. B is the common error of linking low water potential with water entering the cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes cholera.
parts.answer: Bacterium
parts.working: B1 bacterium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how cholera is usually transmitted.
parts.answer: By drinking water (or eating food) contaminated with faeces containing the bacterium.
parts.working: B1 contaminated water / food (sewage / faeces).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two symptoms of cholera.
parts.answer: Severe watery diarrhoea and dehydration (also loss of salts / ions, vomiting).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
