parts.answer: (i) Midday: carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf; oxygen diffuses out. (ii) Night: carbon dioxide diffuses out of the leaf; oxygen diffuses into the leaf.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ in by day; B1 O₂ out by day; B1 CO₂ out at night; B1 O₂ in at night.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the direction of diffusion of carbon dioxide changes between day and night.
parts.answer: In daylight photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide faster than respiration produces it, so the concentration inside the leaf is lower than in the air. At night there is only respiration, so carbon dioxide builds up inside the leaf to a higher concentration than outside.
parts.working: B1 day: photosynthesis rate > respiration so CO₂ lower inside; B1 night: only respiration so CO₂ higher inside.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of diffusion into cubes of agar. The agar contains an alkali and a pink indicator that turns colourless when acid reaches it. Include what you would change and measure, the variables you would control, how you would make the results reliable and a safety precaution.
parts.answer: Cut cubes all exactly 1 cm side from the same block of pink agar. Prepare acid at e.g. 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mol/dm³ by diluting stock acid. Place one cube in the same volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of each concentration at the same temperature, and start a stopwatch. Record the time for the cube to become completely colourless. Repeat three times at each concentration and calculate means; calculate rate as 1 ÷ time. Wear eye protection and handle acid carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV acid concentration with ≥5 values; DV time for cube to become colourless (or depth decolourised in fixed time); same size cubes / cut accurately; same volume of acid; same temperature; same agar batch / indicator; cubes fully covered / not stirred or stirred equally; repeats and mean; rate = 1/time; safety: goggles / avoid skin contact with acid.

stem: A drop of food colouring was placed carefully at the bottom of a beaker of still warm water at 40 °C. After 12 minutes the coloured region had spread 36 mm from the drop. The experiment was repeated in a beaker of cold water at 10 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at which the colour spread in the warm water, in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 3.0 mm per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process that made the colour spread.
parts.answer: diffusion
parts.working: B1 diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the cold beaker the colour spread only 14 mm in 12 minutes. State the independent variable in this experiment.
parts.answer: the temperature of the water
parts.working: B1 temperature.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one reason why the beakers must not be moved or stirred during the experiment.
parts.answer: Movement / stirring would mix the dye by currents (mass flow), so the spread would not be due to diffusion alone.
parts.working: B1 stirring mixes dye / not just diffusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each change, state whether the rate of diffusion of oxygen into a cell will increase, decrease or stay the same.
(i) The temperature rises from 20 °C to 30 °C.
(ii) The cell membrane area in contact with the oxygen is made larger.
(iii) The oxygen concentration outside the cell falls until it equals the concentration inside.
(iv) The distance the oxygen has to travel is doubled.
parts.answer: (i) increase (ii) increase (iii) decrease (no net diffusion when equal) (iv) decrease
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose and amino acids enter the blood from the small intestine partly by diffusion. State two features of the villi that increase the rate of diffusion.
parts.answer: Any two: large surface area (many villi, microvilli); thin walls / one cell thick epithelium (short distance); rich network of capillaries; good blood flow removes absorbed food and keeps a steep gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In coeliac disease, eating gluten damages the lining of the small intestine and the villi become flattened. Explain why people with untreated coeliac disease often lose mass even when they eat plenty of food.
parts.answer: Flattened villi give a much smaller surface area, so the rate of diffusion (absorption) of digested food into the blood is reduced; less glucose and amino acids are absorbed and more food is lost in the faeces; less energy is available and body stores are used.
parts.working: B1 smaller surface area; B1 less absorption / diffusion of digested food into blood; B1 less energy / nutrients so body reserves used / mass lost.

stem: Two cubes of gelatine, of side 2 cm and 4 cm, were left in a coloured dye. After 10 minutes the dye had moved 0.3 cm into each cube from every face, leaving an uncoloured cube in the centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each cube, calculate the percentage of its volume that is still uncoloured. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2 cm cube: 34.3 %; 4 cm cube: 61.4 %
parts.working: M1 uncoloured inner cube side = side − 2 × 0.3 (1.4 cm and 3.4 cm); M1 volume = side³ (2.744 cm³ and 39.304 cm³); A1 2.744 ÷ 8 × 100 = 34.3 %; A1 39.304 ÷ 64 × 100 = 61.4 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results suggest about how far cells in a large animal could be from a supply of oxygen.
parts.answer: Diffusion only reaches a short distance in a given time, so in a large block most of the volume is not reached; cells must be close to a surface or a blood capillary (very short diffusion distance) to receive enough oxygen.
parts.working: B1 diffusion is only effective over short distances / large volume not reached; B1 cells must be near a capillary / exchange surface (need transport system).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens during quiet expiration (breathing out at rest)?
A The diaphragm contracts and flattens.
B The ribs move upwards and outwards.
C The volume of the thorax decreases and the pressure inside it increases.
D The external intercostal muscles contract.
parts.answer: C The volume of the thorax decreases and the pressure inside it increases.
parts.working: In quiet expiration the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax, the ribs move down and in and the diaphragm domes up, so thorax volume falls and pressure rises above atmospheric, pushing air out. A, B and D describe inspiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The air pressure inside the lungs was compared with atmospheric pressure at four moments during breathing. At which moment is air flowing into the lungs?
A lung pressure 0.2 kPa above atmospheric
B lung pressure 0.3 kPa below atmospheric
C lung pressure equal to atmospheric
D lung pressure 0.1 kPa above atmospheric
parts.answer: B lung pressure 0.3 kPa below atmospheric
parts.working: Air flows from higher to lower pressure, so it enters only when lung pressure is below atmospheric (during inspiration). When the pressures are equal (C) there is no air flow; A and D are during expiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The statements describe inspiration but are in the wrong order. Write the letters in the correct order.
P  Air moves into the lungs.
Q  The diaphragm muscles and external intercostal muscles contract.
R  The pressure inside the thorax falls below atmospheric pressure.
S  The diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out.
T  The volume of the thorax increases.
parts.answer: Q, S, T, R, P
parts.working: 3 marks for fully correct order; 2 marks if one pair swapped; 1 mark if Q is first and P is last.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the approximate percentage of carbon dioxide in inspired air and in expired air.
parts.answer: Inspired air: about 0.04 %; expired air: about 4 %.
parts.working: B1 inspired air about 0.04 %; B1 expired air about 4 % (accept 3.5–4.0 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test you could use to show that expired air contains water. Give the result.
parts.answer: Breathe onto blue cobalt chloride paper (it turns pink) or onto anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (it turns from white to blue).
parts.working: B1 named test; B1 correct colour change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the approximate percentage of nitrogen in expired air.

stem:
A student's lung volume was recorded every second while resting.
Time / s: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Lung volume / dm³: 2.5, 2.8, 3.0, 2.7, 2.5, 2.8, 3.0, 2.7, 2.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed in with each breath (the tidal volume).
parts.answer: 0.5 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the breathing rate in breaths per minute.
parts.answer: 15 breaths per minute
parts.working: M1 one breath takes 4 s; A1 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed in per minute.
parts.answer: 7.5 dm³ per minute

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether the diaphragm is contracting or relaxing between 0 s and 2 s. Give a reason using the data.
parts.answer: Contracting: the lung volume is increasing (2.5 to 3.0 dm³), which is inspiration.
parts.working: B1 contracting; B1 volume increasing / breathing in.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of food blocks the trachea of a man eating at a wedding. A first-aider stands behind him and makes a sudden, strong upward push just below his ribs, under the diaphragm. Explain, in terms of volume and pressure, how this can force the food out.
parts.answer: The push forces the diaphragm upwards, which suddenly reduces the volume of the thorax (lungs); the pressure of the air in the lungs rises sharply above atmospheric; the air rushes out through the trachea and pushes the food out.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm pushed up; B1 thorax / lung volume decreases; B1 pressure increases so air forced out carrying the food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the man cannot breathe in while the food completely blocks his trachea, even though his diaphragm still contracts.
parts.answer: The volume of the thorax increases and the pressure falls, but no air can flow in through the blocked trachea, so the lungs cannot fill; the trachea is the only route for air to the lungs.
parts.working: B1 pressure falls but air cannot enter; B1 trachea is the only pathway to the lungs / no air reaches alveoli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In normal breathing, describe how air is made to enter the lungs.
parts.answer: The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, increasing the volume of the thorax, so the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric and air is drawn in.
parts.working: B1 muscles contract / thorax volume increases; B1 pressure falls below atmospheric so air enters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient whose breathing muscles are paralysed is put on a ventilator. The machine pushes air into the trachea through a tube at a pressure higher than atmospheric. Compare how air enters the lungs with the ventilator and in normal breathing.
parts.answer: Ventilator: pressure in the airway is raised above atmospheric so air is pushed in and the lungs and chest expand as a result. Normal breathing: the chest expands first and the pressure in the lungs is lowered below atmospheric, so air is pulled in. In both, air moves from higher to lower pressure.
parts.working: B1 ventilator raises pressure (positive pressure) / pushes air in; B1 normal breathing lowers pressure in thorax (air drawn in); B1 in both, air flows from higher to lower pressure / volume change of lungs in both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the patient breathes out when the ventilator stops pushing air in.
parts.answer: The stretched lungs and chest wall recoil (elastic recoil), reducing the volume and raising the pressure, so air leaves.
parts.working: B1 elastic recoil of lungs/chest decreases volume and raises pressure.

stem:
Two students each took the deepest possible breath and then breathed out as far as possible through a tube into an upturned, calibrated bottle full of water. The volume of water pushed out was recorded.
Student P: 3.1, 3.3, 3.2 dm³
Student Q: 4.7, 4.5, 4.6 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume of air breathed out by each student.
parts.answer: P 3.2 dm³; Q 4.6 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much larger Q's mean volume is than P's, as a percentage of P's mean. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the students were able to breathe out more air in this test than in a normal breath at rest.
parts.answer: In forced expiration the internal intercostal muscles contract to pull the ribs down and in, and the abdominal muscles push the diaphragm further up, so the thorax volume becomes smaller than in quiet expiration.
parts.working: B1 internal intercostal muscles contract; B1 abdominal muscles push diaphragm up / volume reduced more.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the volume collected may be less than the true volume of air breathed out.
parts.answer: Any two: some air escapes round the mouthpiece or nose not closed; some carbon dioxide dissolves in the water; the student did not breathe in fully first; the water level was read inaccurately / bottle not calibrated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid sources of error.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The percentage of oxygen was measured in three samples of air from one person at rest.
Inspired air: 20.9 %
Air from deep in the alveoli: 14.0 %
Expired air: 16.0 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in oxygen percentage between expired air and alveolar air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why expired air contains more oxygen than the air in the alveoli.
parts.answer: Expired air is a mixture of alveolar air and air from the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles; this air did not reach the alveoli, so no oxygen was removed from it.
parts.working: B1 expired air mixes with air in the airways; B1 no gas exchange in trachea / bronchi so this air still has about 20.9 % oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the alveolar air always contains a much higher percentage of carbon dioxide than inspired air.
parts.answer: Blood arriving at the lungs carries carbon dioxide from respiration in body cells; it diffuses from the blood into the alveolar air, where its concentration builds up between breaths.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide from respiration carried in blood; B1 diffuses from blood into alveoli.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of the lungs does NOT help gas exchange in the alveoli?
A thin walls of the alveoli
B a good supply of blood capillaries
C a large total surface area
D a thick layer of mucus lining the alveoli
parts.answer: D a thick layer of mucus lining the alveoli
parts.working: A thick layer would increase the diffusion distance and slow gas exchange; alveoli have only a thin film of moisture. A, B and C all increase the rate of diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly describes the cells lining the trachea?
A goblet cells beat to move mucus down into the lungs; ciliated cells make mucus
B goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; ciliated cells beat to move the mucus up towards the throat
C goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; ciliated cells beat to move the mucus down into the lungs
D goblet cells engulf pathogens; ciliated cells make mucus
parts.answer: B goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; ciliated cells beat to move the mucus up towards the throat
parts.working: Goblet cells secrete mucus, which traps particles and pathogens; cilia beat to sweep the mucus up and away from the lungs to the throat, where it is swallowed. C has the direction wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the structure described.
(i) the tube that carries air from the larynx to the chest and is held open by rings of cartilage
(ii) one of the two tubes that branch from the trachea, each leading to one lung
(iii) the narrow tubes that branch many times inside each lung
(iv) the tiny air sacs where gas exchange takes place
parts.answer: (i) trachea (ii) bronchus (iii) bronchioles (iv) alveoli
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) The trachea divides into two bronchi.
(ii) Most gas exchange happens in the bronchi.
(iii) The walls of the alveoli are only one cell thick.
(iv) Oxygen diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
parts.answer: (i) true (ii) false (iii) true (iv) false
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Correct one of the false statements.
parts.answer: Most gas exchange happens in the alveoli; or oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood.
parts.working: B1 either correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway of an oxygen molecule from the air in an alveolus to the inside of a red blood cell. Name the structures it passes through.
parts.answer: It dissolves in the moisture lining the alveolus, diffuses through the thin wall of the alveolus (one cell thick), then through the wall of the capillary (one cell thick), into the blood plasma and then across the membrane of the red blood cell.
parts.working: B1 dissolves in moisture / film of water; B1 through alveolus wall and capillary wall; B1 through plasma into red blood cell (membrane).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oxygen continues to diffuse in this direction.
parts.answer: Breathing keeps bringing fresh air with a high oxygen concentration into the alveoli, and the blood flow carries oxygenated blood away and brings deoxygenated blood, so a concentration gradient is maintained.
parts.working: B1 ventilation keeps alveolar oxygen high; B1 blood flow removes oxygen / brings blood low in oxygen.

stem: In a healthy lung the distance between the air in an alveolus and the blood is about 0.5 µm. In a patient with pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue thickens the walls so that the distance becomes about 2.5 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the diffusion distance is in the patient.
parts.answer: 5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient becomes breathless when walking upstairs.
parts.answer: The longer diffusion distance means oxygen diffuses into the blood more slowly; less oxygen is supplied to the muscles for aerobic respiration during exercise; the brain detects the build-up of carbon dioxide, so the person breathes faster and deeper / feels breathless.
parts.working: B1 slower diffusion of oxygen (and CO₂); B1 less oxygen for respiration in muscles; B1 carbon dioxide builds up / breathing rate increases / breathless.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the patient's lungs also have a smaller volume than a healthy person's lungs.
parts.answer: The scarred / stiff walls cannot stretch as much, so the alveoli do not inflate fully.
parts.working: B1 stiff tissue cannot expand / alveoli do not fill.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student viewed a prepared slide of lung tissue with a microscope and drew one alveolus. The image of the alveolus measured 25 mm across at a magnification of ×100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the alveolus in µm.
parts.answer: 250 µm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mm; A1 × 1000 = 250 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student says that the alveoli look like empty spaces separated by very thin walls. State how this structure helps gas exchange.
parts.answer: The thin walls give a short diffusion distance; many small alveoli give a very large surface area.
parts.working: B1 thin walls / short distance; B1 large surface area.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature, other than thin walls and large surface area, that the student would expect to see close to each alveolus if the tissue was stained to show blood.
parts.answer: Many blood capillaries (containing red blood cells) surrounding each alveolus.
parts.working: B1 capillaries / rich blood supply.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The trachea of an adult is about 120 mm long. In a healthy person, the cilia move mucus up the trachea at about 5 mm per minute. Scientists found that after several days of breathing heavy winter smog, the rate fell to 1.5 mm per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for mucus to travel the length of the trachea (i) in a healthy person and (ii) after breathing heavily polluted smog.
parts.answer: (i) 24 minutes (ii) 80 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the cells lining the trachea normally protect the gas exchange surfaces.
parts.answer: Goblet cells secrete mucus, which traps dust particles and pathogens; ciliated cells have cilia that beat to move the mucus up the trachea to the throat, where it is swallowed, so the particles and pathogens do not reach the alveoli.
parts.working: B1 goblet cells make mucus; B1 mucus traps particles / pathogens; B1 cilia beat / sweep mucus up to throat away from lungs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why people living in a city during winter smog are more likely to suffer from chest infections.
parts.answer: Mucus is moved more slowly so it stays longer in the airways; trapped pathogens have more time to multiply and reach the lungs / bronchi and cause infection.
parts.working: B1 slower clearance / mucus builds up; B1 pathogens remain longer / reach lungs / breed in mucus.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Lung surface areas and body masses of two mammals:
Mouse: lung surface area 0.07 m², body mass 0.025 kg
Human: lung surface area 70 m², body mass 70 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the lungs per kg of body mass for each mammal.
parts.answer: mouse 2.8 m² per kg; human 1.0 m² per kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mouse needs a larger lung surface area per kg of body mass than the human.
parts.answer: A mouse has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat faster; it must respire faster per kg to keep its body temperature constant, so it needs more oxygen per kg each minute.
parts.working: B1 mouse loses heat faster (large SA:V); B1 higher rate of respiration per kg / more oxygen needed per kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two features, other than a large surface area, that both mammals' gas exchange surfaces must have.
parts.answer: Any two: thin (short diffusion distance); moist; good blood supply; good ventilation with air.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: During an asthma attack, the muscle in the walls of the bronchioles contracts, making them narrower. Name the tubes that lead from the trachea to the bronchioles.
parts.answer: bronchi
parts.working: B1 bronchi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person having an asthma attack feels short of breath.
parts.answer: Narrower bronchioles let less air reach the alveoli each breath, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood (and less carbon dioxide is removed).
parts.working: B1 less air reaches alveoli; B1 less oxygen into blood / less gas exchange.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Extra mucus is also made during an asthma attack. Name the cells that make mucus.
parts.answer: goblet cells
parts.working: B1 goblet cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How does breathing change when a person starts to run?
A The rate increases but the depth stays the same.
B The rate and the depth both increase.
C The depth increases but the rate decreases.
D The rate and depth both stay the same but more oxygen is absorbed per breath.
parts.answer: B The rate and the depth both increase.
parts.working: During physical activity both the breathing rate and the depth of each breath increase, so more air is exchanged per minute. A misses the increase in depth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four athletes had their breathing measured during a training session. Which athlete breathed the largest volume of air per minute?
A 30 breaths per minute, 0.4 dm³ per breath
B 20 breaths per minute, 0.8 dm³ per breath
C 40 breaths per minute, 0.3 dm³ per breath
D 16 breaths per minute, 0.9 dm³ per breath
parts.answer: B 20 breaths per minute, 0.8 dm³ per breath
parts.working: Volume per minute = rate × depth: A 12.0, B 16.0, C 12.0, D 14.4 dm³ per minute. C has the fastest rate but shallow breaths, so a smaller volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student holds her breath for 30 seconds. Name the gas that builds up in her blood.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which organ detects this change.
parts.answer: the brain
parts.working: B1 brain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When she starts breathing again, she breathes faster and more deeply for a short time. Explain why.
parts.answer: The higher carbon dioxide concentration in the blood is detected by the brain, which increases the rate and depth of breathing to remove the extra carbon dioxide (and take in oxygen).
parts.working: B1 high CO₂ detected / brain sends impulses to breathing muscles; B1 faster deeper breathing removes CO₂.

stem:
A student ran on a treadmill at different speeds. Her breathing was measured after 3 minutes at each speed.
Speed / km per hour: 0, 4, 8, 12
Volume per breath / dm³: 0.5, 1.0, 1.8, 2.4
Breathing rate / breaths per minute: 12, 16, 24, 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at each speed.
parts.answer: 0 km/h: 6.0 dm³, 4 km/h: 16.0 dm³, 8 km/h: 43.2 dm³, 12 km/h: 76.8 dm³
parts.working: M1 tidal volume × rate; A1 all four correct (6.0, 16.0, 43.2, 76.8).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the volume per minute is at 12 km/h than at rest.
parts.answer: 12.8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the volume of air breathed per minute increases with running speed.
parts.answer: Faster running needs more energy, so the muscles respire faster; they need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide; the increase in blood carbon dioxide is detected by the brain, which increases the rate and depth of breathing.
parts.working: B1 more (aerobic) respiration in muscles; B1 more oxygen needed / more CO₂ produced; B1 CO₂ detected by brain → rate and depth increase.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Climbers who go to high mountain base camps in Gilgit-Baltistan breathe air that still contains 21 % oxygen, but the air is much less dense, so each breath contains fewer oxygen molecules. Suggest why climbers breathe faster and deeper than normal even when resting at base camp.
parts.answer: Less oxygen enters the blood with each breath, so less oxygen reaches respiring cells; the body responds by increasing the rate and depth of breathing to take in more air per minute, so that enough oxygen is absorbed.
parts.working: B1 fewer oxygen molecules per breath / less oxygen diffuses into blood; B1 cells need oxygen for aerobic respiration; B1 faster, deeper breathing increases volume of air per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why climbing a slope at high altitude makes climbers more breathless than the same climb at sea level.
parts.answer: Exercise increases the demand for oxygen and carbon dioxide production, but each breath supplies less oxygen; breathing has to increase even more to meet the demand.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen needed for muscle respiration; B1 less available per breath so breathing must increase further / breathless.

stem:
A student did step-ups for different lengths of time. After each exercise period she recorded how long it took for her breathing rate to return to its resting value.
Duration of exercise / minutes: 1, 2, 3, 4
Recovery time / minutes: 1.5, 2.5, 4.0, 6.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the duration of exercise and the recovery time.
parts.answer: The longer the exercise, the longer the recovery time; the recovery time increases more steeply for longer exercise (+1.0, +1.5, +2.0 minutes).
parts.working: B1 positive relationship; B1 increases more steeply / not proportional, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in recovery time between 1 minute and 4 minutes of exercise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the breathing rate stays high after the exercise stops.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide (and lactic acid) built up during exercise must be removed; extra oxygen is needed to break down lactic acid (repay the oxygen debt), so breathing stays fast until the blood carbon dioxide concentration returns to normal.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ still high in blood / detected by brain; B1 oxygen needed to remove lactic acid / oxygen debt.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: the same student; type / intensity of exercise (e.g. same step height and stepping rate); starting from rest each time with time to recover; same temperature; same method of counting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the intensity of exercise affects the breathing rate of students. Use step-ups on a bench: intensity can be changed by changing the number of steps per minute (use a metronome). Include what you would change and measure, the variables you would control, how you would make the results reliable and one safety consideration.
parts.answer: Use stepping rates of e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 steps per minute set by a metronome. Before each trial the student rests until the breathing rate is at its resting value; count breaths for 1 minute at rest. Step for a fixed time (e.g. 2 minutes) on the same bench, then immediately count breaths for 1 minute (or count for 30 s and double). Keep the same student(s), bench height and duration. Repeat each intensity three times (or use several students) and calculate means. Stop if the student feels unwell; students with asthma or heart problems should not take part.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV stepping rate with ≥4 values; DV breaths per minute counted for a fixed time immediately after; measure resting rate first / rest between trials until back to resting rate; same duration of exercise; same bench height; same person / similar age, sex, fitness; repeat and calculate mean; safety (stop if dizzy; exclude those with medical conditions).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the flow chart using suitable words.

exercise starts → muscle cells need more ______ → rate of ______ in muscles increases → more ______ is produced and passes into the blood → this is detected by the ______ → rate and ______ of breathing increase
parts.answer: energy; respiration; carbon dioxide; brain; depth
parts.working: 1 mark per gap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During hard exercise the athlete absorbs 3.0 dm³ of oxygen per minute. Each dm³ of air breathed in gives 0.05 dm³ of oxygen to the blood. Calculate the volume of air the athlete must breathe each minute.
parts.answer: 60 dm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each breath has a volume of 2.0 dm³. Calculate the breathing rate needed.
parts.answer: 30 breaths per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: At rest the athlete absorbs 0.25 dm³ of oxygen per minute. Calculate how many times more oxygen is absorbed per minute during hard exercise.
parts.answer: 12 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the muscles need so much more oxygen during hard exercise.
parts.answer: The muscles contract more and need much more energy; this is released by aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen.
parts.working: B1 more energy needed for muscle contraction; B1 aerobic respiration uses oxygen.

stem:
Two swimmers at a club in Karachi swam 200 m at the same speed. One trains every day; the other rarely exercises.
Trained: breathing rate 26 breaths per minute, volume per breath 1.8 dm³
Untrained: breathing rate 40 breaths per minute, volume per breath 1.1 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between the breathing of the two swimmers during the swim.
parts.answer: The trained swimmer's breathing rate rose less (to 26 compared with 40 breaths per minute) and each breath was deeper (1.8 dm³ compared with 1.1 dm³).
parts.working: B1 rate lower in trained swimmer with data; B1 depth greater in trained swimmer with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the trained swimmer can take deeper breaths.
parts.answer: Any two: stronger diaphragm and intercostal muscles; larger lung volume / chest expands more after training; better control of breathing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible suggestions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute by each swimmer during the swim.
parts.answer: trained 46.8 dm³; untrained 44.0 dm³

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student breathes in and out of a paper bag for one minute while sitting still. The percentage of carbon dioxide in the air in the bag rises. Explain why the student's breathing rate and depth increase, even though the student is not exercising.
parts.answer: The air breathed in from the bag has a higher carbon dioxide concentration, so the concentration gradient between the blood and the alveoli is smaller; less carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood, so its concentration in the blood rises; this is detected by the brain, which sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to increase the rate and depth of breathing.
parts.working: B1 more CO₂ in inspired air; B1 smaller gradient / less CO₂ diffuses out of blood; B1 blood CO₂ rises and is detected by brain; B1 brain stimulates breathing muscles (diaphragm/intercostals) → faster, deeper breathing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this experiment should be stopped after a short time.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide would keep rising and oxygen falling in the bag, which could make the student dizzy or ill.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ builds up / O₂ falls → unsafe.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is pollination?
A the fusion of a male nucleus with a female nucleus
B the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma
C the growth of a pollen tube down the style
D the release of seeds from a fruit
parts.answer: B the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma
parts.working: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. A is fertilisation, which happens later, after the pollen tube (C) reaches the ovule.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why do insect-pollinated flowers usually produce nectar?
A To keep the stigma moist so that pollen can germinate
B To attract insects, which feed on it and carry pollen from flower to flower
C To make the pollen grains heavier so that they fall onto the stigma
D To provide food for the developing embryo inside the seed
parts.answer: B To attract insects, which feed on it and carry pollen from flower to flower
parts.working: Nectar is a sugary reward that attracts insects, which brush against the anthers and carry pollen to other flowers. A and C are not functions of nectar (the stigma is not kept moist by nectar and the pollen weight is unchanged); D confuses nectar with stored food in the seed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each part of a flower.
(i) sepal (ii) petal (iii) filament (iv) ovule
parts.answer: (i) protects the flower when it is a bud (ii) attracts insects (for pollination) (iii) holds up / supports the anther (iv) contains the female gamete (egg cell nucleus); becomes the seed after fertilisation
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Two chilli plants, X and Y, are growing in a garden. Plant X has flowers 1 and 2. Plant Y has flowers 3 and 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each transfer of pollen, state whether it is self-pollination or cross-pollination.
(i) from the anther of flower 1 to the stigma of flower 1
(ii) from the anther of flower 1 to the stigma of flower 2
(iii) from the anther of flower 2 to the stigma of flower 3
(iv) from the anther of flower 3 to the stigma of flower 4
parts.answer: (i) self (ii) self (iii) cross (iv) self
parts.working: 1 mark each. Flowers 1 and 2 are on the same plant, so (ii) is self-pollination; (iii) is between different plants, so cross-pollination; flowers 3 and 4 are on the same plant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of the offspring produced after cross-pollination that is less likely after self-pollination.
parts.answer: More genetic variation among the offspring.
parts.working: B1 more variation / new combinations of alleles.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some flowers, the anthers release their pollen several days before the stigma of the same flower is ready to receive pollen. Suggest and explain the advantage of this to the species.
parts.answer: It prevents self-pollination within the same flower, so pollen must come from another plant (cross-pollination); this increases genetic variation in the offspring, so the species is more likely to survive changes in the environment / new diseases.
parts.working: B1 prevents / reduces self-pollination; B1 promotes cross-pollination; B1 more variation → better chance of adapting / surviving environmental change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage to a plant of depending only on cross-pollination.
parts.answer: If pollinators are scarce or there are no other plants of the species nearby, no seeds are produced.
parts.working: B1 depends on pollinators / other plants being present.

stem:
In spring, many people in Islamabad suffer from allergies caused by pollen from paper mulberry trees. The number of pollen grains per m³ of air was recorded each day for one week.
Day: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
Pollen grains per m³: 3200, 4500, 7800, 6100, 1200, 900, 5300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean daily pollen count for the week.
parts.answer: 4143 grains per m³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rain fell on day 5 and day 6. Suggest why the pollen counts were low on these days.
parts.answer: Rain washes pollen out of the air / wet anthers do not release pollen and pollen is not carried far by wind.
parts.working: B1 rain removes pollen from air; B1 wet pollen / anthers not released or not blown.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The paper mulberry tree is wind-pollinated. Explain why wind-pollinated plants release such large numbers of pollen grains.
parts.answer: Pollen is carried randomly by the wind and most grains never land on a stigma of the same species; producing huge numbers makes it likely that some will reach a stigma.
parts.working: B1 transfer by wind is random / most pollen wasted; B1 increases chance some reaches a stigma.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Date palms have separate male trees and female trees. In date orchards in Sindh, farmers climb female trees and tie strands of male flowers among the female flowers. Name this process and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: Hand pollination (artificial pollination). Each tree has flowers of one sex only, so pollen must reach the female flowers from a male tree; wind alone is unreliable and the farmer plants few male trees, so tying male flowers among the female ones makes sure that pollen reaches the stigmas.
parts.working: B1 (artificial / hand) pollination; B1 pollen must come from a different (male) tree / cross-pollination needed; B1 ensures pollen reaches stigmas so more fruits / dates form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why farmers grow only a few male trees in an orchard.
parts.answer: Male trees do not produce fruit; one male tree can provide enough pollen for many female trees, so more space is used for fruit-bearing trees.
parts.working: B1 male trees produce no dates / one male supplies many females.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what develops from the ovary of a date flower after fertilisation.
parts.answer: the fruit (the date)
parts.working: B1 fruit.

stem:
A student studied 150 flowers on mustard plants in a field near Faisalabad. 50 flowers were left open, 50 were covered with fine mesh bags that kept out insects, and 50 were bagged and then hand-pollinated with a brush. The number of flowers that formed fruits was counted.
Open: 48
Bagged: 6
Bagged and hand-pollinated: 45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of flowers that formed fruits in each group.
parts.answer: open 96 %; bagged 12 %; bagged and hand-pollinated 90 %
parts.working: M1 number ÷ 50 × 100; A1 all three correct (96, 12, 90).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the results show about how this plant is normally pollinated.
parts.answer: It is mainly pollinated by insects (animals): when insects were kept out, very few fruits formed.
parts.working: B1 insect pollinated; B1 bagged flowers formed far fewer fruits (12 % compared with 96 %).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the third group, bagged and hand-pollinated, was included.
parts.answer: To show that the bag itself did not stop fruit forming (for example by changing temperature or damaging the flower); when pollen was supplied, fruits formed, so the lack of pollen was the cause.
parts.working: B1 control for effect of the bag; B1 shows lack of pollination (not the bag) caused low fruit set.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a few fruits still formed in the bagged group.
parts.answer: Some self-pollination occurred within the bag (or pollen got in / tiny insects got through the mesh).
parts.working: B1 self-pollination / some pollen entered.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which the pollen of a wind-pollinated flower differs from the pollen of an insect-pollinated flower.
parts.answer: Wind pollen is smaller and lighter; it is smooth (not sticky or spiky).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two comparative points (smaller/lighter; smooth, not sticky or spiky).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each difference helps wind pollination.
parts.answer: Small, light grains are carried further by air currents; smooth, non-sticky grains do not clump together and are easily released and blown away from the anther.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a linked explanation: size/weight → carried far by the wind; smooth, not sticky → not clumped, released easily.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the human male, which tube carries both urine and semen out of the body (at different times)?
A sperm duct
B urethra
C ureter
D oviduct
parts.answer: B urethra
parts.working: The urethra runs through the penis and carries urine from the bladder and semen during ejaculation. The ureter (C) carries urine from kidney to bladder only; the sperm duct (A) carries sperm only.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly compares a human sperm cell with a human egg cell?
A sperm: large, has energy stores, not able to move; egg: small, able to swim
B sperm: small, able to swim using a flagellum, few energy stores; egg: large, not able to swim, has energy stores in its cytoplasm
C sperm: small, 46 chromosomes; egg: large, 23 chromosomes
D sperm: small, able to swim, many energy stores; egg: large, able to swim, few energy stores
parts.answer: B sperm: small, able to swim using a flagellum, few energy stores; egg: large, not able to swim, has energy stores in its cytoplasm
parts.working: A sperm is small and motile (flagellum) with little cytoplasm; an egg is much larger, not motile, with energy stores. Both gametes have 23 chromosomes, so C is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each structure in the male reproductive system.
(i) scrotum (ii) sperm duct (iii) prostate gland (iv) penis
parts.answer: (i) holds the testes outside the body (at a lower temperature) (ii) carries sperm from the testis to the urethra (iii) produces fluid that is added to sperm to make semen (iv) passes semen into the vagina during sexual intercourse (and urine out)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the structures, in order, through which an egg cell passes from where it is released to where an embryo implants.
parts.answer: ovary → oviduct → uterus
parts.working: B1 oviduct; B1 uterus (in correct order after ovary).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where sperm are deposited during sexual intercourse.
parts.answer: the vagina (near the cervix)
parts.working: B1 vagina.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the ring of muscle at the lower end of the uterus.
parts.answer: cervix
parts.working: B1 cervix.

stem:
A fertility clinic tested semen samples from two men.
Man A: 60 million sperm per cm³, volume 3.0 cm³
Man B: 4 million sperm per cm³, volume 2.5 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of sperm in one sample for each man. Give your answers in millions.
parts.answer: man A 180 million; man B 10 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more sperm there are in man A's sample.
parts.answer: 18 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only one sperm fertilises an egg. Suggest why man B is less likely to father a child.
parts.answer: Most sperm die or are lost on the way through the uterus and oviducts and only a few reach the egg; with a low count it is likely that none reach the egg; many sperm may be needed to break through the layers around the egg.
parts.working: B1 most sperm do not reach the oviduct / die on the way; B1 fewer sperm → lower chance any reach / penetrate the egg.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a vasectomy, a small section of each sperm duct is cut and the ends are tied. Explain why the man can no longer father children.
parts.answer: Sperm made in the testes cannot pass along the sperm ducts to the urethra, so the semen contains no sperm and no egg can be fertilised.
parts.working: B1 sperm cannot leave the testes / reach the urethra; B1 no sperm in semen so no fertilisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After a vasectomy, the man still produces semen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Most of the fluid in semen comes from glands such as the prostate gland, which join the pathway after the cut, so fluid is still released.
parts.working: B1 fluid made by prostate gland (and other glands); B1 these add fluid beyond / below the cut point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some infections can scar and block both oviducts. Explain why a woman with blocked oviducts may be unable to become pregnant, even though she ovulates normally.
parts.answer: Sperm cannot travel up the oviduct to reach the egg, and the egg cannot pass along the oviduct; fertilisation normally takes place in the oviduct, so no zygote forms (and an embryo could not reach the uterus).
parts.working: B1 sperm cannot reach the egg; B1 fertilisation normally in oviduct; B1 egg / embryo cannot reach uterus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In in vitro fertilisation (IVF), eggs are collected directly from the ovaries and mixed with sperm in a dish. Embryos are then placed in the uterus. Explain why IVF can help this woman.
parts.answer: IVF bypasses the oviducts: fertilisation happens outside the body, and the embryo is put directly into the uterus, where it can implant.
parts.working: B1 oviducts not needed / bypassed; B1 embryo placed in uterus to implant.

stem: In this question, assume that a sperm swims at 3 mm per minute and must travel 180 mm from the cervix to an egg in the oviduct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for a sperm to swim from the cervix to the egg, in minutes.
parts.answer: 60 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the roles of the mitochondria and the flagellum of a sperm cell.
parts.answer: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration for swimming; the flagellum is a whip-like tail that uses this energy to beat and drive the sperm forward.
parts.working: B1 mitochondria: energy release by respiration for swimming; B1 flagellum: whip-like tail that moves the sperm forward.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After one sperm enters the egg, the jelly coat changes. Explain why this is important.
parts.answer: It stops any other sperm entering the egg, so only one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus and the zygote has the correct number of chromosomes (46).
parts.working: B1 prevents more sperm entering; B1 so zygote has correct chromosome number / only one set from father.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student looked at a stained sample of bull semen with a microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The image of one whole sperm measured 55 mm long at a magnification of ×1000. Calculate the actual length of the sperm in µm.
parts.answer: 55 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student counted the sperm in five squares of a counting slide: 12, 15, 9, 14, 10. Calculate the mean number per square.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted sperm in five squares instead of one.
parts.answer: The sperm are not spread evenly, so a mean of several squares is more representative / reliable.
parts.working: B1 more representative / reliable mean.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one feature of the sperm that the student would see that helps it swim to the egg.
parts.answer: a long flagellum (tail)
parts.working: B1 flagellum.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the function of each part of a human egg cell.
(i) jelly coat (ii) cytoplasm (iii) nucleus
parts.answer: (i) protects the egg / changes after fertilisation so that only one sperm can enter (ii) contains energy stores for the early embryo (iii) contains the genetic material (23 chromosomes) from the mother
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where egg cells are produced.
parts.answer: the ovaries
parts.working: B1 ovary.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone causes the development of breasts and the widening of the hips in girls at puberty?
A testosterone
B oestrogen
C insulin
D adrenaline
parts.answer: B oestrogen
parts.working: Oestrogen from the ovaries controls the female secondary sexual characteristics. Testosterone (A) controls the male ones.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row shows the hormone that triggers ovulation and the gland that secretes it?
A FSH, ovary
B LH, pituitary gland
C progesterone, ovary
D oestrogen, pituitary gland
parts.answer: B LH, pituitary gland
parts.working: A surge of LH from the pituitary gland causes the egg to be released. FSH (A) is also from the pituitary, not the ovary, and stimulates follicle development; progesterone maintains the uterus lining.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three secondary sexual characteristics that develop in girls during puberty.
parts.answer: Any three: breasts develop; hips widen; pubic and underarm hair grows; menstrual cycle begins; more fat deposited under the skin.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes oestrogen.
parts.answer: the ovary
parts.working: B1 ovary.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table for a typical 28-day menstrual cycle.
Days 1–5: ______
Days 6–13: the lining of the uterus ______
Day 14 (about): ______
Days 15–28: the lining of the uterus is ______
parts.answer: Days 1–5: menstruation (the uterus lining breaks down and is lost); days 6–13: thickens / repairs; day 14: ovulation (an egg is released from an ovary); days 15–28: maintained (kept thick, ready for implantation)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem:
The concentration of progesterone in a woman's blood was measured during one 28-day cycle (arbitrary units).
Day: 1, 7, 14, 21, 28
Progesterone: 1, 1, 2, 15, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the day on which progesterone concentration was highest.
parts.answer: day 21
parts.working: B1 day 21.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes progesterone in this cycle.
parts.answer: the ovary
parts.working: B1 ovary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the role of progesterone in the second half of the cycle.
parts.answer: It maintains the thick lining of the uterus (keeps it ready for an embryo to implant) and inhibits the release of FSH and LH.
parts.working: B1 maintains uterus lining; B1 inhibits FSH / LH (prevents another ovulation).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what happens to the uterus lining after day 25 if no embryo implants.
parts.answer: Progesterone concentration falls, so the uterus lining is no longer maintained; it breaks down and is lost in menstruation.
parts.working: B1 progesterone falls; B1 lining breaks down → menstruation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the hormone secreted by the testes and state one secondary sexual characteristic it causes in boys.
parts.answer: Testosterone; any one: growth of facial / body / pubic hair; voice deepens; muscles develop; growth of penis and testes; shoulders broaden.
parts.working: B1 testosterone; B1 any one characteristic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 16-year-old boy's testes produce very little testosterone because of a medical condition. Suggest two ways in which his development would differ from that of other boys of the same age.
parts.answer: Any two: little facial or body hair; voice does not deepen; less muscle development; reproductive organs stay small / no sperm production.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how doctors could treat this condition.
parts.answer: Give him testosterone (hormone treatment, e.g. injections).
parts.working: B1 testosterone / hormone replacement.

stem:
A woman recorded her body temperature every morning before getting up.
Days 10–14: 36.4, 36.3, 36.4, 36.5, 36.4 °C
Day 15: 36.4 °C; day 16: 36.7 °C
Days 17–21: 36.8, 36.9, 36.8, 36.7, 36.8 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean temperature for days 10–14 and for days 17–21, and the difference between them.
parts.answer: 36.40 °C; 36.80 °C; difference 0.40 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Progesterone causes a small rise in body temperature. Use this information to suggest on which day ovulation took place. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: About day 15 (accept day 14 or 15): the temperature rises on day 16, after the progesterone rise that follows ovulation, so ovulation happened just before the rise.
parts.working: B1 day 15 (accept 14–15); B1 temperature rise follows ovulation as progesterone increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why recording temperature alone cannot be used to predict the day of ovulation in advance.
parts.answer: The temperature rises only after ovulation has happened (and illness or room temperature can also change body temperature).
parts.working: B1 rise happens after ovulation / other factors affect temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A school nurse asked ten Year 11 students, who agreed to take part anonymously, the age at which their menstrual cycle started.
Ages / years: 11.5, 12.0, 12.5, 13.0, 12.0, 11.0, 13.5, 12.5, 12.0, 14.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean age at which menstruation started for this group.
parts.answer: 12.4 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of the ages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the hormone that causes the development of the uterus lining during each cycle after puberty.
parts.answer: oestrogen
parts.working: B1 oestrogen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the results from ten students may not represent all girls in the city.
parts.answer: The sample is very small / from one school only.
parts.working: B1 small sample / not random.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the table for the four hormones of the menstrual cycle. For each hormone state where it is made and one role.
FSH; LH; oestrogen; progesterone
parts.answer:
FSH – pituitary gland – stimulates a follicle (egg) to develop in the ovary / stimulates oestrogen secretion.
LH – pituitary gland – causes ovulation.
Oestrogen – ovary – causes the uterus lining to thicken (repair).
Progesterone – ovary – maintains the uterus lining.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hormone with both site and role correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During pregnancy the concentration of progesterone stays high. Explain how this prevents menstruation.
parts.answer: Progesterone maintains the thick uterus lining, so it does not break down; menstruation only happens when progesterone falls.
parts.working: B1 progesterone maintains lining; B1 lining not lost because progesterone does not fall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pregnant woman does not ovulate.
parts.answer: High progesterone (and oestrogen) inhibits the secretion of FSH and LH by the pituitary gland, so no new follicles develop and no LH surge triggers ovulation.
parts.working: B1 FSH / LH inhibited; B1 no follicle development / no LH surge so no ovulation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organ that takes over the secretion of progesterone later in pregnancy.
parts.answer: the placenta
parts.working: B1 placenta.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the offspring produced by asexual reproduction?
A They are genetically identical to each other and to the parent.
B They have genes from two parents.
C They are formed by the fusion of gametes.
D They show more variation than offspring from sexual reproduction.
parts.answer: A They are genetically identical to each other and to the parent.
parts.working: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gametes, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and each other. B and C describe sexual reproduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of statements are both advantages to a species of sexual reproduction rather than asexual reproduction?
1 It produces offspring with genetic variation.
2 Only one parent is needed.
3 The species is more likely to survive a change in the environment.
4 Large numbers of offspring are produced quickly.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 3
C 2 and 4
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1 and 3
parts.working: Variation (1) means some individuals may survive new diseases or conditions (3). Needing one parent (2) and rapid production of many offspring (4) are advantages of asexual reproduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each example is asexual or sexual reproduction.
(i) a bacterium dividing into two
(ii) new garlic plants growing from the cloves of one bulb
(iii) a mango tree growing from a seed
(iv) new ginger shoots growing from pieces of an underground stem (rhizome)
parts.answer: (i) asexual (ii) asexual (iii) sexual (iv) asexual
parts.working: 1 mark each. The seed (iii) forms after fertilisation of an ovule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define sexual reproduction.
parts.answer: A process involving the fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote, producing offspring that are genetically different from each other.
parts.working: B1 fusion of nuclei of (male and female) gametes / forms zygote; B1 offspring genetically different.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dog has 78 chromosomes in each body cell. State the number of chromosomes in (i) a dog sperm cell and (ii) a dog zygote.
parts.working: B1 39 (haploid); B1 78 (diploid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why gametes must have half the number of chromosomes of body cells.
parts.answer: When two gametes fuse at fertilisation their nuclei combine; if gametes were not haploid the chromosome number would double each generation; haploid gametes give a diploid zygote with the normal number.
parts.working: B1 two gametes fuse / nuclei combine; B1 keeps chromosome number constant (diploid zygote) between generations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sugarcane farmers in Pakistan usually plant pieces of stem, called setts, instead of seeds. Give two advantages to the farmer of growing sugarcane from setts.
parts.answer: Any two: all plants are genetically identical to a high-yielding parent, so the crop is uniform and keeps the good features; plants grow faster / establish more quickly than from seed; no pollination needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plant breeders who want to produce a new variety of sugarcane that resists a disease use sexual reproduction. Explain why.
parts.answer: Sexual reproduction mixes genetic material from two parents, giving offspring with new combinations of features (variation); breeders can select individuals that resist the disease; asexual reproduction only produces copies with no new features.
parts.working: B1 two parents / fusion of gametes; B1 variation / new combinations; B1 allows selection of resistant plants (asexual gives only clones).

stem: A small number of yeast cells were added to fruit juice at 5000 cells per cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of yeast cells per cm³ after 9 hours, assuming the number doubles every 90 minutes and no cells die.
parts.answer: 320000 cells per cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Yeast cells reproduce by budding, a type of asexual reproduction. Explain one advantage of this to yeast growing in sugary fruit juice.
parts.answer: It is fast and needs only one parent, so the yeast can quickly increase its population and use the food source before competitors.
parts.working: B1 rapid / one parent / no need to find a mate; B1 can exploit the food quickly / colonise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the population would not keep doubling for several days.
parts.answer: The sugar would be used up and waste products such as ethanol would build up, so the cells would stop dividing or die.
parts.working: B1 food / sugar runs out; B1 toxic waste (ethanol) accumulates / limited space.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identical twins form when a zygote divides into two cells that separate and each develops into a baby. Explain why identical twins are genetically identical.
parts.answer: Both come from the same zygote, formed by one sperm and one egg; the cells divide by mitosis, which produces genetically identical cells.
parts.working: B1 from one zygote / same sperm and egg; B1 mitosis gives identical copies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says, 'Identical twins are produced by asexual reproduction.' Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: The zygote was formed by sexual reproduction – fusion of gametes from two parents; the twins differ genetically from both parents, whereas asexual offspring are identical to their single parent.
parts.working: B1 zygote formed by fusion of gametes / two parents; B1 twins are not identical to the parents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Non-identical twins form when two eggs are each fertilised by a different sperm. Explain why non-identical twins are no more similar genetically than ordinary brothers and sisters.
parts.answer: Each twin comes from a different egg and sperm, each with a different combination of alleles.
parts.working: B1 different gametes / different combination of genes.

stem:
A student took five stem cuttings from one money plant and stood them in jars of water on a windowsill. After 14 days she counted the roots on each cutting.
Number of roots: 8, 11, 9, 12, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of roots per cutting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is sexual or asexual reproduction. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Asexual: only one parent is involved and no gametes fuse.
parts.working: B1 asexual; B1 one parent / no gametes / no fertilisation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using cuttings from one parent plant is useful when testing the effect of a rooting powder on root growth.
parts.answer: All the cuttings are genetically identical, so genetic differences cannot affect the results; any difference is due to the rooting powder (fair test).
parts.working: B1 genetically identical; B1 removes genetic variation as a variable / fairer comparison.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one variable, other than the type of plant, that should be kept the same for all cuttings.
parts.answer: Any one: length of cutting / number of leaves; volume of water; temperature; light; time.
parts.working: B1 any valid variable.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of sexual reproduction to a species.
parts.answer: Any two: produces genetic variation; species can adapt to changes in the environment / more likely to survive new diseases; seeds can be dispersed to new areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of sexual reproduction.
parts.answer: Any two: two parents are needed (finding a mate / pollinator); slower; more energy used (e.g. making flowers, nectar, many gametes); good combinations of features may be lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cheetahs have very little genetic variation; individuals are nearly as alike genetically as identical twins. Suggest why a new disease is a greater threat to cheetahs than to a species with more variation.
parts.answer: If all individuals are genetically similar, any individual that is susceptible means that all are likely to be susceptible; there are unlikely to be any individuals with alleles giving resistance; so the disease could kill most of the population.
parts.working: B1 little variation / all similar; B1 no resistant individuals likely; B1 whole population could be wiped out (species could become extinct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Zoos sometimes move male cheetahs between zoos in different countries for breeding. Explain how this helps to conserve the species.
parts.answer: It allows breeding between less closely related animals, so sexual reproduction combines more different alleles, increasing genetic variation in the offspring.
parts.working: B1 unrelated / different populations; B1 increases variation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these stages in the correct order, starting with fertilisation.
implantation in the lining of the uterus; fetus with recognisable organs; fertilisation in the oviduct; zygote divides to form a ball of cells (embryo)
parts.answer: fertilisation in the oviduct → zygote divides to form a ball of cells (embryo) → implantation in the lining of the uterus → fetus with recognisable organs
parts.working: 2 marks for correct order; 1 mark if one pair reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by implantation.
parts.answer: The embryo (ball of cells) sinks into / attaches to the lining of the uterus.
parts.working: B1 embryo embeds in uterus lining.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fetus does not use its lungs for gas exchange. State how the fetus obtains oxygen.
parts.answer: Oxygen diffuses from the mother's blood into the fetal blood across the placenta and is carried to the fetus in the umbilical cord.
parts.working: B1 from mother's blood by diffusion across placenta; B1 carried through umbilical cord.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other substances, apart from oxygen, that pass from the mother to the fetus.
parts.answer: Any two: glucose; amino acids; water; mineral ions (e.g. iron, calcium); vitamins; fatty acids; antibodies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the waste gas that passes from the fetus to the mother.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) The placenta is attached to the wall of the uterus.
(ii) The blood of the mother flows directly into the fetus.
(iii) Urea passes from the fetus to the mother across the placenta.
(iv) The amniotic fluid supports and protects the fetus.
parts.answer: (i) true (ii) false (iii) true (iv) true
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rubella (German measles) is a mild illness in adults, but if a woman catches it early in pregnancy the virus can damage the developing fetus. Explain how the virus reaches the fetus.
parts.answer: The virus is carried in the mother's blood and can cross the placenta into the fetal blood (then travels through the umbilical cord).
parts.working: B1 virus in mother's blood; B1 crosses the placenta.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many countries vaccinate girls against rubella before they are old enough to become pregnant. Explain how this protects babies born later.
parts.answer: Vaccination gives the girl active immunity: she makes antibodies and memory cells; if she meets the virus while pregnant, the virus is destroyed quickly before it can infect her and cross the placenta.
parts.working: B1 makes antibodies / memory cells; B1 long-term immunity; B1 virus destroyed before it reaches fetus.

stem:
The volume of amniotic fluid around a fetus at different weeks of pregnancy:
Week: 10, 20, 30, 34, 38, 40
Volume / cm³: 30, 350, 800, 1000, 900, 800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the volume of amniotic fluid changes during pregnancy.
parts.answer: It increases rapidly from 30 cm³ at week 10 to a maximum of 1000 cm³ at week 34, then decreases to 800 cm³ at week 40.
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 peak 1000 cm³ at week 34; B1 then decreases, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in volume between week 34 and week 40.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two functions of the amniotic fluid.
parts.answer: Any two: protects the fetus from bumps / shocks (cushions); supports the fetus; allows the fetus to move; keeps temperature steady.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Doctors advise pregnant women in Australia not to drink any alcohol. Explain how alcohol in the mother's blood can affect the fetus.
parts.answer: Alcohol is a small molecule that diffuses across the placenta into the fetal blood; it can damage the developing organs (especially the brain) and slow growth, giving a low birth mass.
parts.working: B1 crosses placenta; B1 enters fetal blood; B1 harms development / brain / growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other substance that can cross the placenta and harm the fetus.
parts.answer: Any one: nicotine; carbon monoxide; some medicinal drugs; heroin.
parts.working: B1 any valid substance (not a pathogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pregnant women are advised to eat foods rich in iron. Explain why extra iron is needed during pregnancy.
parts.answer: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin for the fetus's developing red blood cells and for the mother's increased volume of blood.
parts.working: B1 haemoglobin / red blood cells; B1 for fetus and mother's extra blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why extra calcium is also needed.
parts.answer: For the development of the fetus's bones and teeth.
parts.working: B1 bones / teeth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a balanced diet with enough protein is especially important during pregnancy.
parts.answer: Protein provides amino acids for growth of the fetus (making new cells and tissues) and of the placenta and uterus.
parts.working: B1 amino acids for growth / new cells; B1 of fetus (or placenta).

stem: Near the end of pregnancy, about 500 cm³ of the mother's blood flows through the placenta every minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of mother's blood that flows through the placenta in one day, in dm³.
parts.answer: 720 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this large blood flow helps the fetus to obtain enough oxygen and glucose.
parts.answer: Fresh maternal blood keeps bringing a high concentration of oxygen and glucose, while the fetal blood flow carries them away; this maintains steep concentration gradients across the placenta, so diffusion is fast.
parts.working: B1 maternal blood brings high concentrations; B1 fetal blood removes them; B1 steep gradient maintained so rapid diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one structural feature of the placenta that also increases the rate of exchange.
parts.answer: Many villi giving a large surface area / thin barrier between the two bloods.
parts.working: B1 large surface area (villi) or thin walls.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Concentrations of four substances in the blood on each side of a placenta (arbitrary units):
Oxygen: maternal 12, fetal 6
Glucose: maternal 5.0, fetal 3.5
Urea: maternal 2.0, fetal 3.0
Carbon dioxide: maternal 5, fetal 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to explain the direction in which each substance moves across the placenta.
parts.answer: Oxygen: higher in maternal blood, so diffuses into fetal blood. Glucose: higher in maternal blood, so moves into fetal blood. Urea: higher in fetal blood, so diffuses into maternal blood. Carbon dioxide: higher in fetal blood, so diffuses into maternal blood.
parts.working: 1 mark per substance, each linked to the concentration gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the placenta keeps the two blood supplies separate.
parts.answer: Any two: the mother's blood pressure is higher and could damage the fetal blood vessels; blood groups may be incompatible, causing clotting / agglutination; reduces transfer of some pathogens and toxins.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student modelled the amniotic fluid. Raw eggs were sealed in plastic bags, either dry or completely filled with water, and dropped onto a hard floor from different heights. Five eggs of each type were dropped from each height.
Height / cm: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
Eggs broken, dry bag: 0, 2, 4, 5, 5
Eggs broken, water-filled bag: 0, 0, 0, 1, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total percentage of eggs broken for each type of bag over all the heights.
parts.answer: dry bag 64 %; water bag 12 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the model shows about the function of the amniotic fluid.
parts.answer: Fluid around the egg absorbed the force of the impact, so far fewer eggs broke; similarly amniotic fluid cushions the fetus and protects it from bumps.
parts.working: B1 water absorbs / spreads impact (fewer broken); B1 amniotic fluid protects fetus from mechanical shock.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two ways in which the model is not like a real fetus in the uterus.
parts.answer: Any two: the fetus is also protected by the mother's body wall / uterus muscle / amniotic sac; the fetus is alive and can move; the egg shell is not like fetal tissue; the drops are much harder than knocks to a pregnant woman.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way of making the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Use more eggs at each height / repeat and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 more repeats.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some antibodies in the mother's blood cross the placenta into the fetus. Name the type of immunity this gives the baby.
parts.answer: passive immunity
parts.working: B1 passive (natural) immunity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this immunity is useful to a newborn baby, but only lasts a few months.
parts.answer: The baby's immune system has not yet met many pathogens, so the mother's antibodies protect it immediately against diseases the mother is immune to; the antibodies are not made by the baby and no memory cells are formed, so they are broken down and not replaced.
parts.working: B1 immediate protection while baby's own immune system develops; B1 antibodies are from the mother / baby makes no memory cells; B1 antibodies broken down and not replaced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other way in which a baby can receive antibodies from its mother after birth.
parts.answer: In breast milk.
parts.working: B1 breast milk.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After fertilisation in a flower, state what each structure becomes or what happens to it.
(i) ovule (ii) ovary (iii) petals
parts.answer: (i) seed (ii) fruit (iii) wither and fall off
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is formed when the male nucleus fuses with the female nucleus.
parts.answer: a zygote
parts.working: B1 zygote.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three environmental conditions needed for seeds to germinate.
parts.answer: water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why seeds need water to germinate.
parts.answer: Water makes the seed swell and split the seed coat, and it activates enzymes that break down the stored food so it can be used for growth.
parts.working: B1 activates enzymes / allows reactions; B1 swelling / splits coat / transport of food in solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define fertilisation.
parts.answer: The fusion of the nuclei of a male gamete and a female gamete.
parts.working: B1 fusion of gamete nuclei.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a flowering plant, name the structure that carries the male nucleus from the pollen grain to the ovule.
parts.answer: the pollen tube
parts.working: B1 pollen tube.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the flower in which the female gamete is found.
parts.answer: the ovule (inside the ovary)
parts.working: B1 ovule.

stem:
Groups of 50 wheat seeds were kept on damp paper at different temperatures for 7 days. The percentage that germinated was recorded.
Temperature / °C: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
Germination / %: 6, 30, 64, 84, 92, 80, 40, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for germination from these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of seeds out of 50 that germinated at 15 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of increasing temperature from 5 °C to 25 °C.
parts.answer: Germination increases because enzymes in the seed work faster at higher temperatures (more kinetic energy, more collisions), so stored food is broken down faster for growth.
parts.working: B1 more germination with data; B1 enzyme activity increases / more kinetic energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why germination was so low at 40 °C.
parts.answer: The enzymes are denatured at high temperature (active site changes shape), so the stored food cannot be broken down and the embryo cannot grow.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured; B1 food reserves not digested / no energy or materials for growth.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
40 radish seeds were placed on damp cotton wool at 22 °C. The total number of seeds that had germinated was counted each day.
Day: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total germinated: 0, 4, 15, 28, 34, 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final percentage germination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of seeds that germinated on day 4 only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Half of the seeds that eventually germinated had germinated by a certain day. Between which two days was this?
parts.answer: Between day 3 and day 4 (half of 36 is 18; 15 by day 3, 28 by day 4).
parts.working: M1 half of 36 = 18; A1 between day 3 and day 4.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why 4 of the seeds did not germinate.
parts.answer: Any two: the embryo was dead or damaged; seed was dormant; seed was infected by fungus; seed coat was too hard / impermeable to water; not enough water reached that seed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A seed bank stores seeds of many crop varieties for many years. The seeds are dried and kept in sealed containers at about −18 °C. Explain why the seeds do not germinate during storage.
parts.answer: There is very little water, so enzymes cannot work and food stores are not mobilised; the very low temperature slows / stops enzyme activity; the sealed container limits oxygen (and stops water entering).
parts.working: B1 lack of water; B1 low temperature – enzymes inactive; B1 sealed / little oxygen (no respiration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the seeds are not simply stored at room temperature.
parts.answer: At room temperature respiration continues slowly and uses up stored food, and fungi may grow, so the seeds would lose viability / die sooner.
parts.working: B1 respiration uses up food stores / enzymes active; B1 seeds die / lose ability to germinate (or fungal decay).

stem: In this question, a pollen tube grows down a style 9.0 mm long at a steady rate of 1.2 mm per hour.

parts.label: a
