parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the pollen tube to reach the ovule. Give your answer in hours and minutes.
parts.answer: 7 hours 30 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens when the pollen tube reaches the ovule.
parts.answer: The tube enters the ovule (through a small hole); the male nucleus passes from the tube into the ovule; it fuses with the female nucleus (egg cell) – fertilisation – forming a zygote.
parts.working: B1 tube enters ovule; B1 male nucleus moves into ovule; B1 fuses with female nucleus / fertilisation / zygote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the pollen tube grows more slowly on a cold day.
parts.answer: Enzyme activity / respiration in the tube is slower at low temperature.
parts.working: B1 slower enzyme reactions.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer in Punjab sowed maize seeds, then heavy rain flooded the field for four days. Very few seeds germinated. Explain why.
parts.answer: Water filled the air spaces in the soil, so little oxygen reached the seeds; germinating seeds need oxygen for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth; without enough energy the embryo could not grow (and may have died from anaerobic respiration products).
parts.working: B1 waterlogging removes air / oxygen; B1 oxygen needed for aerobic respiration; B1 energy needed for germination / growth (anaerobic respiration insufficient).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seeds sown too deep in dry, compacted soil also often fail to grow into seedlings. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Any two: food stores run out before the shoot reaches light to photosynthesise; little oxygen in compacted soil; dry soil supplies too little water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

stem:
Bean seeds were germinated in soil in light. Every 2 days, 10 seedlings were dried in an oven and weighed.
Day: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Dry mass of 10 seedlings / g: 2.40, 2.30, 2.15, 2.10, 2.35, 2.80

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass between day 0 and day 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dry mass decreased during the first 6 days.
parts.answer: Stored food in the seed was broken down and used in respiration to release energy for growth; carbon dioxide and water were lost, so dry mass fell; no photosynthesis yet.
parts.working: B1 stored food used in respiration; B1 no photosynthesis yet / CO₂ lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dry mass increased after day 6.
parts.answer: The leaves had grown above the soil and turned green, so the seedlings photosynthesised faster than they respired, making new organic substances.
parts.working: B1 leaves / photosynthesis begin; B1 photosynthesis > respiration so organic matter gained.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why dry mass rather than fresh mass was measured.
parts.answer: Fresh mass changes greatly with the water content (seeds absorb water), so it does not show the amount of organic material.
parts.working: B1 water content varies.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student wanted to find out whether mung bean seeds need light to germinate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should set up the experiment so that the only difference between the dishes is the light.
parts.answer: Use two identical dishes with the same number (e.g. 20) of the same type of mung beans on cotton wool soaked with the same volume of water; keep both at the same temperature; put one in light and cover the other with a box / put it in a dark cupboard at the same temperature.
parts.working: B1 same number and type of seeds; B1 same water / cotton wool; B1 same temperature, only light differs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After 4 days, 18 out of 20 seeds had germinated in the light and 19 out of 20 in the dark. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: Light is not needed for germination of mung beans.
parts.working: B1 light not needed / no effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The seedlings in the dark were taller and yellow. Suggest why they were yellow.
parts.answer: No chlorophyll was made in the dark.
parts.working: B1 no chlorophyll (light needed to make it).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one way to improve the reliability of the results.
parts.answer: Use more seeds / repeat with more dishes and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 more seeds or repeats.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 20 dry chickpea seeds had a mass of 6.0 g. After soaking in water for 12 hours their mass was 10.5 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the use of the water absorbed by the seeds during germination.
parts.answer: Any two: activates enzymes; allows enzymes to digest stored starch/protein; transports dissolved food to the growing embryo; makes cells swell / bursts seed coat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The soaked chickpeas were then kept in a sealed jar with no air. Predict whether they would germinate, and explain.
parts.answer: No (or very few): there is no oxygen for aerobic respiration, so not enough energy is released for growth.
parts.working: B1 no germination; B1 oxygen needed for respiration / energy.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.

After pollination, a pollen grain on the ______ grows a tube down through the ______ to the ovary. A male ______ travels down the tube and fuses with a female nucleus inside an ______. This is called ______. The ovule then develops into a ______.
parts.answer: stigma; style; nucleus (gamete); ovule; fertilisation; seed
parts.working: 1 mark for each gap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes HIV infection.
parts.answer: a virus
parts.working: B1 virus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the disease that HIV infection may lead to.
parts.answer: AIDS
parts.working: B1 AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one body fluid through which HIV can be passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Any one: blood; semen; vaginal fluid; breast milk.
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether HIV can be passed on in each of these ways. Answer yes or no.
(i) sharing a needle to inject drugs
(ii) a mosquito bite
(iii) from a mother to her baby during birth
(iv) shaking hands
(v) receiving a transfusion of blood that has not been screened
parts.answer: (i) yes (ii) no (iii) yes (iv) no (v) yes
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient with HIV asks a doctor for antibiotics. Explain why antibiotics will not cure HIV.
parts.answer: HIV is a virus; antibiotics only kill bacteria (or stop their growth) and do not affect viruses.
parts.working: B1 HIV is a virus; B1 antibiotics do not affect viruses / only work on bacteria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: There is no cure for HIV, but antiretroviral drugs can be taken. Suggest one benefit of taking these drugs every day.
parts.answer: They slow down the reproduction of the virus, so the person stays healthy for longer / is less likely to develop AIDS / less likely to pass HIV on.
parts.working: B1 any valid benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using a condom during sexual intercourse reduces the spread of sexually transmitted infections.
parts.answer: It acts as a barrier, preventing the exchange of body fluids (semen, vaginal fluid) that contain the pathogens.
parts.working: B1 barrier; B1 prevents contact with / exchange of body fluids containing pathogens.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two other ways in which the spread of HIV can be controlled in a country.
parts.answer: Any two: screening donated blood; using sterile / single-use needles and syringes; testing people and treating those infected; education about how HIV is spread; limiting the number of sexual partners; treating infected pregnant women.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

stem:
Estimated number of new HIV infections per year in one country:
2010: 14 000
2015: 20 000
2020: 25 000
2023: 26 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in new infections per year between 2010 and 2023. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in the data after 2015.
parts.answer: New infections continued to rise, but the increase slowed (5000 from 2015 to 2020, then only 1000 from 2020 to 2023).
parts.working: B1 still increasing; B1 rate of increase slowing, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two measures the government could take to reduce the number of new infections.
parts.answer: Any two: free testing and treatment; education campaigns; providing condoms; needle-exchange programmes / single-use syringes in clinics; screening all blood donations; treating pregnant women with HIV.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: An outbreak of HIV occurred among children in one district. Investigators found that some clinics had reused the same syringes and needles on many patients. Explain how this spread HIV.
parts.answer: Blood containing HIV from an infected patient remained in / on the syringe or needle; when it was used on the next patient, the virus entered their blood directly.
parts.working: B1 infected blood left on needle / syringe; B1 enters bloodstream of next patient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two actions that health authorities could take to prevent this happening again.
parts.answer: Any two: use only single-use / auto-disable syringes; train and inspect clinic staff; safe disposal in sharps boxes; sterilise reusable equipment properly; test and treat children and families affected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

stem: HIV infects and destroys some types of lymphocyte. A person's lymphocyte count fell from 1000 per mm³ to 200 per mm³ over 8 years without treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean decrease in lymphocyte count per year.
parts.answer: 100 per mm³ per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: The person felt healthy for most of the 8 years. Explain why it is important for people who may have been exposed to HIV to be tested, even if they feel well.
parts.answer: HIV may cause no symptoms for many years, but the virus is present in body fluids, so the person can pass it on without knowing; testing allows them to start treatment early to slow damage to the immune system and to take precautions to protect others.
parts.working: B1 no symptoms for years; B1 can still transmit HIV; B1 early treatment / prevent spread.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person with a lymphocyte count of 200 per mm³ is likely to develop serious infections such as tuberculosis.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes make antibodies; with very few lymphocytes the immune system cannot make enough antibodies to destroy pathogens, so infections that are normally controlled develop.
parts.working: B1 lymphocytes make antibodies / fight pathogens; B1 weakened immune system cannot destroy pathogens.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In one study, about 30 % of babies born to mothers with HIV were infected when the mothers had no treatment, but only 2 % were infected when the mothers took antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of babies, out of 500, expected to be infected (i) without treatment and (ii) with treatment, and the number of infections prevented.
parts.answer: (i) 150 (ii) 10; 140 prevented

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three ways in which HIV may pass from a mother to her baby.
parts.answer: Across the placenta (during pregnancy); during birth (contact with blood and body fluids); in breast milk.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A common test for HIV detects antibodies against HIV in the blood. Explain why a person who was infected one week ago may test negative.
parts.answer: It takes time for the immune system (lymphocytes) to make enough antibodies to be detected; after one week there may not yet be enough antibodies.
parts.working: B1 antibodies take time to be produced; B1 too few to detect yet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this person should be tested again some weeks later and should take precautions in the meantime.
parts.answer: By then antibodies would be detectable, giving a reliable result; meanwhile the virus may still be present and the person could pass it on.
parts.working: B1 later test reliable once antibodies produced; B1 can still transmit HIV in the meantime.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) HIV is a bacterium.
(ii) AIDS can develop in a person infected with HIV.
(iii) HIV can be passed on in breast milk.
(iv) HIV infection can be cured with antibiotics.
parts.answer: (i) false (ii) true (iii) true (iv) false
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: In a health survey, 75 out of 12 500 people in the general population tested positive for HIV. In a separate survey of 800 people who inject drugs, 304 tested positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people testing positive (i) in the general population sample and (ii) among people who inject drugs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the percentage is among people who inject drugs. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 63 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why people who inject drugs have a much higher chance of being infected with HIV.
parts.answer: Needles and syringes are often shared; a needle used by an infected person contains blood with HIV, which is injected directly into the next person's blood.
parts.working: B1 sharing needles; B1 infected blood enters bloodstream directly.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a bacterium. State how gonorrhoea can be treated.
parts.answer: with antibiotics
parts.working: B1 antibiotics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some strains of the bacterium that causes gonorrhoea are now resistant to several antibiotics. Explain why this makes it more important to prevent its spread.
parts.answer: Resistant infections are difficult or impossible to treat with the usual antibiotics, so infected people may stay ill or suffer complications and continue to spread it; prevention avoids the need for treatment.
parts.working: B1 harder to treat / antibiotics ineffective; B1 infection lasts longer / spreads further, so prevention needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a person can be infected with an STI and pass it on without knowing.
parts.answer: Many STIs cause few or no symptoms for a long time.
parts.working: B1 no / few symptoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all blood donated to a blood bank is tested for HIV before it is used.
parts.answer: Blood from an infected donor contains HIV; a transfusion puts the blood directly into the patient's bloodstream, so the patient would be infected.
parts.working: B1 infected blood contains virus; B1 transfused directly into patient's blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nurses wear gloves when taking blood and put used needles into a puncture-proof sharps box. Explain how each precaution reduces the risk of HIV infection.
parts.answer: Gloves stop infected blood touching cuts in the nurse's skin; the sharps box prevents needlestick injuries that could inject infected blood.
parts.working: B1 gloves – barrier to blood entering cuts; B1 sharps box – prevents needle injuries / reuse.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A course of antibiotics would kill which of these organisms in a patient?
A HIV
B the influenza virus
C Salmonella, a bacterium that causes food poisoning
D the measles virus
parts.answer: C Salmonella, a bacterium that causes food poisoning
parts.working: Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect viruses. A, B and D are all viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A patient stopped taking an antibiotic after 2 days of a 7-day course. A week later the infection returned and the same antibiotic no longer worked. What is the best explanation?
A The patient's body became immune to the antibiotic.
B The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate so that they became resistant.
C The bacteria that survived the short course were the most resistant ones, and they multiplied.
D The antibiotic had been broken down by the patient's white blood cells.
parts.answer: C The bacteria that survived the short course were the most resistant ones, and they multiplied.
parts.working: A short course kills the most susceptible bacteria; the more resistant ones survive and reproduce, so the new population is mostly resistant. B is the common error: the antibiotic does not cause the mutation; it selects resistant bacteria that already exist. A is wrong because resistance belongs to the bacteria, not the patient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Typhoid is caused by a bacterium carried in contaminated water and food. Since 2016, a strain resistant to most commonly used antibiotics has spread in parts of Sindh. Explain why infections with this strain are more dangerous than infections with non-resistant strains.
parts.answer: Most antibiotics no longer kill the bacteria, so the infection is harder to treat; patients may need expensive drugs given in hospital and are more likely to suffer complications or die.
parts.working: B1 usual antibiotics ineffective; B1 longer / more serious illness, fewer treatment options.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing the number of people infected with this strain.
parts.answer: Any two: provide clean drinking water and good sanitation; good hygiene / hand washing and safe food preparation; vaccinate children against typhoid; use antibiotics only when prescribed and complete the course.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why doctors were told to use the remaining effective antibiotics only for confirmed cases.
parts.answer: Unnecessary use of these antibiotics would select for bacteria resistant to them too; keeping their use to essential cases slows the development of resistance so they stay effective.
parts.working: B1 overuse selects for resistance; B1 keeps antibiotics effective for longer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which drug relieves the symptoms of an infection, such as pain and fever, but does not kill the pathogen?
A paracetamol
B penicillin
C amoxicillin
D streptomycin
parts.answer: A paracetamol
parts.working: Paracetamol is a painkiller that reduces pain and fever but does not kill pathogens. B, C and D are antibiotics, which kill bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term drug.
parts.answer: Any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into the body; B1 modifies / affects chemical reactions in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a drug used as a medicine and one example of a drug that people take for other reasons.
parts.answer: Medicine: any one, e.g. paracetamol, an antibiotic such as penicillin, insulin. Other: any one, e.g. caffeine, nicotine, alcohol.
parts.working: B1 medicinal drug; B1 non-medicinal drug.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these drugs could be used to treat a bacterial infection?
paracetamol; penicillin; caffeine; insulin; nicotine
parts.answer: penicillin
parts.working: B1 penicillin only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Insulin is a hormone made in the pancreas. Explain why insulin injected by a person with type 1 diabetes is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into the body that modifies chemical reactions in the body – it causes glucose to be converted to glycogen in the liver (lowering blood glucose).
parts.working: B1 taken into the body; B1 affects reactions / lowers blood glucose / glucose → glycogen.

stem:
Daphnia (water fleas) are tiny transparent animals whose heart can be seen beating under a microscope. A student placed a Daphnia in pond water containing different concentrations of caffeine and counted the heart beats in 15 seconds.
Caffeine concentration / %: 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04
Beats in 15 s: 50, 56, 63, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute at each concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate between 0 % and 0.04 % caffeine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Caffeine is a drug. Use the results to explain why.
parts.answer: Caffeine was taken into the Daphnia's body and changed the rate of its heart beat, showing that it affects chemical reactions / processes in the body.
parts.working: B1 taken into body; B1 changed heart rate / body reactions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature of the water; size / age of Daphnia; time in the solution before counting; volume of solution; light intensity under the microscope.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student counted the heart beats of Daphnia in 15 seconds in different concentrations of ethanol. A new Daphnia was used for each concentration, and three counts were made for each.
Ethanol / %: 0 – 66, 64, 65; 1 – 58, 60, 59; 2 – 52, 51, 36; 3 – 44, 45, 46; 4 – 38, 37, 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean for that concentration without it.
parts.answer: 36 at 2 % ethanol; mean 51.5 beats

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean heart rate between 0 % and 4 % ethanol. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ethanol (alcohol) is described as a depressant drug. Explain how these results support this description.
parts.answer: As the ethanol concentration increased, the heart rate decreased; ethanol slows down body processes, which is what a depressant does.
parts.working: B1 heart rate falls as concentration rises, with data; B1 depressant slows body activity.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the student used a different Daphnia for each concentration, and one problem this causes.
parts.answer: Reason: ethanol from one test could still affect the animal in the next test. Problem: different Daphnia may have different natural heart rates (size, age), so the comparison is less fair.
parts.working: B1 avoids carry-over effect / harm to one animal; B1 individual variation in heart rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measured her reaction time by catching a falling ruler. The distance the ruler fell before she caught it was recorded five times before, and five times 30 minutes after, drinking a cup of coffee.
Before / cm: 18, 20, 19, 21, 17
After / cm: 15, 16, 14, 17, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance before and after drinking the coffee.
parts.answer: before 19 cm; after 15 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shorter distance means a faster reaction. State the effect of the coffee on the student's reaction time.
parts.answer: The reaction became faster (reaction time decreased).
parts.working: B1 faster reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the drug in coffee that probably caused this effect.
parts.answer: caffeine
parts.working: B1 caffeine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the results from one student do not prove that coffee speeds up reactions for everyone.
parts.answer: Only one person was tested; the student may also have improved with practice.
parts.working: B1 one person / practice effect / no control.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A study in Australia measured the reaction time of volunteers in a driving simulator after drinking different amounts of alcohol.
Blood alcohol concentration / %: 0, 0.05, 0.08, 0.12
Reaction time / s: 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in reaction time at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 % compared with no alcohol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car travels at 25 m per second. Calculate the extra distance it travels before the driver reacts, at 0.08 % blood alcohol compared with no alcohol.
parts.working: M1 extra time 0.10 s; A1 25 × 0.10 = 2.5 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why alcohol is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is taken into the body and affects chemical reactions / the nervous system (slows reactions).
parts.working: B1 substance taken in that modifies body reactions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why many countries set a legal limit for blood alcohol when driving.
parts.answer: Slower reactions make accidents more likely / drivers cannot stop in time.
parts.working: B1 slower reactions → more accidents.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In this question, a doctor tells a parent to give paracetamol syrup at a dose of 15 mg per kg of body mass. The child has a mass of 18 kg. The syrup contains 120 mg of paracetamol in every 5 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dose of paracetamol for the child, in mg.
parts.answer: 270 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of syrup that contains this dose. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dose of a drug for children is calculated from body mass.
parts.answer: A smaller body has less blood / tissue, so the same amount of drug would give a higher concentration in the body; too high a concentration can be harmful (e.g. paracetamol can damage the liver).
parts.working: B1 smaller body → higher concentration from same dose; B1 risk of harm / overdose (liver damage).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has developed a new drug to lower blood pressure. Before it can be sold it is tested on volunteers. Explain why each of these features of the trial is used.
(i) One group of volunteers is given a placebo (a tablet that looks the same but contains no drug).
(ii) Neither the volunteers nor the doctors know who is given the drug and who is given the placebo.
(iii) Several thousand volunteers take part.
(iv) The drug is first tested at very low doses on a small number of healthy volunteers.
parts.answer: (i) To compare with the drug group, so any effect caused just by taking a tablet / believing you are treated can be separated from the effect of the drug. (ii) So that expectations cannot affect the results or how they are recorded (double-blind; removes bias). (iii) To make the results reliable / reduce the effect of individual variation and to detect rare side effects. (iv) To check that the drug is safe / find side effects before larger doses and patients are used.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a drug that works well in a trial may not be approved for use.
parts.answer: It may have serious side effects / be no better than existing drugs.
parts.working: B1 harmful side effects or not better than existing treatment.

stem: In a trial of a new drug for influenza, 400 patients were given the drug and 400 were given a placebo. The mean time to recover was 4.2 days for the drug group and 5.6 days for the placebo group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the mean time to recover in the group given the drug.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the trial included patients of different ages and of both sexes.
parts.answer: So that the results apply to the whole population, and so that any effect that depends on age or sex is detected.
parts.working: B1 results can be generalised to the wider population; B1 shows whether the drug works differently for different groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the new drug is described as an antiviral drug rather than an antibiotic.
parts.answer: It acts against viruses (influenza is caused by a virus); antibiotics only work against bacteria.
parts.working: B1 acts on virus / antibiotics only work on bacteria.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many medicines first came from plants: aspirin was developed from a chemical in willow bark, and quinine, used to treat malaria, comes from the bark of the cinchona tree. Suggest why scientists want to protect large areas of tropical forest, even where no medicines have yet been found.
parts.answer: Forests contain huge numbers of plant species, many not yet studied; some may contain chemicals that could be developed into new drugs; if the forest is destroyed these species may become extinct before they are tested, and the potential medicines are lost.
parts.working: B1 high biodiversity / many unstudied species; B1 may contain useful drug chemicals; B1 extinction would lose them permanently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Malaria is caused by a single-celled organism, not a bacterium. Suggest why quinine is not described as an antibiotic.
parts.answer: Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria; quinine acts against the malaria parasite, which is not a bacterium.
parts.working: B1 antibiotics act on bacteria only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tobacco contains nicotine. Explain why nicotine is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into the body (absorbed into the blood from the lungs) and it affects chemical reactions / the nervous system in the body.
parts.working: B1 taken into body; B1 affects body reactions / nervous system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one property of nicotine that makes it difficult for smokers to stop.
parts.answer: It is addictive.
parts.working: B1 addictive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two other harmful substances in tobacco smoke.
parts.answer: Any two: tar; carbon monoxide; smoke particles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tobacco smoke contains carbon monoxide. Explain how carbon monoxide reduces the amount of oxygen carried by the blood.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells (very strongly, and does not easily leave), so less haemoglobin is available to carry oxygen.
parts.working: B1 combines with haemoglobin; B1 less haemoglobin available for oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a smoker becomes breathless during exercise more quickly than a non-smoker.
parts.answer: Less oxygen reaches the muscles, so less aerobic respiration and more anaerobic respiration occur; carbon dioxide / lactic acid build up faster, so breathing has to increase more.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen to muscles; B1 more anaerobic respiration / faster build-up of CO₂ → breathless.

stem:
Deaths from lung cancer per 100 000 men per year, by number of cigarettes smoked per day:
Non-smokers: 10
1–14 per day: 78
15–24 per day: 127
25 or more per day: 251

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for those who smoked 25 or more cigarettes a day than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 25.1 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: The more cigarettes smoked per day, the higher the death rate from lung cancer; even light smokers (1–14 a day) have a death rate about 8 times that of non-smokers.
parts.working: B1 positive relationship; B1 data quote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says that these data prove that smoking causes lung cancer. Explain why the data alone do not prove this, and suggest what other evidence would help.
parts.answer: The data show a correlation; another factor (for example, working with harmful dust or air pollution) could be linked with both smoking and cancer. Evidence that would help: the cancer rate falls in people who stop smoking; laboratory evidence that chemicals in tar cause cancer in cells; the pattern is the same in many different countries and groups.
parts.working: B1 correlation is not proof of cause; B1 other factors could be involved; B1 any one valid extra evidence.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Caffeine content of some drinks:
Cup of tea: 40 mg
Cup of coffee: 95 mg
Can of cola: 35 mg
Can of energy drink: 80 mg
In one day, a student in Karachi drank two cups of tea, one can of energy drink and one can of cola.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of caffeine the student drank in one day.
parts.answer: 195 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate by how much the student exceeded the guideline of 100 mg per day used in this question.
parts.answer: 95 mg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Caffeine is a stimulant. Suggest why drinking an energy drink late in the evening may affect a student's sleep.
parts.answer: Caffeine increases the activity of the nervous system / keeps the student alert, so it is harder to fall asleep.
parts.working: B1 keeps alert / stimulates nervous system.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why salbutamol is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into the body that affects chemical processes in the body: it changes the activity of the muscle in the walls of the bronchioles, making it relax.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into the body; B1 modifies body processes (relaxes bronchiole muscle).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how relaxing these muscles helps a person with asthma to breathe.
parts.answer: The bronchioles become wider, so more air reaches the alveoli in each breath and more oxygen can diffuse into the blood.
parts.working: B1 bronchioles wider / less constricted; B1 more air (and oxygen) reaches the alveoli for gas exchange.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the drug is inhaled straight into the lungs rather than swallowed as a tablet.
parts.answer: It acts directly on the bronchioles, so it works quickly and less of it reaches the rest of the body, reducing side effects.
parts.working: B1 acts directly where needed (quick action) and fewer side effects elsewhere in the body.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Salbutamol is a drug in an inhaler. It is used to treat asthma and relaxes the muscles in the walls of the bronchioles.
In this question, the concentration of a drug in the blood halves every 4 hours. Just after one dose, the concentration is 80 mg/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the drug in the blood 12 hours after the dose.
parts.answer: 10 mg/dm³
parts.working: M1 three half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10; A1 10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The drug is effective only when its concentration is above 15 mg/dm³. Calculate the concentration at 8 hours and state whether the drug is still effective at 8 hours and at 12 hours.
parts.answer: 20 mg/dm³ at 8 hours; effective at 8 hours (20 > 15) but not at 12 hours (10 < 15)
parts.working: B1 80 → 40 → 20 at 8 h; B1 effective at 8 h, not at 12 h.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the label tells the patient to take the drug at regular intervals rather than taking the whole day's dose at once.
parts.answer: The drug is broken down / removed from the body over time; regular doses keep the concentration above the effective level but below a harmful (toxic) level all day.
parts.working: B1 concentration falls as drug is broken down / excreted; B1 regular doses keep it within the effective, safe range.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dentist injects a local anaesthetic into a patient's gum before filling a tooth. The patient cannot feel pain in that area for about two hours. State why the anaesthetic is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance put into the body that changes how the body works – it stops nerve impulses from the gum (affects body reactions).
parts.working: B1 substance taken into body; B1 affects body processes / stops pain impulses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the effect wears off after about two hours.
parts.answer: The drug is carried away in the blood and broken down / removed.
parts.working: B1 drug removed / broken down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person who drinks large amounts of alcohol over many years may develop liver damage. Name the organ that breaks down alcohol in the body.
parts.answer: the liver
parts.working: B1 liver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why heavy, long-term drinking damages this organ.
parts.answer: The liver has to break down large amounts of alcohol (a toxin) continuously; its cells are damaged and replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), so it cannot carry out its other functions.
parts.working: B1 liver cells break down alcohol / toxin; B1 cells damaged / scar tissue / cirrhosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying that a person is addicted to a drug.
parts.answer: The person feels a strong need to keep taking the drug and suffers unpleasant withdrawal symptoms if they stop.
parts.working: B1 need / craving to keep taking it; B1 withdrawal symptoms when stopped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some athletes illegally take anabolic steroids, drugs similar to the hormone testosterone, to build muscle. Explain why these substances are drugs.
parts.answer: They are taken into the body and modify chemical reactions (increase protein synthesis / muscle growth).
parts.working: B1 taken in and modify body reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why sports organisations ban anabolic steroids.
parts.answer: Any two: gives an unfair advantage; harmful side effects (e.g. damage to the liver or heart); athletes may feel pressured to take them to compete.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Testosterone normally controls the production of sperm. Suggest why male athletes who take large doses of steroids may produce fewer sperm.
parts.answer: The high level of steroid in the blood causes the body to reduce its own hormone signals (negative feedback), so the testes make less testosterone and fewer sperm.
parts.working: B1 body detects high hormone level / reduces own production; B1 testes produce less / fewer sperm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether drinking a caffeinated drink affects the reaction time of students. Use the ruler-drop test. Include what you would change and measure, how you would make it a fair test, how you would make the results reliable and one ethical or safety consideration.
parts.answer: Use a group of e.g. 20 volunteer students. Measure each student's reaction time with the ruler-drop test (catch distance), 5 times, and calculate a mean. Then give half the students a drink containing caffeine and the other half an identical-tasting drink without caffeine (decaffeinated – a placebo), without telling them which. After 30 minutes repeat the ruler test 5 times. Keep the same ruler, same dropping height, same hand, same person dropping, no warning before dropping. Compare the change in mean distance for the two groups. Practise beforehand so learning does not affect results. Use a small, safe amount of caffeine; students with heart conditions or who avoid caffeine should not take part; get consent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV caffeine / no caffeine (or caffeine dose); DV distance ruler falls / reaction time; measured before and after a fixed time; placebo / decaffeinated drink for control group; volunteers do not know which drink (blind); same hand, ruler, starting position, dropper; practice trials to reduce learning effect; repeats and means / large group; ethics: consent, small safe dose, exclude those with health conditions.

stem: In a survey at a college, 240 students were asked about their drinks. 96 said they drank at least one drink containing caffeine every day. Of these 96, 29 reported having trouble falling asleep.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of students who drank at least one caffeinated drink every day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of these daily drinkers who reported trouble sleeping. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what extra information would be needed to decide whether caffeine causes the trouble sleeping.
parts.answer: The percentage of students who do not drink caffeine who also have trouble sleeping (a comparison group); and information on other causes, e.g. screen use or exam stress / the time of day they drink caffeine.
parts.working: B1 compare with non-drinkers; B1 other factors / timing.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Stimulants speed up the activity of the nervous system and depressants slow it down. Classify each drug as a stimulant or a depressant.
(i) caffeine (ii) alcohol (iii) nicotine (iv) heroin
parts.answer: (i) stimulant (ii) depressant (iii) stimulant (iv) depressant
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many drugs work by affecting enzymes. Penicillin stops an enzyme that bacteria use to build their cell walls. Explain why penicillin kills bacteria but does not harm human cells.
parts.answer: Without the enzyme, bacteria cannot build cell walls properly, so the growing bacteria burst / die; human cells have no cell wall and do not use this enzyme, so they are not affected.
parts.working: B1 bacterial cell wall not made / weak; B1 bacteria burst / die; B1 human cells have no cell wall / no such enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the definition of a drug to explain why a substance that inhibits an enzyme is a drug.
parts.answer: Enzymes control chemical reactions in the body, so inhibiting one modifies / affects chemical reactions.
parts.working: B1 link enzyme → chemical reactions modified.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why penicillin has no effect on a viral infection.
parts.answer: Viruses have no cell walls and do not have their own enzymes for making them (they reproduce inside host cells).
parts.working: B1 viruses have no cell wall / not cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: People are advised not to flush unused medicines down the toilet but to return them to a pharmacy. Suggest two harmful effects of medicines entering rivers.
parts.answer: Any two: antibiotics in the water may lead to resistant bacteria developing in the environment; hormones from medicines can affect the development / reproduction of fish; drugs may be taken in by other organisms and affect their body reactions / be passed along food chains.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics in river water could make it harder to treat human infections in future.
parts.answer: Low concentrations of antibiotic kill sensitive bacteria but allow resistant ones to survive and multiply (selection); resistant bacteria can then infect people.
parts.working: B1 selects for resistant bacteria; B1 resistant bacteria may infect humans / spread resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Medicine labels state the dose and how often to take it. Explain why a patient should not take more than the stated dose.
parts.answer: Too much of a drug can be harmful / poisonous (toxic) and may damage organs such as the liver; a larger dose does not make the treatment work faster.
parts.working: B1 overdose harmful / toxic; B1 example of harm or no extra benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why medicines should be kept out of reach of young children.
parts.answer: Children may swallow them; their small body mass means even a small amount could be a dangerous dose.
parts.working: B1 accidental overdose / small body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Athlete's foot is a skin infection caused by a fungus. It is treated with an antifungal cream. Explain why the antifungal cream is a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into (applied to and absorbed by) the body that affects chemical reactions – it kills the fungus / stops it growing.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into the body; B1 modifies chemical reactions / kills fungus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of drug used to treat infections caused by bacteria.
parts.answer: antibiotics
parts.working: B1 antibiotic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one type of pathogen that is not affected by antibiotics.
parts.answer: viruses
parts.working: B1 virus (accept fungi).
